# INTRODUCTION

In introducing the first volume of Śārṅgadeva’s <term>Ocean of Music</term> <note>original: "Saṅgitaratnākara"</note>, containing the first <term>chapter</term> <note>original: "adhyāya"</note>, along with the two commentaries, namely, Kallinātha’s <term>Treasure of Art</term> <note>original: "Kalānidhi"</note> and Siṁhabhūpāla’s <term>Moon of Nectar</term> <note>original: "Sudhākara"</note>, my first duty is to record the gratitude of the Adyar Library to that great scholar, the late Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastri, who undertook the edition of this important work. He had corrected the entire material for all the seven chapters of the work for the press and the first chapter was completely printed before his death. In the normal course, this Introduction would have come from his pen. Having regard to his solid erudition, his profound knowledge of music both on the practical and the theoretical side, his wide reading, his deep insight into subjects allied to music like dancing, I must confess that the present Introduction is only a poor substitute for what could have been expected from him.

The <italic>Ocean of Music</italic> of Śārṅgadeva is one of the most important works on music now available. It is besides, one of the longest works on music in Sanskrit. It is a very comprehensive exposition of the subject, dealing with all aspects. Ever since it was written it has remained the standard work on music; it has been

drawn upon profusely, as authority, by all subsequent writers on the subject. Perhaps it has superseded many earlier works and obscured them; and they have disappeared from the field. But it has never been superseded till now.

A complete edition of the work was undertaken by Kalivara Vedāntavāgis'a and S'ārada Prasāda Ghosha from Calcutta with the commentary of Siṃhabhūpāla <note>A 14th-century royal commentator also known as Bhūpāla</note> some time back, and the first volume containing the *Chapter on Notes* <note>original: "Svarādhyāya"; the first section of the work dealing with sound and musical pitches</note> was published in 1879 from the New Arya Press, Calcutta.¹ In the Preface to that edition², it had been promised that the remaining portions too would be published; but it does not seem that any further progress had been made in that direction. At that time they had access only to a very defective copy of the commentary of Kallinātha <note>A 15th-century commentator at the Vijayanagara court</note>, which, as they say, was “very unintelligible, owing to numerous clerical mistakes.” ³ As for Siṃhabhūpāla’s commentary appearing in this edition, there is no indication of the source of the manuscripts. The Preface does not mention the point at all. Evidently they must have had access to a complete copy, since they had projected a complete edition. The manuscripts known to us and utilised for this edition will be noticed in the course of this introduction.

The text of the *Ocean of Music* <note>original: "Saṅgītaratnākara"; the definitive 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on Indian music and dance</note> with the commentary of Kallinātha has been edited in the Anandasrama <note>A famous research institute and publishing house in Pune</note>

# Preface

Sanskrit Series as No. 35 in 1896.<sup>1</sup> In preparing this present edition, Pandit Subrahmanya Sastri has made use of both the editions. The text has been compared with manuscripts available in the various libraries in and near Madras and the commentary of Kallinātha <note>A 15th-century commentator known for his detailed explanations of musical theory.</note> has been compared with the manuscript in the Tanjore Palace Library.<sup>2</sup> The printed editions have been carefully compared with these manuscripts and the readings have been improved.

The plan was to add an English translation of the text at the end of each volume for the portion contained in it. It is very unfortunate that the late Pandit Subrahmanya Sastri was not able to prepare the translation. That work has devolved on me, along with the responsibility to see through the press the matter for the later portions which he had got ready. The English translation for the first <term>chapter</term> <note>original: "adhyāya"</note> is ready. The delay in issuing this first volume, which had been printed more than a year ago, is due to the time taken for getting the English translation ready. At this stage, the problem of printing-paper became a very acute one <note>Likely referring to shortages during the World War II era.</note> and it is not found possible at present to print the English translation. Therefore the first volume containing the first <term>chapter</term> <note>original: "adhyāya"</note> is being issued, along with the commentaries and also appendices. The second and the third <term>chapters</term> <note>original: "adhyāyas"</note> have been printed and the printing of the fourth <term>chapter</term> <note>original: "adhyāya"</note> has begun and the second volume containing these three <term>chapters</term> <note>original: "adhyāyas"</note>

will appear very soon. Unfortunately we have to hold up printing any further matter on account of difficulty in securing the needed paper. It is proposed to publish the remaining portion in a few convenient volumes and the English translation will appear in a separate volume for the entire text.

    The appendices added in this volume from page 293 illustrate certain details given in the text. Of these the <term>Svaraprastāras<note>Permutations and combinations of musical notes</note></term> from page 297 and the next one on p. 394 are given at the end of the whole work in the <note>The Anandasrama Sanskrit Series is a famous collection of Indian texts published in Pune.</note>Anandasrama edition; since the matter relates to the first <term>adhyāya<note>chapter</note></term>, it is given at the end of this volume containing the <term>adhyāya</term>. It is hoped that these and the other appendices which were prepared by Pandit Subrahmanya Sastri, and the index of half verses will be of help to the readers in making use of the book.

    As is well known, the <term>Saṅgītaratnākara<note>Literally "The Ocean of Music," a 13th-century treatise that is the foundation of Indian musicology.</note></term> is divided into seven <term>adhyāyas</term> dealing with:

| | | |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1. Musical Notes | 4. Compositions | 7. Dance |
| 2. Melodic Modes | 5. Rhythm and Meter | |
| 3. Miscellaneous Topics | 6. Musical Instruments | |

    The first <term>adhyāya</term> containing the <term>Svara<note>Musical notes or sound</note></term> is divided into eight sections, called <term>prakaraṇas</term> and they deal with:

1. Summary of the subject matter
2. The origin of the human body <note>This section describes the physiological basis of sound production.</note>
3. Sound, its locations, microtones, notes, classes, families, presiding deities, seers, meters, and emotional flavors.
4. Scales, modes, sequences, and melodic variations.

<summary>The editor explains the publication delays due to paper shortages and outlines the structural organization of the Saṅgītaratnākara, specifically detailing the contents of the first chapter on musical notes.</summary>
<keywords>Saṅgītaratnākara, musicology, Svara, Indian classical music, Pandit Subrahmanya Sastri, music theory structure</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the editorial introduction regarding the structural divisions of the Saṅgītaratnākara and begins the biographical sketch of its author, Śārṅgadeva.</meta>

5. Common Tones <note>original: "Sādhāraṇa"; refers to overlapping notes between different scales</note>
6. Melodic Ornamentation <note>original: "Varṇālaṅkāra"; the "color" or movement of notes and their artistic embellishments</note>
7. Melodic Types <note>original: "Jāti"; the ancient classification of melodies that preceded the modern Raga system</note>
8. Song Styles <note>original: "Gīti"</note>

In the Calcutta edition,¹ the first of these chapters <note>original: "prakaraṇas"</note> is called the Introductory section and the rest of the book <note>original: "adhyāya"</note> is divided into seven sections. In the Preface² there, the fifth section is called Common Tones and the Melodic Ornamentation is spoken of as the fourth; but in the text itself the order of these sections is as given in the present edition. I am adding a detailed list of contents, which, it is hoped, will be of use to the readers to understand the whole subject matter at a glance.

Śārṅgadeva, the author of the *Ocean of Music* <note>original: "Saṅgītaratnākara"; the most influential 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on Indian music and dance</note>, gives some information about himself in the beginning of the work,³ before he begins the summary of the work, in the first chapter of the first book. The first verse is an auspicious invocation <note>original: "maṅgala"</note>. Then he speaks of his family,⁴ which traces its origin to Kashmir.⁵ The family goes back to the sage Vṛṣagaṇa.⁶ In that family there was one Bhāskara,⁷ who migrated to the south.⁸ His son

Many commentaries are known to have been written on this work of Śārṅgadeva. The editors of the work from Calcutta say <note>Preface, p. 4.</note> that they have known of seven commentaries, of which four are in Sanskrit, one in Hindi and two in Telugu. But they had seen only two of the Sanskrit commentaries (evidently those by Kallinātha and Siṁhabhūpāla) and the one in Hindi. The late Dr. M. Krishnamacharyar mentions the following commentaries on it, in his *Classical Sanskrit Literature* <note>paragraph 1004, page 853.</note> : Siṁhabhūpāla, Keśava, Kallinātha, Haṁsabhūpāla, Chandrikā, and the Hindi commentary by Gaṅgārāma. Of these the commentaries by Siṁhabhūpāla and Kallinātha will be taken up for detailed consideration presently.

The commentary by Keśava is called *Kaustubha* <term>Kaustubha: literally 'jewel', a common title for scholarly works</term>, according to Dr. Krishnamacharyar. <note>foot-note 2 on p. 853.</note> A commentary by Keśava is mentioned in the *Saṅgītasudhā* <note>The *Saṅgītasudhā* (Nectar of Music) by Govinda Dīkṣita mentions Keśava’s commentary in the following verse: "The two Brahmins, Keśava and Kallinātha, who set out here to make this [work] clear." Edition of Music Academy, Madras, No. 1, p. 152, verse 408.</note>

seems to be the work of Kes'ava.<sup>1</sup> The commentary in Hindi is by Gaṅgārāma, of which there is a good manuscript in the Tanjore Palace Library <note>Now known as the Saraswathi Mahal Library, a famous repository of medieval manuscripts in Tamil Nadu</note>.<sup>2</sup> A Tamil translation of the work also is available in the Tanjore Palace Library.<sup>3</sup>

Of the two important commentaries, those by Kallinātha <note>A 15th-century commentator known for his exhaustive 'Kalanidhi' (The Treasure of Art)</note> and Siṁhabhūpāla <note>A 14th-century king of the Recherla dynasty and author of the 'Sudhakara' (The Moon) commentary</note>, the commentary of Siṁhabhūpāla is earlier. Siṁhabhūpāla belongs to the Recherla dynasty. His father was Anapota, who had a younger brother called Mada. They built up a strong kingdom and they divided the kingdom between themselves, the northern part going to Anapota with the capital at Rajukonda <note>The King's Hill</note> and the southern part to Mada with the capital at Devarakonda <note>The God's Hill</note>.<sup>4</sup> Anapota had two sons; Devagiris'vara <note>The Lord of the Divine Mountain</note> was the elder, who must have died young since it is Siṁhabhūpāla who succeeded Anapota.<sup>5</sup> About Siṁhabhūpāla there is enough material available in his own works. In the commentary on the *Jewel-Mine of Music* <note>original: "Saṅgītaratnākara"</note> itself, there is not much information available. the science of music.<sup>1</sup> <note>original: "saṅgītāgamasanavidbhirakhilaiḥ sārdhaṃ vicārya sphuṭam" — verse 9 from the start of his commentary, meaning "having clearly discussed with all those who know the essence of the musical tradition."</note> He adds that he has studied all the subjects also.<sup>2</sup> <note>original: "vidyājātaviśāradaḥ" — meaning "an expert in the various branches of knowledge."</note> But he has written other works which are now available in print.

A great <term>Alaṅkāra<note>A branch of Sanskrit literature focusing on poetics, rhetoric, and the aesthetics of literature</note></term> work called *Rasārṇavasudhākara* <note>The Moon-nectar of the Ocean of Sentiment</note> by Siṁhabhūpāla has been published in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series by the late <term>Mahāmahopādhyāya<note>A prestigious honorary title for eminent scholars, literally meaning "The Great Great Teacher"</note></term> Dr. T. Ganapati Sastri as No. 50 in 1916. Here there is a long introductory portion<sup>3</sup> <note>verses 1-44</note> where the author gives much information about himself. There is the caste born of the feet of Viṣṇu <note>the Śūdra caste, described in traditional Vedic cosmology as emerging from the feet of the cosmic being</note>.<sup>4</sup> <note>original: "tasya (viṣṇoḥ) pādāmbujājjāto varṇaḥ" — "the caste born from the lotus-feet of him (Vishnu)."</note> Belonging to that caste there is the dynasty of Recalla <note>Recherla</note> where there was the king named Dacana.<sup>5</sup> <note>original: "tatra recalla-vaṃśāndhi-śaradrākā-sudhākaraḥ | kalānidhir-udāraśrīr-āsīd dācana-nāyakaḥ ||" — "In that place lived the leader Dacana, who was like a full moon in the autumn sky over the ocean of the Recherla dynasty, a treasure-house of the arts and possessed of noble splendor." The name of the dynasty is *Recerla* and the double 'll' in the printed edition is likely a typo for 'rlla'.</note> He defeated the Pāṇḍya king,<sup>6</sup> <note>original: "yasyāsidhārāmāgeṇa durgeṇāpi raṇāṅgaṇe | pāṇḍyarājakanyākāñ-jayalakṣmīrupāgatā ||" — "On the battlefield, the Goddess of Victory came to him—as if she were the daughter of the Pandya king—by way of the difficult path of his sword's edge."</note> and he had the Title of Khaḍga-nārāyaṇa <note>The Sword-Narayana, equating the king's prowess with the deity Vishnu/Narayana</note>.<sup>7</sup> <note>original: "khaḍganārāyaṇe yasmin" — "in whom [there was the title] Sword-Narayana."</note> His wife was Vocamāmbā<sup>8</sup> <note>original: "tasya bhāryā mahābhāgyā . . . vocamāmbā guṇodārā" — "His wife was of great fortune . . . Vocamamba, noble in virtues."</note> who belonged to the Tāmarasa <note>Lotus</note> dynasty.<sup>9</sup> <note>original: "jātā tāmarasanvayāt" — "Born of the Tamarasa (Lotus) lineage."</note> They had three sons,<sup>10</sup> <note>original: "tayorabhavan . . . putrāstrayaḥ" — "To them were born . . . three sons."</note>

<page-num>XIV</page-num>

Siṅga Prabhu, Vennama Nayaka, and Reca.¹ Siṅga became the king² after the death of Dacana. His brother Reca had a son named Nāgaya Nāyaka³ who had the Title of <term>Kuṭhārirāya<note>Literally "The Axe-like King," likely a title signifying military prowess or a specific ancestral conquest</note></term>⁴ and who was also called <term>Rāhuttarāya<note>A title meaning "Lord of the Horsemen" or "Chief of the Cavalry"</note></term>.⁵ Siṅga Prabhu had two sons named Ananta and Mādhava.⁶ This Mādhava had many sons⁷ of whom Vedagirīndra was the eldest.⁸ The elder brother of Madhava, namely, Ananta became known as Anapota also.⁹ His wife was Annamāmbā.¹⁰ They had two sons;¹¹ the elder was Devagirīśvara¹² and the second was Siṅgabhūpati.¹³ He lived in his ancestral city of <term>Rājācala<note>Identified with the historical fort-city of Rajukonda in present-day Telangana</note></term>.¹⁴ His kingdom lay between the <term>Vidhya<note>Referring to the Vindhya mountain range in central India</note></term> mountains and the Śrīśaila.¹⁵

<page-num>XV</page-num>

Another work of Siṁhabhūpāla is *Kuvalayāvalī* or *Ratnapāñcālikā*, published in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series by Dr. L. A. Ravi Varma as No. 146 in 1941. This is a small drama in four Acts. In the Prologue the author is mentioned as Śrī Śiṅgabhūpāla,¹ otherwise known as <term>Khaḍganārāyaṇa<note>A royal title meaning "The Vishnu of the Sword," suggesting divine martial prowess</note></term>² who lived at the capital city named <term>Rājaśaila<note>Literally "The Royal Mountain," identified as the fortress of Rajukonda</note></term>.³ His mother was Annamātā.⁴ It is also stated there that one Viśveśvara had spoken very highly of his poetry.⁵ The Viśveśvara mentioned in the Prologue must be the author of *Camatkāracandrikā*; in the colophon <note>A concluding statement in a manuscript providing details about its production</note> of this work there is the mention of Siṁhabhūpāla.⁶

There is a Telugu work called *Velugoṭivārivaṃśāvali* <note>A genealogical history of the Velugoti family</note>.⁷ In the Introduction to that work, Dr. Venkata Ramanayya deals with Siṁhabhūpāla on pages 13 ff.

² By Khaḍganārāyaṇa. <note>original: "khaḍganārāyaṇena"</note> p. 2. l. 8. His grandfather too had this Title. See note 7 on p. XIII above. Perhaps this is a Family Title.

<page-num>XVI</page-num>

Simhabhūpāla is a versatile scholar and a prolific writer. Apart from his *Kuvalayāvalī* and *Rasārṇavasudhākara*, both published in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series, he must have written many other works. In the *Rasārṇavasudhākara*, he mentions a work called *Kandarpasambhava* <note>The Birth of the God of Love</note> as his own composition.¹ In the whole of this *Rasārṇavasudhākara*, he quotes from his own works about twenty-five verses in illustration of various statements he makes, with the remark, "as in my own" <note>original: "yathā mamaiva"</note>. A few of them are traceable to his *Kuvalayāvalī* as is mentioned in the Preface to that drama in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series. We have as yet no information about the other verses quoted from his works.

In Aufrecht’s *Catalogus Catalogorum* <note>The "Catalog of Catalogs," a massive 19th-century effort to list all known Sanskrit manuscripts</note>, there is an entry of *Nāṭakaparibhāṣā* <note>Definitions of Dramaturgy</note> as a work of Siṅgadharaṇīsena. The entry is made on p. 284 as found in Buhler’s Report and on p. 791 as found in the India Office. The manuscripts in the India Office are described by Eggeling under Nos. 1201 and 1202. Evidently the author is Siṅgadharaṇīśa <note>A variant of the King's name meaning "Singa, Lord of the Earth"</note> and Siṅgadharaṇīsena must be the <term>Instrumental Singular<note>A grammatical case in Sanskrit indicating "by" or "with"</note></term> form with *sa* for *śa*.² It is not a separate work; it is only a part of Simhabhūpāla’s *Rasārṇavasudhākara* beginning from verse 290 on p. 298.

There is no reason to believe that the *Rasārṇavasudhākara* was written by Viśveśvara <note>A scholar-poet who some critics suggested might have been the true author behind the King's name</note> on the ground that—

¹ He says: "As in my own *Kandarpasambhava*:" <note>original: "yathā kandarpasambhave mamaiva"</note>
> O Uma, at that moment, the craftsman of passion, seeking to unify the hearts of both, caused them to melt through the heat of love, as if by a searingly hot sigh.
->P. 151, under verse 112.<-

² Eggeling gives the name as Siṅgadharaṇīśa.

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument for King Siṁhabhūpāla’s genuine authorship, shifting from cataloging specific manuscripts to a broader defense of the intellectual capabilities and cultural roles of historical Indian monarchs.</meta>

<page-num>XVII</page-num>
<page-type>preface</page-type>

In the *Camatkāracandrikā* <note>Moonlight of Wonders</note>, the scholar Viśveśvara refers the reader to the *Rasārṇavasudhākara* <note>The Moon of the Ocean of Aesthetic Emotion</note> for further details.¹ It is becoming a fashion nowadays to attribute all works bearing the name of a king to some court poet or court scholar. Unless there is definite evidence—as in the case of the *Saṅgītasudhā* <note>The Nectar of Music</note>, which is assigned to King Raghunātha but mentioned as being written by Govinda Dīkṣita by his son Veṅkaṭamakhin²—we must accept that the king himself wrote these works.

The kings in ancient and even in medieval India were not mere figureheads in administration; nor were they mere administrators. They were the true representatives of the civilization of the country. In their intellectual equipment, in their cultural accomplishments, and in every aspect of their lives, they represented civilization in its ideal form. They maintained **Dharma** <note>A foundational Sanskrit term for duty, cosmic order, and the moral law that sustains civilization</note>, which is another word for civilization; they lived according to **Dharma** also. Besides being warriors, conquerors, and rulers, they were learned scholars, poets, philosophers, and authors, as well as patrons of learning and the arts. 

They recognized only a unified Indian **Dharma** or civilization without any racial prejudices. Siṁhabhūpāla himself says that he belonged to the lowest caste³ <note>He likely refers to the Shudra varna, emphasizing that his royal power comes from merit and duty rather than the highest social birth</note>; at the same time, he honored the Brahmins <note>The priestly and scholarly class</note> and protected religion. Neither caste distinction nor sectarian differences interfered with the unity of culture under the rule of those great Indian kings.

---

¹ Cf. Dr. M. Krishnamacharyar's *Classical Sanskrit Literature*, para 879, p. 771.
² See note 1 on p. XI. above.
³ See note 4 on p. XIII. above.

<summary>This page defends the intellectual legacy of King Siṁhabhūpāla, arguing that ancient Indian kings were genuine scholars and poets who embodied the ideals of Dharma.</summary>
<keywords>authorship, kingship, Dharma, Siṁhabhūpāla, cultural unity, Brahmins, Rasārṇavasudhākara, patronage</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the defense of King Siṁhabhūpāla’s authorship by refuting specific scholarly objections raised by Dr. M. Krishnamacharyar regarding the identity of the author of two major works.</meta>

<page-num>XVIII</page-num>
<page-type>preface</page-type>

Dr. M. Krishnamacharyar says that Siṁhabhūpāla, who wrote the commentary on the *Saṅgītaratnākara* <note>The Jewel Mine of Music, a foundational 13th-century treatise on Indian music</note>, is different from the author of *Rasārṇavasudhākara* <note>The Moon of the Ocean of Aesthetic Emotion, a work on dramaturgy and poetry</note>¹. He does not give any explanation. It is true that while he gives an elaborate description of his ancestry in the introductory portion of the *Rasārṇavasudhākara*, he gives little information about himself in his commentary. This must be due to the fact that he wrote the commentary after he wrote the *Rasārṇavasudhākara*. It is not possible at this stage to investigate the point on the basis of any internal evidence. I must wait for that till the whole of the commentary is published. But the **colophon** <note>A statement at the end of a manuscript or book chapter providing details about its authorship and production</note> in the two works proves the identity of the authors beyond any doubt.² The question of a work called *Nāṭakaparibhāṣa* <note>Technical Definitions of Drama</note>, the question of *Rasārṇavasudhākara* having been written by another person who was a favourite in the court, and the question of the authors of the two works being different—such questions should not have been raised, and if the points had been properly investigated such doubts would not have been raised. But since they are found in works well known and relied on by many, it has become necessary for me to investigate the points and make certain remarks on them.

¹ See *Classical Sanskrit Literature*, footnote 1, p. 853.
² The colophon in *Rasārṇavasudhākara* read as follows :
> Thus, in the work named the *Rasārṇavasudhākara* <note>The Moon of the Ocean of Aesthetic Emotion</note> composed by the illustrious King Siṁhabhūpāla—who is the son of the glorious King Yanapota, the lord of the Andhra territory, and a hero as mighty as Bhima <note>A legendary hero from the Mahabharata known for his incredible physical strength</note>... <note>original: "iti śrīmadandhramaṇḍalādhīśvarapratigaṇḍabhairavaśrīyanapotanarendranandanabhujabalabhīmaśrīśiṅghabhūpālaviracite rasārṇavasudhākaranāmni etc."</note>

This may be compared with the colophon at the end of the first chapter of the commentary. Further, the identity of the names *Sudhākara* <note>The "Moon," literally meaning "The Mine of Nectar"</note> in both works too point out to the identity of the authors.

<summary>The author disputes Dr. Krishnamacharyar’s claim that King Siṁhabhūpāla did not write both the Saṅgītaratnākara commentary and the Rasārṇavasudhākara, citing matching colophons and titles as evidence of a single author.</summary>

<page-num>XIX</page-num>
<page-type>preface</page-type>

Three manuscripts of Siṃhabhūpāla's commentary on the *Saṅgītaratnākara* <note>The "Jewel Mine of Music," a foundational 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on music and dance</note> have come to our notice. One is in the collection at the Fort at Bikaner and we were able to secure a transcript of it.¹ There is another work in the Oriental Library at Baroda and for this also, we were able to have a transcript.² The third is in the Bhandarkar Research Institute, Poona.³ It is found that this last manuscript consists of a few stray leaves and so we did not utilise it. Another manuscript is known to exist in Kashmere.⁴ We tried very much to secure a loan or a transcript of it. But we are informed that the manuscript is not available there.

Kallinātha <note>A prominent 15th-century scholar and commentator who wrote under the patronage of the Vijayanagara Empire</note> also gives some information about himself in the introductory portion of his commentary.⁵ He speaks about the Karṇātaka country⁶ with the Kāverī and the Kṛṣṇā <note>Two major rivers of Southern India</note> on the south and the north of the country,⁷ which extends to the eastern and the western coasts.⁸ Here on the banks of the

<page-num>XX</page-num>
<page-type>preface</page-type>

Tungabhadrā <note>A major river in Southern India</note> there is the city called Vidyānagari (Vijayanagar)¹ where there ruled the king Devarāya, son of Vijaya of the Yadava dynasty.² Devarāya’s son was Immaḍi Devarāya.³ Kallinātha lived there at that time.⁴ His grandfather was Vallabhadeva;⁵ his mother was Nārāyaṇī⁶ and father Lakṣmīdhara.⁷ He belonged to the <term>Ṣāṇḍilya Gotra <note>A traditional Brahmin lineage or clan tracing its descent to the ancient sage Shāndilya</note></term>.⁸ Under the orders of the king, he commented on the <term>Sangītaratnākara <note>The "Ocean of Music," a definitive 13th-century treatise on Indian musicology</note></term>.⁹

Vijaya I, mentioned by Kallinātha, reigned from 1418 to 1423; his son Devaraya II reigned from 1423 to 1446.¹⁰ Immaḍi Devarāya reigned from 1446 to 1465. Thus Kallinātha must have lived in the second half of the fifteenth century.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific biography and lineage of the commentator Kallinātha (concluded on page XX) to a discussion of the primary author, S'árṅgadeva, and the broader institutional context of the Adyar Library’s musicological publications.</meta>

<page-num>XXI</page-num>
<page-type>preface</page-type>

S'árṅgadeva, the author of the <term>Saṅgītaratnākara <note>The "Ocean of Music," the most definitive 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on Indian music and dance.</note></term>, mentions many previous writers on the subject in verses 15 to 19 in the first <term>prakaraṇa <note>A section or subdivision of a chapter.</note></term> of the first <term>adhyāya <note>A primary chapter or book division.</note></term>. Of these authorities, some are very well known. A detailed notice of them will be more appropriate when the whole book is out. He must have eclipsed most of them. He styles himself as <term>Nis'saṅka <note>original: "निःशङ्क"; meaning "The Doubtless" or "Free from doubts."</note></term>. He also refers to himself as <term>Karaṇāgraṇīḥ <note>original: "करणाग्रणीः"; meaning "Chief of the Department of Records" or "Accountant-General."</note></term>, which shows that he was the accountant-general of his king. Thus the author of the original was a high official in the service of the king; the commentator Kallinātha was a prominent figure in the royal court, held in high esteem by the king; the other commentator is a king. This shows what a close relation there existed between the government and the culture of the country.

The Adyar Library has already published two works on Music, the <term>Melarāgamālikā <note>A "Garland of Ragas and Scales" describing the 72 melakarta scales of Carnatic music.</note></term> of Mahāvaidyanātha S'ivan and the <term>Saṅgrahacūḍāmaṇi <note>The "Crest-gem of Compendiums," a musical manual attributed to Govinda.</note></term>, which were both edited by the late Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastri and which appeared as Nos. 16 and 17 in the Adyar Library Series. The <term>Rāgavibodha <note>The "Awakening of Ragas," a 17th-century work focusing on musical notation and performance.</note></term> of Somanātha is already available in more than one edition and there is also an English translation. But the book is known to be out of print. The Adyar Library has already started printing a fresh edition of the work prepared by the late Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastri, where he has been able to improve the readings in many places. This edition will be out very soon.

The plan of the Adyar Library is to publish works in all aspects of ancient Indian Culture, of which we

<summary>This page discusses S'árṅgadeva's professional status as a high-ranking state official and highlights the historic synergy between Indian government patronage and the preservation of musical culture. It also lists several significant musicological texts published by the Adyar Library under the editorship of S. Subrahmanya Sastri.</summary>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface from page XXI, moving from the historical context of the author S'árṅgadeva to the philosophical underpinnings of Indian music as a religious practice, and beginning the acknowledgments for the current edition.</meta>

<page-num>XXII</page-num>
<page-type>preface</page-type>

...consider music and other fine arts as very important ones. In India, music did not develop as a secular entertainment; music in India is a fundamental phase of religion; rather music has become a religion itself, with a philosophy attached to it. The musical notes are the physical manifestations of the Highest Reality termed the Divine Sound (<term>Nāda-Brahman <note>original: "नादब्रह्मन्"; the concept that the entire universe is a manifestation of sacred sound.</note></term>). Music is not a mere accompaniment in religious worship; it is religious worship itself, like sacrificial rituals (<term>Yāgas <note>Ancient Vedic fire sacrifices and ceremonial offerings.</note></term>) and Temple worship. In India there has never been an antithesis between aesthetics and morality; there has never been developed an aesthetic doctrine which was not acceptable to the most orthodox follower of religion. Thus the *<term>Saṅgītaratnākara <note>The "Jewel-mine of Music," the most influential 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on Indian music and dance.</note></term>* and other works on music undertaken for publication by the Adyar Library are presentations of orthodox phases of Hindu religion and of Indian civilization as much as the commentaries on the <term>Vedas <note>The most ancient and foundational scriptures of Hinduism.</note></term> and the works on religion and philosophy like the *<term>Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā <note>A sacred text of the Vaishnava tradition dealing with the power of God and ritual philosophy.</note></term>* and the *<term>Vedāntaparibhāṣā <note>A classic 17th-century manual explaining the logic and knowledge-theory of the Vedanta school of philosophy.</note></term>*. Through our publications we desire to exhibit the unity of Indian culture and the harmony that exists among the various phases of the Culture.

Now what remains for me is to acknowledge the help that has been received in the preparation of this edition. Our gratitude to Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastri, who prepared the edition, is far beyond words to be adequately expressed. His whole life was spent in scholarly pursuits; it is a great privilege for me to be able to associate myself with this great work even in this very humble capacity. Dr. G. Srinivasa Murti...

<summary>This page explains that in Indian tradition, music is not mere entertainment but a sacred philosophy and a form of religious worship equivalent to ritual. It also begins the editor's acknowledgments, specifically thanking Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastri for his lifelong scholarship.</summary>

The air <note>original: "maruta"</note> born there is the vital breath called **Prana** <note>the life-force</note>, which moves through the locations of the navel, heart, nose, and mouth, and is the cause of the pronunciation of sounds. # The Ocean of Music
### [Exposition of Terms]

The "place" refers to the sacred syllable *Om* <note>original: "Pranava"</note>. Following that, in the phrase "according to the rules," the word "according to" <note>original: "anu"</note> functions as a prepositional particle. Grammatically, this requires the word "Sacred Sound" <note>original: "Shruti-padam"</note> to take the second case ending <note>referring to a rule in Panini's grammar: "karmapravacaniya-yukte dvitiya"</note>. The term "delightful" <note>original: "ranjakah"</note> describes how the sound absorbs everything else into its own essence, much like a potent dye <note>original: "maha-rajana"</note>.

Alternatively, "Sacred Sound" <note>original: "Shruti-padam"</note> can refer to the secondary sentences of the scriptures. Their "place" or goal is the "Great Saying" <note>original: "Mahavakya"</note>—the entire philosophical context beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this [existence] was alone" <note>original: "Sadev somyedam agra asit" from the Chandogya Upanishad</note> and concluding with "That thou art" <note>original: "Tat tvam asi"</note>. By "following," it means that after hearing these truths, one proceeds through a sequence of verbal understanding. Once the sense of separation is removed and the unity between "That" and "Thou" <note>referring to the soul and the absolute</note> is practiced, the truth is realized. 

When we say "this one," the word "this" refers to what is known through the scriptures. However, using the pointer "this" indicates that after hearing and reflecting, it becomes a direct mental perception. "He shines by himself" <note>original: "svayam rajate"</note> means he radiates with his own light. Upon realization, when the limiting conditions of mental activity are destroyed, he shines eternally in his true nature. As stated in the *Yoga of Yajnavalkya* <note>original: "Yoga-Yajnavalkya," a foundational text on yoga and breath control</note>:

> “Controlling the breath with the mind, chanting the sacred syllable Om, 
> one should sit in a secret place with senses conquered and mind focused. 
> When that breath reaches the central channel <note>original: "Sushumna," the primary energy channel in the spine</note>, O beautiful-faced one, 
> the wise one, having chanted the mantra, should hold it within the heart. 
> When the space within the body is filled with breath, 
> then the Soul shines there like the sun <note>original: "vikartanah"</note> in the sky. 
> Whatever he sees, he should see all that as the Self within the Self.”

<margin>are perceived.</margin>
The division of Scales <term>Gram: literally 'village'; in music, it refers to a fundamental scale or collection of notes</term>, the arrangement of melodic movements <term>Varna: 'color' or 'order'; refers to the four types of melodic movements like ascending or descending</term>, and the classes of ornaments <term>Alankara: musical decorations or embellishments</term>. 

By the word "Scale" <note>original: "Gram"</note>, the worlds or people <gloss>people</gloss> are indicated. Their "division" refers to their classification. "Melodic movements" or "colors" <note>original: "Varna"</note> here refers to social classes like the Brahmins; their "arrangement" refers to the way they are organized. The "classes of ornaments" are those generated by the ascending and descending order of notes, which serve to decorate the melodic patterns.

It then begins to define fundamental musical terms like Grama (scale) and Varna (melodic movement) using double meanings that link music to social and cosmic order.</summary>

# Collection of Music: Chapter 1
## The First Chapter: Concerning the Nature of Notes

The sequence of these scales, divisions, and so forth, is "that from which they arise"—this is the implied meaning <note>original: "adhyahara"</note>. This follows the rule of the grammarians: "Where no other action is specified, the verb 'to be' is understood." By this, the relationship of the world to the Lord is shown to be an indirect attribute <note>original: "tatastha-lakshana," a technical term in Vedanta meaning a property that defines something without being its permanent essence</note>. This is just as it is presented in the "Aphorism on Origin" <note>referring to the *Brahma Sutras* 1.1.2</note> concerning the scriptural sentence "From which [all these beings are born]," and in the sacred verse <note>original: "shruti"</note> that states: "His mouth became the Brahmin."

"The Body of Sound" <note>original: "nada-tanu"</note> means one whose physical form is sound itself. This is based on the scripture: "Having created that, He then entered into it." I bow to that Lord Shankara <note>a name for Shiva, literally 'The Granter of Happiness'</note> for the sake of "delight" <note>original: "mude"</note>, meaning the attainment of unsurpassed bliss—He who is "exaltedly praised by the world" <note>original: "uddhurajagadgitam"</note>, meaning the entire universe sings his praises in a grand and exalted manner.

However, from the perspective of the musical notes <note>original: "svara"</note> being discussed:

In the "heart-lotus" of the wise who know these matters, sound resides in the "lower register" <note>original: "mandra-sthana"</note>. This is the exact meaning of the term "Knot of Brahma" <note>original: "brahma-granthi," a psychic center in the subtle body located near the heart</note>. Through the "mind" <note>original: "citta"</note>, which is impelled by the soul’s desire to speak, sound is produced. 

"The place of Microtones" <note>original: "shruti-padam" / "shruti"</note>: the microtones are those subtle divisions of the scale like *Chandovati* <note>the name of one of the 22 shrutis</note> which manifest the primary notes like *Shadja* <note>the fundamental note, 'Sa'</note>. "Place" <note>original: "padam"</note> here is a collective noun referring to their various locations. The sound <note>original: "nada"</note> produced by the striking of the air—drawn by the mind—against the diagonal channels connected to the main upward-flowing channel <note>original: "nadis" of the subtle body</note> is designated by the word "place," because it resides within those locations.

"Thereafter," it becomes "delightful" <note>original: "ranjaka"</note> by flowing without interruption. This is because it is the producer of its own form from its cause, the microtones, and because it generates pleasure in the heart of the listener. This "Note" <note>original: "svara"</note> is that which is experienced as famous in the scientific treatises. It is said to "shine by itself" <note>original: "svayam rajate"</note>, meaning that in actual musical performance, it shines forth without needing any external or auxiliary cause. By this similarity of syllables, the etymology of the word "Note" <note>svara = svayam (self) + rajate (shines)</note> is demonstrated.

Regarding "Scales" <note>original: "grama"</note> and the rest:
*   **Scales:** These are the *Shadja-grama* and others.
*   **Divisions:** Their internal groupings.
*   **Melodic Movements:** <note>original: "varna"</note> The steady, ascending, descending, and wandering patterns.
*   **Ornamentations:** <note>original: "alamkara"</note> Musical figures like the "Bright" <note>original: "prasanna"</note> and others.
*   **Melodic Types:** <note>original: "jati"</note> The ancient parent scales like *Shadji*.

The sequence of all these—the scales, divisions, and so forth, whose characteristics will be described later—arises from the Note as their fundamental cause. 

"Body of Sound" means having the nature of sound. "Exaltedly praised by the world": "Song" <note>original: "gita"</note> is a specific composition of notes; since the exalted songs of the world arise from Him, He is so named. I praise that Shankara, the granter of happiness, for the manifestation of bliss. || 1 ||

->(Sudhakara's Commentary)<-

> His outer form shines as he plays the flute-song, surrounded by his companions,
> His head adorned with a serpent, he marks the rhythm with claps, eager to perform the dance upon the stage of the earth.

<summary>This page provides a dual philosophical and technical commentary on the origin of sound, linking the deity Shiva (as the Body of Sound) to the physical and metaphysical production of musical notes and scales within the human body.</summary>
<keywords>Nada, Svara, Grama, Brahma-granthi, Shruti, Shankara, music theory, etymology of Svara, microtones, subtle body</keywords>

# The Ocean of Music [The Nature of...
## Page 6

Thus, revealing Himself through a unique grace and having embraced the art of music, <gloss>1</gloss> may the Lotus-eyed One <note>original: "Padmekshana," an epithet for Lord Vishnu</note>, who protects the three worlds at every step, protect you all. (1)
<gloss>1: Variant reading: "...having accepted music, the protector of the three worlds"</gloss>

May the vast source of the Goddess of Fortune <note>original: "Shri," referring to Lakshmi</note> lead to the prosperity of the worlds. I believe the god Mukunda <note>an epithet for Vishnu</note> became four-armed just so he could embrace the expansive breasts of Shri. (2)

We meditate in our hearts upon that Elephant-Faced God <note>original: "Gajanana," or Ganesha</note>, who—as if seeking victory for his father <note>Lord Shiva</note>—bears the sun in the guise of his frontal lobes reddened with vermilion, and carries the Yamuna river in the form of the dark stream of rutting-ichor flowing from his temples. (3)

I bow to that Treasure of the Worlds <note>referring to the Goddess Parvati</note>, who is the very life of the Great Lord <note>Shiva</note> and the fruit of the penances of the Snow-Mountain <note>Himalaya</note>, so that the darkness of doubt may be pacified. (4)

Because the texts composed by the Sage Bharata <note>the legendary author of the Natyashastra</note> and others were so difficult to grasp, the entire tradition of music <note>original: "sangita-paddhati"</note> had fallen into decay and ruin before the time of Sharngadeva. (5)

That tradition was clearly unified and restored by Sharngadeva. Like a sacrificial pillar <note>original: "yupa"</note> in the temple of the *Ocean of Music*, it stands as a monument to his self-sufficiency and wisdom. (6)

Mindful of the author’s generosity and with a heart full of compassion, <gloss>2</gloss> King Simhabhupala now strives to turn this text into a "Path for Elephants" <note>a metaphor for making a difficult subject broad, smooth, and easy for everyone to follow</note>. (7)
<gloss>2: This [work].</gloss>

King Simhabhupala, the lamp of his royal lineage, expands upon this commentary—which clearly reveals the meaning of the book named *The Ocean of Music* <note>original: "Sangita Ratnakara"</note>—and calls his work *The Nectar-Source of Music* <note>original: "Sangita Sudhakara"</note>. (8)

The sacred science <note>original: "shastra"</note> composed by Bharata and the ancient masters is difficult to perceive. After long study and clear deliberation with all the experts who know the essence of the musical traditions <note>original: "sangita-agama"</note>, the noble-hearted King Simhabhupala, a master of all the arts, explains *The Ocean of Music* out of a desire to favor the world. (9)

It is possible for someone to take a little knowledge and expand it into a brand new work. However, it is truly difficult to provide a proper arrangement and explanation even for a text that seems accessible. (10)

In this text, which is extremely deep, complex, and understood only by a few, <gloss>3</gloss> King Simhabhupala is the only one truly all-knowing and skilled in providing a complete explanation. (11)

# [The Compendium: Section 1]
## Chapter 1: The Nature of Musical Notes

->Those who know theory possess no confidence without musical practice,<-
->and those who know practice but are devoid of scriptural knowledge behave poorly in assemblies.<-
->Therefore, wise men of great intellect should not look down upon this work by King Simhabhupala,<-
->who knows both practice and theory with perfect clarity, thinking it merely "new." (12)<-

->He who praises without understanding the essence does not truly offer us praise,<-
->just as a deaf person’s praise does nothing for a singer.<-
->The foremost among the wise, speaking with a certain mind, brings joy;<-
->for in a gathering, the offering of fine points <note>original: "curna," literally "powder." In a medical sense, it calms the body; in a literary sense, it refers to refined, clear explanations</note> calms the disturbances of men. (13)<-

->Who, out of pride—even if superior in all qualities—would dare to explain the *Ocean of Music*?<-
->Nonetheless, I make this attempt to please those who possess insight. (14)<-

Believing that the musical scriptures composed by the likes of the sages <term>Bharata, Dattila, and Kohala: the legendary founding fathers of Indian music and drama theory</term> possess secrets difficult to grasp for those on earth with limited intellect, the supremely compassionate Sharngadeva—whose mind is devoted to the lotus feet of the Moon-Crested Lord <note>original: "Shishirakirana-bharana," an epithet for the god Shiva</note>—desired to compose the *Ocean of Music* <note>original: "Sangita-ratnakara"</note>, the very essence of music, for the benefit of the world. 

To ensure a completion free from obstacles and to allow the work to spread through his disciples and their pupils, he performs an auspicious invocation <term>Mangalacharana: a prayer at the start of a manuscript to ensure its successful completion</term>, as prescribed by tradition and scripture. In a single verse, he also explains the subject matter, the purpose, and the relationship between them, beginning with the words "The Knot of Brahma" <note>original: "Brahma-granthi"</note>. 

Thinking that the word *Brahma*—which reminds one of the Supreme Soul, the destroyer of all obstacles—will serve as an auspicious opening by its very placement, he uses the term *Brahma* first, as it is the cause of liberation and the nature of Sound <term>Nada: in Indian philosophy, sound is seen as a divine, primordial energy</term>. 

He says: **I bow** <note>original: "vande"</note>. This means "I salute" or "I praise," for the linguistic root *vad* signifies both salutation and praise. If he had used words like "I prostrate" <note>original: "namati"</note> or "I laud" <note>original: "stauti"</note>, only one of those meanings would be obtained, not both; hence the use of "I bow" <note>original: "vande"</note>. 

Here, the three-fold nature of salutation—mental, vocal, and physical—is understood because no specific qualifier is given. Or rather, a connection should be made with the word "with the mind" <note>original: "cittena"</note> in the first line, because a mental salutation is the primary one as it is performed with faith, according to the scripture: "Whatever one does with knowledge and faith..." Since the vocal salutation is established by the very act of writing the book, and for the faithful, vocal salutation is inseparable from physical salutation, all three types of salutation are successfully established. 

To whom do I bow? To **Shankara**, which means "the Lord." Or, *Shankara* is he who "bestows bliss" <note>original: "sham karoti iti shankarah"</note>; the Lord alone provides happiness independently. By this definition, we exclude kings and others who only provide happiness conditionally <note>i.e., kings only give rewards if they are pleased or if certain conditions are met, whereas God's grace is seen as absolute</note>.

# *The Ocean of Music* [The Meaning of the Words]

Now, one might object: even those who are supremely compassionate and act without self-interest still strive to bring joy to others. To address this [and explain why the author offers praise], he says:

**"Udgura"** and so on. **Udgura** means praised or sung by the world. Although the root word <note>original: "Gai," the Sanskrit verbal root for singing</note> refers to the act of making sound, because the subject here is the Lord, it is understood to mean "praise."

What is the nature of this Lord? He is **Nadatana**, meaning his body or essence is **Nada** <term>Nada: the primordial, metaphysical sound that is considered the substance of the universe</term>. This is because he is described as **Shabdabrahma** <note>original: "Shabdabrahma," or the Absolute manifest as Sound</note>. Or, one might view **Nada** as the effect, which points toward its cause, Space; thus, his essence is Space. Space is also one of the eight forms of the Supreme Lord. This definition is used because the Supreme Lord is the cause of sound, and his grace is what allows for the completion of this vast work of words.

The word "Him" is used to establish a relationship, for according to the rule, "He" and "That" are eternally connected. Him, who? He from whom **Grama** <term>Grama: literally "villages," but in music theory refers to the fundamental scales or collections of notes</term> and the rest originate. 

By the word **Grama**, we should understand the worlds such as Earth, or alternatively, the cities, towns, and villages. **Vibhaga** [Divisions] refers to material wealth like grain, or the distinct separation of the "villages," following the Vedic scripture: "This is the bridge, the boundary, so that these worlds do not collide."

From Him also come:
*   **Varnas** <note>original: "varna" can mean musical syllables, colors, or social classes</note>: the Brahmins and other social orders.
*   **Rachana** [Arrangements]: the creation of two-footed, four-footed, and six-footed beings.
*   **Alankaras** [Ornaments]: such as bracelets and crowns.
*   **Jatis** <note>original: "jati" refers to musical modes as well as biological species or castes</note>: the categories of being, such as "cowness" or "horseness."
*   **Krama** [Sequence]: the stages of life like childhood, or the cycle of creation and destruction, or the sequence of the seasons.

Because the grammar uses the source-case <note>original: "panchami," the ablative case used to indicate origin</note>, we understand these all "originate" from Him. Here, one may treat "Scales, Divisions, Notes, Arrangements, Ornaments, and Modes" as a compound group followed by "Sequence," meaning the "Sequence associated with these things." Or, it means the sequence or orderly arrangement of everything from the "Scales" to the "Modes" originates from Him.

He further distinguishes the Lord: He is **Svaprakasha**, meaning He who shines by His own light. But what does "Self-luminous" mean? It is that which is fit for immediate, direct experience while not being an object of external knowledge. As stated in the *Tattvapradipika* <note>A famous 13th-century treatise on Advaita Vedanta philosophy</note>:

> "When that which is fit for immediate experience is established as our very self, how could a definition of Self-luminosity be impossible?"

Where does He shine? In the **lotus-heart of the wise**. This follows the teaching: "The Person the size of a thumb resides in the center of the self."

One might ask: how can the all-pervasive Supreme Self have the physical property of residing in a heart? To this, he says: **Anuranjaka** [The Purifier/Resonator]. Even though the Supreme Lord is all-pervading, He manifests within the lotus-heart of living beings. As the sage Vyasa said: "It is a matter of manifestation." 

How is He manifested in the heart? By the **Chitta** [the mind/consciousness]. Of what kind? By that which follows the movement of the breath through the **Brahma-granthi**. The **Brahma-granthi** <term>The Knot of Brahma: a vital psychic center in the subtle body where the three main energy channels (Ida, Pingala, and Sushumna) meet</term> is the junction where the central channel meets the side channels; the "wind" or breath that arises there and travels with it is the means of this manifestation.

# [Compendium 1] First Chapter: On Musical Notes

The suffix indicates an "Indra-pratyaya" <note>A grammatical term referring to a specific derivative form</note>. The compound **"following the wind"** <note>original: "marutanugatina"</note> is broken down as "one who follows the wind." This refers to the well-known principle among Yogis that the mind and the breath <note>original: "maruta," the vital air or Prana</note> always move together. This was also expressed by the poet Sriharsha in his work *The Life of Nala*:

> “O Bhaimi, though you have gone outside through the nostrils as breath, you dwell within the heart; it is no wonder that the mind does not seize wealth there, for the mind and breath function as one.”

The connection here is: I bow to this specific Supreme Lord for the sake of **joy** <note>original: "mude," meaning happiness or spiritual bliss</note>. From another perspective, I bow to **Song**. "Song" <note>original: "Gitam"</note> is defined as a pleasing arrangement of musical notes, as will be explained later: “A pleasing arrangement of notes is called Song.” Since Song is the primary subject, the term "Song" here also implies instrumental music and dance; thus, the text hints that the subject of this entire book is **Musicology** <term>Sangita: the triple art of vocal music, instrumental music, and dance</term>. If Musicology were not the intended subject, mentioning it at the beginning as an object of praise and salutation would be logically inconsistent.

Alternatively, I bow to the **Body of Sound**. I bow to that arrangement of notes whose very form is Sound <term>Nada: the primordial vibration that manifests as musical sound</term>. What is its nature? It is **sung by the exalted world**, meaning it has been produced or celebrated by the great beings of the universe. For what purpose? For **joy** (bliss). What else is its nature? It is **Shankara**, meaning "that which creates happiness" <note>The author derives the name of the god Shiva from "Sham" (happiness) and "Kara" (maker)</note>. By this, the author shows the primary purpose of the work: the causal relationship between the subject (music) and the result (happiness).

To whom does this refer? To Him from whom the **Scales** and other elements originate. **Scales** <term>Grama: literally 'villages', the fundamental collections of notes</term> are groups of musical notes. There are three: the Shadja-grama, the Madhyama-grama, and the Gandhara-grama. **Division** <note>original: "vibhaga"</note> refers to their distinct separation. **Melodic Movement** <term>Varna: the functional act of singing</term> is fourfold—steady, ascending, descending, and wandering—as will be stated later: “The act of singing is called Varna.” This refers to its structure, its execution, or its beauty. **Ornaments** <term>Alankara: specific sequences of notes that decorate a melody</term> are distinct arrangements of notes like the "low-register" sequences and others. **Melodic Types** <term>Jati: the ancient precursors to the Raga system</term> are eighteen in number, beginning with *Shadji*: seven are "pure" and eleven are "modified," such as *Shadja-kaishiki*. The connection here is that the orderly sequence of all these elements arises from Him.

This sound **shines by itself**, because it grants joy without depending on anything else. This also explains the etymology of the word **Note** <term>Swara: derived from 'Sva' (self) and 'Raj' (to shine)</term>. What is its nature? It is **pleasing to the wise**, creating a sense of devotion or passion in those who understand the essence of music. Where does it shine? In the **heart-lotus**. The "heart-lotus" is a general term; it implies the three locations where musical sound is generated: the heart, the throat, and the head. By what is it perceived? By the **mind**, because the mind is the cause of the production of sound, as will be said later: “The self, desiring to speak, prompts the mind...” The description **born from the knot of Brahma** <note>original: "Brahmagranthija"</note> is used as before <note>Referring to the psychic center in the lower torso where the breath and fire meet to create sound</note>. || 1 ||

# 10 The Ocean of Music [Word-meanings]

There is an auspicious home, a noble lineage born in the beautiful land of Kashmir. It originated from the sage Vrishanaga and its fame has reached the very corners of the world. || 2 ||

This lineage was adorned by the leaders of the twice-born <note>original: "dvijendra," referring to Brahmins</note>, who were the foremost among those of religious mind, masters of the ocean of Vedic knowledge, and who appeared like the Creator <note>original: "Brahma"</note> himself in human form. || 3 ||

In that family, there was Bhaskara, a treasury of brilliance who shone like the sun. To grace the southern region, he made his "southern journey" <note>original: "dakshinayana," a pun referring both to the sun's seasonal movement and his own migration to Southern India</note>. || 4 ||

His son was the venerable Sodhala, possessed of great humility and profound intellect. By serving the King Bhillama <note>Bhillama V, founder of the Yadava/Seuna dynasty of Devagiri</note>, <gloss>1</gloss> whose prosperity was ever-increasing, he attained a fame that soothed the sorrows of the entire world. He also held a position of great victory and high status under the illustrious King Singhana <note>Singhana II, the most powerful ruler of the Yadava dynasty</note>. || 5 ||

King Singhana Deva alone is the conqueror of the circle of the earth. The rows of his toenails are painted by the <gloss>2</gloss> rising radiance of the sapphires in the crowns of kings who bow before him. He is the leader of monarchs; the fire of his majesty, though pervading the whole universe, intensely burns only the hearts of his enemies. || 6 ||

Having pleased that virtuous king who was a lover of excellence, Sodhala—the leader of the wise—satisfied the learned Brahmins with a multitude of virtues and acts of service. || 7 ||

What did he not give? What did he not know? What wealth did he not possess? What religious duty did he not perform? And by what virtues did he not shine? || 8 ||

From that Sodhala, as the moon is born from the Milk Ocean, was born **Sharngadeva** <note>The author of this treatise</note>. He stands above all others, his hands ever-shining with constant generosity <note>original: "kara," a pun meaning both "hands" and "rays of the moon"</note>. || 9 ||

# 10 The Ocean of Music [Lineage and Authorities]

->**Sadasiva, Shiva, Brahma, Bharata, and the sage Kashyapa;**<-
->**Matanga, Yashtika, Durga, Shakti, Shardula, and Kohala; || 15 ||**<-
->**Vishakhila, Dattila, as well as Kambala and Ashvatara;**<-

<note>original: "yajvabhih"</note> **By the sacrificers:** This means the lineage was adorned by those who perform Vedic rituals. It implies that such noble people were born into this family.

The author now describes the distinguished founding ancestor born in that family: **"There"** <note>original: "tatra"</note>. There was a man named Bhaskara, who was like the sun in his brilliance, a treasury of light, and a vessel of spiritual splendor <term>brahma-varchasa: the luster or power acquired through Vedic study and lifestyle</term>; or, in another sense, a vessel of physical beauty. He performed a **"southward journey"** <note>original: "dakshinayana"</note>, moving from the land of Kashmir toward the southern regions; or, alternatively, it means he made the "arrival of the gift" <note>original: "dakshina"</note> possible by finding worthy recipients for his charity, thus fulfilling the desires of those skilled in receiving such offerings. In the context of the sun, the term "southward journey" refers to the well-known winter solstice.

The author of this treatise now speaks of his father: **"His"** <note>original: "tasya"</note>. He refers to King Bhillama <note>A king of the Yadava dynasty</note> in the city of Jaitra <note>Likely Jaitrapala, or a city named after him</note>.

He describes his own master, King Singhana <note>original: "Siddhana-bhupa"</note>: **"The one"** <note>original: "eka"</note>. The fire of this king’s majesty, although it pervades the entire universe, burns only the hearts of his enemies. Here, the author uses a poetic figure of speech <term>visheshokti: a poetic ornament where the cause is present but the expected effect is restricted</term>.

He describes the power of King Singhana's favor: **"Having pleased him"** <note>original: "tam prasadya"</note>. Having gladdened King Singhana through a multitude of virtues. He uses the phrase "one who loves virtue" as a significant descriptor, employing a poetic device <term>parikaralankara: the use of significant adjectives to enhance the meaning</term>. Through various means of service—providing wealth, clothing, and other resources—what did he not give? The meaning is that the king gave everything.

From this man named Sodhala, who was like a salt-ocean <note>symbolizing vastness and depth</note>, Sharngadeva was born, just as the moon was born from the churning of the cosmic ocean. Regarding the phrase **"Above and beyond"** <note>original: "uparyupari"</note>: the word "above" is repeated for emphasis, governing the following nouns in the grammatical second case.

To demonstrate the unique quality of this book, the author describes himself as **"Having heard"** <note>original: "shruta"</note> the ancient wisdom. He reveals his own scholarship as **"Various"** <note>original: "nana"</note>. His association with learning is explained by his connection to Kashmir, the dwelling place of Saraswati <note>the goddess of wisdom</note>, as Sharngadeva himself was born in the Kashmiri tradition.

**"He"** <note>original: "sa"</note>: That Sharngadeva reveals—which is to say, composes—the *Ocean of Music* <note>original: "Sangita Ratnakara"</note>. He does this **"for the attainment of ultimate liberation"** <note>original: "nihshreyasa-aptaye"</note>. This is because specific ancient song forms like the *Madraka* and others, which will be discussed in the sections on compositions, were ordained by the Creator to be used in the praise of Shiva as a means to achieve spiritual moksha <note>liberation from the cycle of rebirth</note>. || 2–14 ||

# 13 The Compendium 1] First Chapter: The Nature of Notes

->**Anjaneya, Matrigupta, Ravana, and Nandikeshvara;**<-

**Commentary:** From the mention of "Sadasiva, Shiva, etc." <note>referring to verses 15-16 on the previous page</note> up to the phrase "extracted this essence." "Extracted essence" <note>original: *saroddhara*</note> refers to the **butter** <note>original: *navanita*</note>; this is a metaphorical description of the work. Alternatively, "extraction of the essence" can be read as a functional description of the labor performed in this work. || 15—20 ||

<term>(Su.)</term> <note>This refers to the *Sudhakara* commentary by Simhabhupala</note> An objection might be raised: "Since there already exist works on music composed by Sadasiva, Bharata, and others, why undergo the trouble of creating this new work? <gloss>original marginalia: Why this modern creation?</gloss> Is it not a fruitless effort?" To this, the author replies: **"Sadasiva..."** etc. By churning the ocean of their collective doctrines, he has "extracted this essence." Therefore, because those ancient works are vast, difficult to comprehend, and numerous, they are impossible for short-lived humans to fully digest. Through this work, the realization of the secrets of all music is achieved with very little effort; thus, this endeavor is not in vain. Furthermore, by stating it was created after consulting these authoritative scriptures, the author implies that wise seekers should accept this work as an authentic standard, as it is firmly rooted in tradition. || 15—20 ||

<term>(Ka.)</term> <note>This refers to the *Kalanidhi* commentary by Kallinatha</note> Now, regarding the vow: "The broad-minded author reveals the *Sangita Ratnakara* (The Ocean of Music)." In common worldly usage, the word **Music** <term>Sangita: traditionally encompassing vocal, instrumental, and dance</term> often brings to mind only singing as the primary subject of the book, but not...

# 14 Sangita-Ratnakara: [The Nature of Substances]

->**It is twofold: *Marga* [the Path] and *Deshi* [the Regional]. *Marga* is said to be that**<-
->**which was sought out by Brahma <gloss>1</gloss> and others, and performed by the sage Bharata and his followers. || 22 ||**<-
->**When performed before Lord Shiva, it bestows certain prosperity.**<-
->**But that which pleases the hearts of people in various regions according to their taste is *Deshi*. || 23 ||**<-

Wishing to resolve the doubt that "Sangita" might only refer to instrumental music and dance, the author explains the meaning of the word: **"Song, instrument..."** If only vocal music were meant to be discussed, he would have used only the word "Song" <note>original: *Gita*</note> rather than the word with the prefix "Sam-" <note>The prefix *sam-* in Sanskrit implies "together," "complete," or "perfect."</note>. Now, one might argue that the prefix is used merely to denote the "perfection" of the song; however, this is not the case. Since there is a specific definition stating, "A melodic arrangement of notes that is pleasing is called *Gita*," the perfection of the song is already established by the word *Gita* alone. 

When the prefix *Sam-* is used with the word for song, it does not add a new quality to the song itself. Instead, because it is a general term, it characterizes the connection of song with instrumental music and—as both of these find expression in it—with dance <gloss>2</gloss>. Therefore, wherever the word *Sangita* is used, one should understand that the "Triad of the Theater" <note>original: *tauryatrika*, referring to the triple symphony of voice, instrument, and dance</note> is intended. Occasionally, the word *Sangita* is used to refer to song alone; this is a figure of speech where a part is referred to by the name of the whole, much like how a piece of cloth might be called "clothing." || 21 ||

<term>(Su.)</term> <note>This refers to the *Sudhakara* commentary by King Simhabhupala</note> It has been stated that this "Treatise on Music" is being composed. In response to the question "What is this Sangita?", the author says: **"Song..."** An objection might be raised: "If Sangita refers only to the collection of the three, then each individual element—song, instrument, or dance—would not be 'Sangita'." This is not so, for the definition of the word *Sangita* applies to any one of the three—song, instrument, or dance—individually as well. || 21 ||

<term>(Ka.)</term> <note>This refers to the *Kalanidhi* commentary by Kallinatha</note> After declaring that music is of two types, *Marga* and *Deshi*, the author provides their definitions along with their etymologies: **"Marga, Deshi, and so on."** It is called *Marga* because it was "sought" <note>original: *margitattvat*; from the root *marg*, to seek</note>. This "seeking" was done by Brahma and the other gods. As it is said: "I shall create this Veda known as Theater, along with its history..."

---

<margin>1</margin> By Brahma <note>original: *Virinchi*</note> and others.
<margin>2</margin> By being manifested <note>original: *vyangyatvena*</note>.

It also provides a linguistic analysis of the word "Sangita," explaining why it encompasses the triad of song, instrument, and dance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introductory definitions of the Sangita-Ratnakara. Having defined the triad of music (song, instrument, and dance) and introduced the categories of Marga (celestial) and Deshi (regional), the author now focuses on why vocal music (Gita) is the most important of the three and details its divine origin in the Sama Veda.</meta>

# -Compendium: 1] First Chapter: On Musical Notes

->**Song, instrumental music, and dance: these [when performed for pleasure] are termed *Deshi* [Regional Music]. It is said that dance follows the instrument, and the instrument follows the song. || 24 ||**<-
->**Therefore, because of its primacy, song is explained here at the beginning. The Grandfather <gloss>Brahma</gloss> extracted this song from the *Sama Veda*. || 25 ||**<-

The author begins with the phrase "I will [explain]," and notes that these arts were created after searching through the four Vedas. The term *Margita* <note>original: *mārgitaḥ*</note> is a form derived from the verbal root *marg*—meaning "to search" or "to seek"—in the sense of a completed action. The word *Marga* [The Path/Celestial Music] is likewise derived from that same root. Regarding the term *Deshi* [Regional Music]: the word "region" <note>original: *desha*</note> refers here to the people who live in those various lands. It is a technical name given by the ancient Masters to the activities of singing and performing that are carried out by such people according to their own tastes and pleasures.

Since the term "music" <term>Sangita: the unified triad of song, instrument, and dance</term> applies to all three, and since dance is considered a limb of the theater, a question arises as to why they are presented in this specific order. To establish the primacy of song over the other two, the author cites authority: "One should perform the movements of the limbs according to the measure of the song and the instrument," and "Song is born from and colored by the four types of instruments; [yet] it is what is sung." Because the other two depend upon it, the author establishes the primacy of song and vows to explain it first, stating: "Dance follows the instrument..." || 22—24 ||

**(Su.)** <note>This refers to the *Sudhakara* commentary by Simhabhupala.</note> Having described the two-fold nature of music as *Marga* and *Deshi*, he explains the definition of *Marga*: "That which was sought." "Sought" means searched for or discovered. By this, the etymology of the word *Marga* is also indicated. He then provides the definition of *Deshi* and states the reason for describing song first. || 22—24 ||

**(Ka.)** <note>This refers to the *Kalanidhi* commentary by Kallinatha.</note> The author demonstrates that song is worthy of acceptance because of its Vedic nature, as it is a collection drawn from the *Sama Veda*. This relationship exists because song, like the Veda, is composed of musical notes <term>Svara: a musical note or pitch</term>. In the *Sama Veda*, there are seven notes known as: *Krushta* [High], *Prathama* [First], *Dvitiya* [Second], *Tritiya* [Third], *Chaturtha* [Fourth], *Mandra* [Low], and *Atisvarya* [Extremely Resonant]. In this system of music, however, these same notes are given names beginning with *Shadja* <note>The seven notes of the Indian scale: Shadja, Rishabha, Gandhara, Madhyama, Panchama, Dhaivata, and Nishada.</note> and so on, as appropriate. The implication is that even though the Creator <gloss>Brahma</gloss> extracted this from the Vedas, his purpose in creating this collection was to make it "accessible to all castes" <note>While the Vedas were traditionally restricted to certain groups, the arts were intended to be a "Fifth Veda" available to everyone.</note>. || 25 ||

<summary>This page establishes the hierarchy of the musical arts, placing vocal music (Gita) at the top because instrumental music and dance depend on it. It also traces the origins of musical notes to the Sama Veda and explains the etymological roots of Marga and Deshi music.</summary>
<keywords>Sangita, Gita, Veda, Brahma, Marga, Deshi, Svara, Shadja, Sama Veda, musical hierarchy</keywords>

# 1. The Compendium of Music: Section on Notes

->**By song, the All-Knowing Lord <gloss>Shiva</gloss>, the Consort of Parvati, is pleased. Even the Infinite One <gloss>Krishna</gloss>, the Lord of the Gopis, is brought under the spell of the sound of the flute. <note>original: "vamsha-dhvani-vasham gatah"</note> || 26 ||**<-

->**Brahma <gloss>the Creator</gloss> is devoted to the chanting of the *Sama Veda*, and Saraswati <gloss>Goddess of Wisdom</gloss> is attached to her *Veena* <note>The Veena is a traditional Indian plucked string instrument, often associated with divine music.</note>. What then can be said of others—be they celestial spirits, heavenly musicians, gods, demons, or humans? || 27 ||**<-

->**Even a tiny infant, lying in a cradle, who has never tasted the pleasures of the world, will stop crying and experience the height of joy upon drinking the nectar of song. || 28 ||**<-

->**How marvelous it is that even a beast of the forest, a young deer that feeds on grass, is so enchanted by the music of the hunter that it will surrender its very life. <note>This refers to the ancient Indian trope of hunters using melodic songs to lure and mesmerize deer.</note> || 29 ||**<-

->**Who is capable of praising the true greatness of this song? It is the one and only means for attaining the four goals of life: Virtue, Prosperity, Pleasure, and Liberation. <term>Purusharthas: the four fundamental aims of human existence—Dharma, Artha, Kama, and Moksha</term> || 30 ||**<-

---

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** The author explains that song has its source in the *Sama Veda* with the phrase "from the Sama Veda." The word *sanjagraha* means that the Creator stated it in a summarized form. [25]

**(Kalanidhi Commentary)** This art of song is to be embraced not merely because it is "Vedic" <note>meaning scriptural or sacred</note>, but because it has the power to manifest an inner bliss that dissolves all other thoughts. It is beloved by everyone, from the all-knowing Lord Shiva down to the simplest animals. [26–29]

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** The author describes the purpose of song starting with "By song." He praises song by mentioning the "unknowing" infant. Here, the word "enchanted" <note>original: *lubdha*</note> means "devoted to" or "infatuated," and "hunter" <note>original: *lubdhaka*</note> refers to one who stalks game. [26–29]

**(Kalanidhi Commentary)** Though there are specific, distinct methods for achieving Virtue, Prosperity, Pleasure, and Liberation, this single path—music—is the most beautiful and delightful way to reach them. Because of this, the author states that no one is truly capable of describing its full greatness.

# 1. Section on Notes
<meta>Chapter 1: Summary of contents</meta>

->In this first chapter, the Section on Notes, the following are presented:<-
->The nature of the body, the manifestation of sound, the locations of resonance, and the microtones; || 31 ||<-
->Then the seven pure notes, and these twelve modified ones,<-
->the lineages, the castes, the colors, the continents, the ancestral seers, and the presiding deities. || 32 ||<-

Regarding the phrase "of that" <note>This refers back to Verse 30, discussing "of that song."</note>: The fact that song is a means for achieving Virtue <term>Dharma: the moral and cosmic order</term> is established in the section on the Horse Sacrifice <note>The Ashvamedha is one of the most significant royal rituals of the Vedic period.</note> by the scripture which states: "Two Brahmins, singers of the *Veena*, should sing... another Brahmin should sing." This is further proved by the inclusion of song and related arts as integral parts of the worship of the gods. 

The fact that it is a means for Prosperity <term>Artha: worldly success and wealth</term> is seen through common experience in the world. Its role as a means for Pleasure <term>Kama: desire, sensory and aesthetic enjoyment</term> is established both by the Vedas, which state, "Therefore, women desire the one who sings," and by worldly observation. 

Finally, its role as a means for Liberation <term>Moksha: release from the cycle of rebirth</term> is confirmed—

> The one who knows the inner truth of playing the *Veena*, who is expert in microtones and melodic types, and who understands rhythm, travels the path to liberation without effort.

—according to the *Yajnavalkya Smriti* <note>An influential legal and ethical text of ancient India.</note>, and because it is said regarding songs such as the *Madraka* <note>An ancient form of structured song or hymn.</note> used in praise of Shiva: "The Creator ordained these for the praise of Shiva to lead to liberation." || 30 ||

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** Regarding "Virtue, Prosperity, etc.": Song sung for the purpose of worshipping the Supreme Lord is the cause of Virtue. As will be stated later regarding the proper execution of melodic types <term>Jatis: the ancient precursors to Ragas</term>: "Even the slayer of a Brahmin is purified of sin by these melodic types." Music is a means of Prosperity for those who live by song <note>This refers to professional musicians and court performers.</note>. It is a means for Pleasure because it serves as an "exciting determinant" <note>original: "uddipana-vibhava"</note> for the romantic sentiment <gloss>shringara</gloss>. The capacity for songs like the *Madraka* to lead to Liberation will also be discussed later. || 30 ||

**(Kalanidhi Commentary)** Desiring to summarize the topics of each chapter in this *Ratnakara* <gloss>Ocean of Music</gloss>, the author first pledges to present the topics in the Section on Notes, starting with "the body," through the verse beginning with "In this [Section on Notes]..." The intent is to show that "this much of a compendium of topics is being presented."

->The meters and ritual applications, the classes of microtones associated with the notes,<-
->the scales, the melodic modes, the tonal sequences—both pure and fragmentary—and their calculation; || 33 ||<-
->the permutations, the "mountain of fragments" table, and the methods for discovering lost or specific sequences;<-
