**Regarding the "Section on Notes"** <note>original: "Svaragatadhyaya"</note>: The phrase "pertaining to notes" <note>original: "svaragata"</note> refers to those things that follow or are associated with the notes. These are to be understood as the microtones, scales, modes, tonal sequences, melodic movements, ornaments, melodic types, song styles, and so on, which are discussed in this chapter. 

The word "Chapter" <term>Adhyaya: a division of a book</term> is derived from the root meaning "to study." Technically, it is formed with a suffix denoting an abstract state, meaning "the act of studying itself is a chapter." Alternatively, using different grammatical rules <note>Referring to the Sanskrit grammatical rule *Akartari cha karaka-samjnayam*, Pāṇini 3.3.19</note>, it can mean "that through which the intended meaning is studied" (the instrument) or "that in which the meaning is studied" (the location). 

Or, we might say that under the heading of "study" <note>prefix *adhi*</note>, the word for "going" <note>root *i*</note> becomes *aya*, and *aya* signifies the "comprehension of meaning." Therefore, a chapter is a book or section composed for the purpose of comprehending meaning. Or, *aya* refers to the meaning that is "gone toward" (attained), and the book concerned with that meaning is a chapter.

Now, a doubt might be raised: "Previously, you promised that the discussion of Song would take priority. But now, in this first 'Section on Notes,' you are prioritizing the discussion of the body and other such topics. Since the promise and the actual discussion cover different subjects, isn't there a contradiction?"

This is not a flaw. Because the body and other foundational topics are indirectly helpful to the production of song, explaining what pertains to the notes is, in another way, the explanation of song itself. Thus, there is no contradiction. Among the thirty topics mentioned—beginning with the body—the order of presentation for some is determined by their cause-and-effect relationship, while for others, the order is not strictly fixed. This point will be further clarified later. || 31–36 ||

# [Summary 1] First Chapter on Notes <term>Svaragatadhyaya</term>

->The rules for the fingers, and their various divisions such as "Even" <note>original: *yugma*</note> and so on;<-
->The cyclical repetitions <term>Parivarta</term>, the tempo <term>Laya</term>, the regulation of tempo <term>Yati</term>, and the ancient song-forms <term>Gitaka</term>. || 46 ||<-
->Songs such as the *Chandakas*, the collection of rhythmic components <note>original: *talanga*</note>,<-
->The limbs of songs <note>original: *gitanga*</note>, and the regional rhythms <term>Deshi-talas</term> will be told in their true essence. || 47 ||<-
->By the fearless Sharngadeva <note>Nishanka, meaning "the one without doubts," is a title for the author</note>, the mathematical permutations of rhythms <term>Pratyaya</term> will also be explained;<-
->In the sixth chapter, various kinds of musical instruments <note>original: *vadya*</note> will be discussed. || 48 ||<-
->In the seventh, dancing <note>original: *nartanam*</note>, as well as the various aesthetic flavors <term>Rasa</term> and emotional states <term>Bhava</term>, in their proper order. ||<-

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** He explains the summary of the subject matter for the fifth chapter with the words: "In the Chapter on Rhythm" <term>Taladhyaya</term>. The ancient rhythms <term>Marga-talas</term> are those like the *Chaccatputa*. The "Units" <term>Kalas</term> are the silent actions of time-keeping. The "Beats" <term>Patas</term> are the actions performed with sound. The "Paths" <term>Margas</term> are the four types beginning with *Dhruva*. The "Eight-fold Units" are also those starting with *Dhruva*. "Rotation" <term>Parivarta</term> refers to the repetition of a foot-segment or rhythmic section. "Tempo" <term>Laya</term> is the duration of time that exists between rhythmic actions. "Regulation" <term>Yati</term> is the rule that governs the flow or tendency of that tempo. The "Songs" <term>Gitas</term> refer to the seven ancient forms like *Madraka*. The "Regional Rhythms" <term>Deshi-talas</term> are the one hundred and twenty varieties, beginning with *Adi-tala*. Those methods by which the quantity and nature of a rhythm are realized are called "Permutations" <term>Pratyayas</term>, such as expanding a rhythm <term>Prastara</term>, finding a lost rhythmic structure <term>Nashta</term>, or identifying a specific rhythmic pattern by its number <term>Uddishta</term>. || 44—47 ||

**(Kalanidhi Commentary)** He notes that in the sixth chapter, musical instruments of four types (stringed instruments and so on) are discussed according to their many sub-varieties: "In the sixth, various kinds..." In the seventh, he mentions the topics to be established: "In the seventh..." "Dancing" <term>Nartanam</term> is a general term used here to include dramatic acting <term>Natya</term>, representational dance <term>Nritya</term>, and pure rhythmic dance <term>Nritta</term>, all of which are forms of limb movement. "Various aesthetic flavors and states": The aesthetic flavors <term>Rasas</term> are the nine, beginning with the Erotic <term>Shringara</term>. The "States" <term>Bhavas</term> are of five kinds, including the determinants <term>Vibhavas</term> and others. "In order" means according to the sequence in which they were first listed. || 48, 48 ||

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** He states the summary of contents for the sixth and seventh chapters: "In the sixth..." || 48, 48 ||

->Thus ends the first section, called the Summary of Subject Matter, in the first chapter, the Chapter on Notes. || 1 ||<-

### Section Two: The Genesis of the Human Body <term>Pindotpatti-prakaranam</term>

->Song is composed of sound; instrumental music is celebrated for the manifestation of that sound.<-
->Dance follows both of these; therefore, this triad<gloss>1</gloss> is dependent on sound. || 1 ||<-
->Through sound, the syllable is manifested; from the syllable, the word; from the word, speech.<-
->Through speech, all the affairs of this world are conducted; therefore, the whole world is dependent on sound. || 2 ||<-
->Sound is said to be of two types<gloss>2</gloss>: "Struck" <term>Ahata</term> and "Unstruck" <term>Anahata</term>.<-
->This sound manifests within the body; therefore, the body will now be described. || 3 ||<-

**(Kallinatha's Commentary)** One might ask: "Since sound <term>Nada</term> is the primary cause of song, the nature of notes <term>Svara</term> should be explained first. Why bother with a description of the human body?" Anticipating this doubt, the author explains that sound cannot manifest without a body. To resolve this, he begins describing the body with the phrase "Song is composed of sound." This is the point: not only are song, instrumental music, and dance dependent on sound, but since all human interaction is rooted in speech—which itself depends on sound—the body, which serves as the foundation for that sound, must be described first. || 1–3 ||

**(Simhabhupala's Commentary)** Having thus provided a summary of the contents, the author now praises sound in order to describe the body—the place where sound is manifested—beginning with "Song is...". "Composed of sound" means that sound is its "soul" or its very essence. Instrumental music, such as that played on the *Vina* <note>a plucked string instrument</note>, is praised or attains its beauty through the manifestation of sound. Dance follows "both of these" <note>song and instruments</note>, because it is said that "one should support the song with the movement of the limbs." Therefore, the "triad"—meaning the three forms of song, dance, and instrumental music—is dependent on or requires sound. || Not only do song, dance, and instrumental music depend on sound, but the entire world does, as he states with "Through sound...". Through sound (as audible tone), syllables like "ka" and others are made manifest. What is this sound? It is that which reaches the path of the ear from a distance before specific syllables are recognized, and which imparts qualities such as softness or loudness to the syllables; that is what is called "sound." From the syllable comes the "word," such as "pot" <note>original: *ghata*</note>. From the word comes "speech," which is a sentence consisting of a collection of words...

<gloss>2</gloss> or: "in two ways."

# Chapter One: On Notes

->There exists Brahman, the essence of consciousness and bliss, self-luminous and stainless.<-
->The Lord, also called the Sign<gloss>lingam; the point where the universe dissolves</gloss>, without a second, unborn, and all-pervasive. || 4 ||<-
->Changeless, formless, the Lord of all, and eternal.<-

...from speech. From the sentence comes the word, and from the word comes this worldly behavior. Therefore, the entire world is dependent on sound. Matanga also stated in the *Brihaddeshi*<note>original: "Bṛhaddeśī"; an influential 6th–9th century text on music</note>:

> "Without sound, there is no song; without sound, there are no notes.
> Without sound, there is no dance; therefore, the world is sound-natured.
> Brahma is said to be the form of sound; Vishnu<note>original: "Janārdana"</note> is the form of sound.
> The Supreme Power <term>Shakti</term> is the form of sound; the Great Lord Shiva<note>original: "Maheśvara"</note> is the form of sound.
> Regarding the 'Abode of Brahman' <term>Brahma-sthana</term> and what is known as the 'Knot of Brahma' <term>Brahma-granthi</term><note>A yogic center in the body, usually located near the navel or heart</note>,
> Breath <term>Prana</term> resides within them; from that breath, fire is born.
> From the union of fire and wind, sound is produced.
> From sound, the point <term>Bindu</term> is born, and from that, all speech."

The author now describes the two types of sound: "Struck" <term>Ahata</term>. Both types of sound manifest and become apparent within the "pot" <note>a common metaphor for the human body</note>. || 1–3 ||

**(Kallinatha's Commentary)** That body is subject to the actions <term>Karma</term> of the soul. Since the soul being investigated seeks its own source, Brahman, the author defines its nature now that it is being inquired upon, starting with: "There exists Brahman." "Consciousness and bliss" means the nature of knowledge and happiness. "Self-luminous" means shining by its own light. "Stainless" means without any coating or impurity. "Lord" means independent. "The Sign" <term>Lingam</term> because it is where the world dissolves <note>original: "prapañca-layanāl-liṅgam"</note>. "Without a second" means lacking any other entity similar to itself. "Unborn" means without birth. "All-pervasive" means all-encompassing. "Changeless" means it is free from the six states of being: being born, existing, growing, changing, decaying, and perishing...

[Commentary]: [The previous description means] free from modifications <note>original: "vikārāḥ"; refers to the six changes of state: birth, existence, growth, maturity, decay, and death</note>. Formless means devoid of physical shape. Lord of All means the creator of the entire world. Eternal means without destruction. All-powerful means endowed with the powers of will, knowledge, action, and enjoyment. All-knowing means the knower of all things—past, future, and present. This is the "Brahman" spoken of in the Upanishads <note>Ancient philosophical texts that form the theoretical basis of Hinduism</note>. Having described the nature of Brahman, the author now describes the individual souls <term>Jiva</term> through their identity with It and their connection to the body, using the phrase "those known as its parts." They are "parts" or portions of that Brahman. || 4, 5 ||

->Limited by beginningless ignorance, like sparks from a fire,<-
->they are differentiated by beginningless actions, like fire is divided by its fuel. || 6 ||<-

**The Nectar of Logic <term>Sudhakara</term>**
[Commentary]: Having promised to describe the nature of the body, the author now states its root cause with the word "There exists." This means it exists at all times and in all places; it is eternal and pervasive. The word Brahman is used because of its "greatness" <note>original: "bṛhattvāt"</note> or its "power to expand" <note>original: "bṛṃhaṇatvāt"</note>. It is of the nature of pure consciousness and bliss, according to the scripture <term>Shruti</term>: "Brahman is knowledge and bliss." It is "Self-luminous," meaning it shines by its own light, as the scripture says: "When He shines, everything shines after Him; by His light all this is illumined."

The word "Stainless" <term>Niranjana</term> means free from the smear of ignorance <term>Avidya</term>, because ignorance resides in the individual soul. Even if one argues that ignorance resides in Brahman, the term "Stainless" suggests it does not delude its own source. "The Lord" <term>Ishvara</term> is He who is capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise. The "Sign" <term>Lingam</term> refers to the primary cause. "Without a second" means it is free from the three types of difference <note>original: "sajātīya-vijātīya-svagata-bheda"; differences between members of the same species, different species, or within the parts of a single object</note>. "Unborn" means it has no prior cause. "All-pervasive" means it is either widespread or capable of all things. "Changeless" means it is free from all modifications mentioned by the grammarian Yaska <note>An ancient linguist (c. 6th-5th century BCE) who defined the six stages of existence</note>, such as being born, existing, growing, maturing, decaying, and perishing.

"Formless" means not limited by a physical body. "Lord of All" means the ruler even of beings like Brahma <note>The creator god, distinct from the abstract Brahman</note>. "Eternal" means indestructible. "All-powerful" means that within Him exists the power called Illusion <term>Maya</term>, which is the cause of the entire manifested universe. "All-knowing" means possessing direct perception of all objects. "Its parts" means they are not different from It, just as sparks of fire are not different from the fire itself in their essence as heat. Alternatively, following the aphorism "The soul is a part, because of the mention of variety," the author accepts the view that the individual soul and the Supreme Soul share a relationship of part and whole. || 4–5 ||

**The Moon of Art <term>Kalanidhi</term>**
"Limited by beginningless ignorance": Beginningless ignorance refers to "Primal Ignorance" <term>Mula-avidya</term>, which is essentially the lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of the Foundation (Brahman). Those who are "limited" or defined by that ignorance are called "individual souls" <term>Jiva</term>. For an entity whose true nature is Existence, Consciousness, Bliss, and Pervasiveness, the condition of ignorance acts as a limiting factor...

# CHAPTER ONE: SOUND AND NOTES
### [2. THE GENESIS OF THE BODY—CONTINUED]

->Controlled by merit and demerit, which yield pleasure and pain,<-
->they attain a body of a specific species, a lifespan, and experiences born of action. || 7 ||<-
->In every birth they obtain these; yet they possess another [form] as well:<-
->the subtle body <term>linga-sharira</term>, which is held to be imperishable until final liberation. || 8 ||<-
->The wise know this [subtle body] to consist of the subtle elements, senses, vital breaths, and states.<-
->The Unborn Lord creates this world for the experience of individual souls. || 9 ||<-
->That Soul, the Supreme Soul, then withdraws the world to provide rest.<-
->This cycle of creation and dissolution is accepted as a beginningless flow. || 10 ||<-

**The Nectar of Logic <term>Sudhakara</term>**
[Commentary]: The designation "individual soul" <term>Jiva</term> is a result of ignorance <term>Avidya</term>. It is caused by superimposing certain qualities—such as being a sufferer, being limited, or having partial knowledge—onto that which is actually pure being and all-knowing. To explain this, the author provides an analogy: **"as sparks from a fire."** The word "parts" should be understood here. Just as sparks of fire—which is essentially light—are designated as "parts" when they are limited by external conditions <term>upadhi</term> <note>A limiting adjunct or "container" that makes the infinite appear finite, like a jar limiting the space inside it</note> such as wood, grass, or gems <gloss>1</gloss>, so too are these souls.

Regarding the phrase **"by those actions"**: This refers to the individual souls. They are governed by actions <term>karma</term> in the form of merit <term>punya</term> and demerit <term>papa</term>, which respectively grant pleasure and pain. That meritorious actions grant pleasure is known from Scripture <term>Shruti</term>: "He indeed causes him to perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds." That sinful actions grant pain is also from Scripture: "He indeed causes him to perform bad deeds whom He wishes to lead downward." 

Regarding the phrase **"beginningless"**: Because ignorance—the limiting condition that makes the Soul appear as an individual—is beginningless, the actions performed by that soul are also considered beginningless. This follows the logic that "individuals colored by their mental impressions belong to a single continuous origin." 

**"Controlled"** means being bound. In every birth, they obtain a body belonging to a specific species (such as being human), a lifespan, and experiences born of their past actions. By saying "controlled by actions," it is established that the attainment of a body is entirely a result of one's own past deeds.

# CHAPTER ONE: SOUND AND NOTES
### [2. THE GENESIS OF THE BODY—CONTINUED]

The adjective **"born of action"** <term>karmajam</term> is used here to state that the agency of individual souls is fixed and necessary regarding worldly activities performed in this life that yield visible results, such as agriculture and similar labors. The text states **"they possess"**; this refers to those souls who are currently limited by a physical, "gross" body. Besides that physical body, there is **"another"**—a subtle, unmanifest "sign-body" <term>linga-sharira</term>. This is established by sacred scriptures which state, **"The person is the size of a thumb."** <note>original: "angushtha-matrah purushah" — a famous Upanishadic description of the soul residing in the heart.</note> 

This subtle body is considered **"imperishable"** in the sense that it lasts until liberation—that is, until the final realization of one's true nature. It is indestructible because the soul's own ignorance <term>avidya</term> and its latent impressions <term>vasana</term> have not yet been severed. This subtle body consists of the subtle elements, the senses, and the vital breaths. Specifically: 
*   **The elements:** Earth and the others in their subtle forms.
*   **The senses:** Sight and the others.
*   **The breaths:** The five vital airs, beginning with <term>Prana</term>.

The nature of this subtle body is the "collection" or assembly of these unmanifest forms alongside the internal sense, which is the **mind**. 

Some thinkers maintain that **"the world was never unlike this,"** <note>A reference to the Mimamsa school of philosophy, which argues the universe is eternal and was never created.</note> accepting the eternity of the world as a continuous flow. To refute that view, the author describes how the Supreme Soul is the actual agent of the world’s creation and dissolution for a specific purpose. He says, **"For [the souls]"**: the world—composed of elements and the objects made from them—exists for the **"experience"** (the feeling of pleasure and pain) of those individual souls who identify with the two types of bodies (physical and subtle) mentioned before. 

The **"Unborn"** <term>Ajah</term> is the Supreme Soul. The word "Supreme" implies that he has attained the status of Lord <term>Ishwara</term> in relation to the lower individual souls. "That Soul" refers back to the previously mentioned Brahman. The word "and" indicates a sequence: he creates, and he also **"withdraws"** (dissolves) the world. After the world has existed for a time, he dissolves it for the sake of **"rest"**—this should be understood as being for the benefit of the souls, since both creation and dissolution are for their sake. To show that souls are beginningless, he describes the two processes as a **"beginningless flow."** While a specific cycle of creation has a beginning, the "series" or "flow" <term>pravaha</term> is eternal. || 6—10 ||

**The Nectar of Logic <term>Sudhakara</term>**
[Commentary]: One might object: "This is a flawed analogy. Sparks are different from fire because they possess contradictory qualities like being large or small." To answer this, the author says: **"wood and so on."** The phrase "and so on" includes the fuel of the fire, or even the different conditions of fire, such as lightning or fire in water <note>A reference to "submarine fire" or volcanic heat.</note>. Therefore, the "difference" seen in sparks is caused by external conditions <term>upadhi</term> and is not an essential, ultimate difference. 

He then explains how these souls are bound by their actions: **"they [are bound] by actions."** Now, if Brahman...

# [2. THE GENESIS OF THE BODY—CONTINUED]

### These souls are not distinct from the Self, nor is the world distinct from the Self. 
### While creating through His Power, He remains non-different, just as gold remains gold in the form of an earring. || 11 || 
### Others say He creates through Ignorance, just as a rope [appears to be] a snake.

As for the question of how distinct souls are bound by the bondage of action <term>karma</term>, the text says: **"By beginningless..."** Those souls, in every birth, attain a body, a lifespan, and experiences produced by the activity of their past actions, associated with various species—such as being human, a cow, and so on—appropriate to those respective births. 

Now, if souls are tied to a physical "gross" body, how can they attain multiple births, given that the physical body is seen to perish? To this, he says: **"They have another..."** <note>original: "teṣām asty aparam"</note> This refers to the period until liberation <term>moksha</term>, taking liberation as the final boundary. To the question of what kind of thing this "sign-body" <term>linga-sharira</term> is, he says: **"Subtle..."** It consists of the five subtle elements and the eleven senses; thus, it is the "body of sixteen parts." <note>The sixteen parts are the 5 elements of perception (earth, water, fire, air, ether), the 5 senses of perception, the 5 organs of action, and the mind.</note>

But what is the purpose of the Supreme Lord’s creation and destruction of the world? To this, he says: **"For the sake of the souls."** Since both the souls and the Lord are beginningless, this line of questioning does not apply. He says: **"This very thing..."** The combination of creation and destruction is accepted as a **"beginningless flow"** <term>pravaha-anaditva</term>. || 6—10 ||

**(Kallinatha)** Having explained the non-difference of the individual souls and the Self through the relationship of "part and whole," the author now explains the non-difference of the world and the Self through the relationship of "cause and effect," following the doctrine of **"difference-in-non-difference"** <term>bhedabheda</term> with an illustration: **"These souls,"** etc. This Self, while creating the world through His **"Power"**—His inherent power of action—is non-different from it. By changing the grammatical case, the word "world" should be understood as connected here. This means there is an identity <term>tadatyam</term> between them, just as there is between gold and an earring. As they say:

> "In the form of the effect, there is manifoldness; in the form of the cause, there is non-difference. 
> Just as there is non-difference in the nature of gold, there is difference in the nature of earrings and such." <note>original: "kāryarūpeṇa nānātvam abhedaḥ kāraṇātmanā..."</note>

Now, relying on the primary Non-Dualist <term>Vedantin</term> view, he says: **"He creates..."** etc. **"Others"** refers to other Non-Dualists. **"Through Ignorance"** <term>avidya</term> means through the lack of knowledge of the underlying substratum. The illustration for this is: **"Just as a rope [appears to be] a snake."** By this, he shows that the world is a **"transformation of Brahman"** <term>brahma-vivarta</term>, meaning it appears as something other than what it truly is, without actually changing its essence. || 11, 11- ||

# [2. THE GENESIS OF THE BODY—CONTINUED]

### From the Self first came Space, from that Air, and from that Fire. || 12 ||
### From Fire came Water, and from that Earth was born. 
### These are the great elements; they are the body of the Radiant One, the expansive Creator. || 13 ||

(Sudhakara) Regarding the question of whether the Supreme Lord is different or non-different from the world, the text says: **"Like light."** While creating the world through His power, the Supreme Lord <note>original: "asau parameśvaraḥ"</note> is not distinct. Through what kind of power? Like light, it is both different and non-different from the Self. Just as light is said to be different from the sun—as in "the sun’s light"—it is also described as non-different, as in "the sun is light." 

He gives another example: **"Gold."** Gold is non-different from an earring in its essence as gold, yet different in its specific form as an earring. According to the view of the followers of Non-dualism <term>Vedanta</term>, he describes the world as a product of Ignorance <term>avidya</term> by saying: **"He creates."** Just as a rope, due to one's own ignorance, "creates" an imagined snake (thinking "this is a snake"), so too the Supreme Lord creates the world of space and other elements through the ignorance of His own nature as the underlying reality <term>adhishthana</term>. || 11, 11- ||

(Kallinatha) He describes the physical body <term>pinda</term> and its various divisions through the sequence of the creation of the elements, beginning with: **"From the Self, first..."** This means that from the Self, who is the ultimate cause, Space <term>akasha</term> was produced "first"—that is, before air and the other elements. The word "then" <note>original: "tataḥ"</note> refers back to Space; from that Space, acting as the cause, Air was produced. **"From that, Fire"**—here too, it means Fire was born from Air. 

Thus says the Scripture <term>shruti</term>: "From the Self, Space was born; from Space, Air," and so on. <note>This is a famous passage from the Taittiriya Upanishad, 2.1.1, detailing the "chain of creation."</note> These elements—Space and the others—are the "great elements" <term>mahabhutas</term>. The connection is that this is the **"body"** of the Radiant One <term>Viraj</term>, which is the expansive Creator <term>Brahman</term> when associated with the great elements. 

The word **"this"** <note>original: "eṣā"</note> is used to point to something present before us, because the collection of elements is perceptible to all people in the world. Regarding the **"Radiant One"**: the Self, having created the great elements and entered into them, is called the "Radiant One" <term>Viraj</term> because of His identification with them. In the phrase "these [elements] are this body," the use of different grammatical genders is explained by the rule: "Pronouns establishing the identity between a subject and a predicate may take the gender of either," thus justifying the linguistic structure of the verse. || 12, 13 ||

<summary>This page outlines the Vedic cosmology of the five elements—Space, Air, Fire, Water, and Earth—explaining how they evolve from the Self to form the cosmic body of the Creator.</summary>
<keywords>Cosmology, Five Elements, Mahabhuta, Viraj, Brahman, Vedanta, Creation, Atman</keywords>

29 | The Ocean of Music <term>Sangita Ratnakara</term>
# [1. THE CHAPTER ON THE SELF]
## [2. THE GENESIS OF THE BODY—CONTINUED]

### The Supreme Reality created the Creator-God and, having bestowed the Vedas upon him, caused the material world to be created from the words of those Vedas. || 14 ||

### By His command, the Creator-God produced the Lords of Beings <term>Prajapatis</term> through the power of mind alone. From them, the creation of physical bodies through seed is described. || 15 ||

### Physical bodies are of four kinds, based on their origin: from sweat, from the earth, from a womb, or from an egg. Lice and similar creatures come from sweat; vines and plants spring from the earth; || 16 ||

### Humans and other mammals come from the womb, and birds and similar creatures from the egg.

(Sudhakara) He explains the sequence of creation beginning with the phrase: **"From the Self."** He states that the body of the Cosmic Being <term>Virat</term> is composed of the five great elements: **"The great elements..."** || 12, 13 ||

(Kallinatha) Regarding the verse **"The Supreme Reality created the Creator-God"**: The Supreme Reality, in the form of the Cosmic Being <term>Virat</term>, created the four-faced Creator-God <note>original: "Brahmanam"</note>. Furthermore, that Supreme Reality gave the Vedas—the *Rig Veda* and others—to that four-faced Creator. Here, the Supreme is the "instigating agent" while the Creator-God is the "direct agent" who performs the work. Through the **"words of the Vedas"**—for the Veda is defined as that through which virtue and vice are known <note>original: "vedyete anena dharmādharmāviti vedaḥ"</note>—the material world was created. These Vedic words act as names for the archetypal forms; they serve as the "reminders" of the objects that existed in previous cosmic cycles <note>The text suggests that creation is a recurring cycle, and the Vedas provide the blueprint from the last cycle.</note>. Thus, he caused the creation of the physical realm—the body, the senses, and so on—made of the five gross elements. || 14 ||

(Sudhakara) One might ask: "It is common knowledge that the Golden Embryo <term>Hiranyagarbha</term> is the creator of the world; why then is the Supreme Lord called the creator?" To this, he says: **"The Supreme Reality."** The Supreme Lord created the Golden Embryo <term>Hiranyagarbha</term> and, having given him the Vedas, brought forth the material universe—that is, He inspired the Creator-God to create. The phrase **"From the words of the Vedas"** implies that He created by first recalling the Vedic words <note>original: "lyablope pañcamī"</note>. This is supported by scripture <term>shruti</term>: "He who fashioned the Creator-God in the beginning and who delivered the Vedas to him." Consequently, the Golden Embryo is the "direct agent," while the Supreme Lord is the "instigating agent." || 14 ||

(Kallinatha) He describes the sequence of material creation from the four-faced Creator, who is the direct agent: **"By His command."** This refers to the command of the Cosmic Being <term>Virat</term>. From those Lords of Beings <term>Prajapatis</term> came the creation "through seed," referring to forms produced from the transformation of reproductive fluid.

->Among these, the human body is described here because of its utility for musical sound <term>Nada</term>. || 17 ||<-

->The soul <term>Kshetrajna</term>, residing in space, comes from space into the air; from the air into smoke, then into mist, and from mist it abides in the clouds. || 18 ||<-

***

By the word **"seed,"** the **"blood"** is also implied. **"Born from sweat"** etc. refers to an easily understood meaning. The phrase **"lice and others"** is a grammatical compound <note>original: "bahuvrīhi"</note> indicating a group where lice are the first example. || 15–16 ||

(Sudhakara) In response to the question, "What did the Creator create?", he says: **"By His command."** This refers to Daksha and the other Lords of Beings <term>Prajapatis</term>. In response to "What was produced from them?", he says: **"From them, however."** This refers to the **"seed-born"** creation produced from reproductive fluid. He then describes the fourfold nature of bodies: **"Born from sweat,"** etc. In response to "What is produced from what?", he says: **"Lice and others."** || 15, 16 ||

(Kallinatha) Among the four types of bodies mentioned, why focus only on the human? Plants and similar life forms are excluded because they are non-conscious; lice and similar creatures are excluded because they are too minute; birds and similar beings are excluded because they lack the complete system of essential tissues <term>dhatus</term> and energy channels <term>nadis</term>. Even among those born from a womb, such as animals, while they possess the full system of tissues and channels, they lack the capacity for articulate speech <note>original: "uccāraṇa-śakti"</note> due to their horizontal posture and nature. By the process of elimination, only the human body is useful for musical sound. Therefore, he states that its origin is now being determined with the words: **"Among these."** || 17 ||

(Sudhakara) He explains the reason for describing the human body specifically among all those forms with the phrase: **"Among these."** || 17 ||

(Kallinatha) Regarding the human body, he describes the descent of the soul <term>Jiva</term> into the womb through a sequence beginning with space, starting from the verse **"The soul, residing in space"** and ending with the phrase **"entering the womb."** The "Field" <term>Kshetra</term> refers to the body. The "Knower of the Field" <term>Kshetrajna</term> is the soul who knows this body through the sense of "I am" or "this is mine." As was said by the Lord <note>referring to Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita</note>:

> "This body, O son of Kunti, is called the Field;
> he who knows it is called the Knower of the Field by those who understand such things."

३१ | [Genesis 2] First Chapter: The Chapter on Notes

->Nourished by the oblation, the Sun, which has absorbed the essence of the earth with its rays during summer, deposits that concentrated fluid into the cloud; the rain-cloud then holds it. || 19 ||<-

->When it rains, the soul descends with the rain to the earth; it then enters the trees and medicinal herbs that grow from the earth, remaining unobserved. || 20 ||<-

->From these plants, food is produced. That food, consumed by men, is transformed into semen. This is then infused into the "temple of love" <note>the womb or reproductive organ</note> of a woman whose menstrual fluid is pure. || 21 ||<-

->If this semen, being pure, enters the womb along with the pure menstrual fluid...<-

It is said that a cloud <note>original: "abhra"</note> is a collection of smoke, light, and air; when it contains water, it is specifically called a rain-cloud <note>original: "megha"</note>. Regarding the phrase **"by the oblation"**: an oblation <term>āhuti</term> refers to the materials like fuel-sticks and clarified butter offered into the fire by sacrificers using sacred chants for the sake of the deities. The Sun <term>Bhānu</term>, having been nourished and satisfied by this, absorbs the essence <note>moisture/water</note> from the earth with its rays during the summer. **"Concentrated fluid"** means water. The soul enters the **"trees and herbs born from the earth"**—this is the grammatical connection. It is **"unobserved"** because it is invisible to the eyes. **"From these"** refers to the medicinal herbs. **"Food"** <note>original: "annam"</note> refers to that which is eaten, such as cooked rice. When men eat this food, it becomes the reproductive seed. **"Of a woman whose menstrual fluid is pure"**: "menstrual fluid" <term>ārtava</term> refers to the reproductive blood. It is described as having the "appearance of liquid lac or rabbit’s blood, and which leaves no stain when washed." This defines pure menstrual fluid. Regarding the phrase **"if it is pure"**: semen <term>śukra</term> is also defined by the authorities as "strong, white, heavy, oily, sweet, and abundant; appearing like clarified butter, honey, or oil; it is fit for conception." Regarding the **"action of the soul"**: semen does not begin the formation of an embryo simply by entering the womb. Rather, it is "impelled by the soul’s karma"—meaning it is driven by the past actions <term>prārabdha karma</term> of the soul that is about to inhabit the new body. It is joined with the activity necessary for physical existence. Here, the word **"embryo"** <term>garbha</term> refers to the combination of semen and menstrual fluid that has entered the womb as the material cause of the body. || 18–22 ||

(Sudhakara) He explains the method of origin: **"The knower of the field."** The "knower of the field" <term>Kṣetrajña</term> is the self or soul. A "cloud-fragment" <note>original: "abhra"</note> refers to a piece of cloud that does not rain, while a "cloud" <note>original: "megha"</note> is one that does rain. Now, one might ask how water gets into the cloud—

### The Ocean of Music [The Chapter on the Body—

->Driven by the soul's past actions <term>karma</term>, it then begins the formation of the embryo. || 22 ||<-
->In the first month, a liquid state called *kalala* <term>a jelly-like embryonic stage</term> is produced.<-
->In the second month, there is a solid mass <gloss>1</gloss>, a fleshy knot, or a slightly firm swelling. || 23 ||<-
->These are the preceding stages, respectively, for males, females, and the neuter.<-
->In the third month, five sprouts are recognized: the two hands, the two feet, and the head. || 24 ||<-

---

The author says—**"By the oblation."** Nourished—meaning satiated or satisfied—by the oblation <term>āhuti</term> prescribed in sacrifices and other rituals, the Sun <term>Bhānu</term>, having absorbed the essence <note>moisture</note> with its rays, deposits that concentrated fluid into the cloud. Regarding the entry of the soul into medicinal herbs along with the water rained from the clouds, he says—**"in the rain-cloud."** Regarding the soul's entry into the womb from the herbs via food and semen, he says—**"from these"** [referring to verses 18–22].

(Kallinātha) In the manner described, starting from the first month and continuing until the ninth, the author shows the different states of the embryo residing in the womb, beginning with the words **"a liquid state."** **"Called *kalala*"** means that which has the name *kalala*. *Kalala* <note>original: "kalalam"</note> refers to the fluid state of the combination of semen and menstrual blood which has not yet attained firmness. **"In the second"**: a **"solid mass"** <term>piṇḍa</term> is the early state of a male to be born; a **"fleshy knot"** <term>peśī</term> is the early state of a female to be born; and a **"slightly firm swelling"** <term>arbuda</term> is the early state of a neuter being to be born. This is the sequence. **"Solid"** means possessing hardness; a **"fleshy knot"** is square-shaped and consisting mostly of muscle; **"slightly firm"** is described as such because it occupies a middle ground between the solid mass and the fleshy knot. An **"arbuda"** is shaped like the bud of a Silk-Cotton tree <term>Śālmali</term>. As the ancient authorities say:

> "A *peśī* is known to be square, while a *piṇḍa* is known as a solid sphere; 
> physicians recognize an *arbuda* by its resemblance to the bud of the Silk-Cotton tree."

**"In the third"**: From the aforementioned solid mass and other forms, the **"hands, feet, and head"** appear. The term "hands, feet, and head" <note>original: "kara-aṅghri-śirasaḥ"</note> is treated as a single collective unit in the grammar because they are parts of a living being.

->At that same time, all major limbs and minor parts appear in subtle form,<-
->excepting the beard, teeth, and such, which emerge after birth.¹ || 25 ||<-
->This is the natural state; any other is considered a modification by the wise.<-

Regarding the **"Sprouts"**: Even as the sprouts are just beginning to form, they are already considered the hands, feet, and head. This designation is used because the author is speaking of the limbs that are intended to be there, following the **logic of the thread and the cloth** <term>sūtra-śāṭaka-nyāya</term> <note>A philosophical principle where a finished product's name is applied to its materials; just as one might point to threads on a loom and call them "a cloth," the early sprouts are called "limbs" because that is their destiny.</note>. "At the same time" refers to the stage when these sprouts appear.

**"Major limbs and minor parts"**: Within the "sprout" of the head, the parts such as the neck, eyes, nose, and ears exist. In the two sprouts of the hands, there are the parts including the elbows, wrists, and fingers. In the sprouts of the feet, there are the thighs, knees, shins, ankles, and toes. These are "subtle," meaning they exist in an unmanifest or microscopic form.

**"This is the natural state"**: The production of these major and minor parts in subtle form during the sprout stage—excluding things like the beard and teeth which are only produced after birth—is called **Nature** <term>prakṛti</term>. This is the universal nature of all creatures born from a womb.

**"Any other is a modification"**: **Modification** <term>vikṛti</term> <note>original: "vikṛtiḥ"; refers here to congenital anomalies or deviations from the biological norm.</note> refers to cases where the beard or teeth appear prematurely at the same time as the limbs, or when certain limbs fail to form, or form in the wrong place, or when the number of fingers is more or less than the norm.

**"In the fourth"**: This refers to the **distinctness** of those major and minor parts—their differentiation and individual clarity. There is also the distinctness of the **dispositions** <term>bhāva</term>, such as bravery and other internal qualities of the soul, which were previously dormant and now become manifest. || 23–27 ||

(Su.) <note>Abbreviation for the commentator Simhabhūpāla</note> The author describes the specific states of the fetus month by month with the word **"Liquidity."** He explains the preceding states for males, females, and the neuter respectively with the words **"In the second."** A mass resembling a muscle <term>peśī</term> indicates a male; a hard mass indicates a female; and a tumor-like <term>arbuda</term> or soft mass indicates a neuter state. Regarding the phrase "beard, teeth, and such," the word "such" refers to...

### Saṅgītaratnākara [Section on the Origin of the Body]

<margin>Skin and memory</margin>

->Meditating on the means of liberation, the fetus remains dedicated to spiritual practice.<-
->In the eighth month, skin and memory are perfected, as is the vital essence that resides in the heart. || 36 ||<-
->This essence is pure, yellowish-red, and is considered the very cause of life. It moves restlessly, running from the mother to the fetus and back again. || 37 ||<-
->Therefore, a child born in the eighth month does not survive, being devoid of this vital essence. Any brief survival is like the twitching of a severed limb due to residual momentum. || 38 ||<-
->The time for birth occurs from the ninth month onward. Another vessel, called the *para*, is connected to the mother's nutrient-carrying channel. || 39 ||<-

**[Commentary]**
Out of a desire to abandon the cycle of rebirth <note>original: saṃsāra-jihāsayā</note>, there is repeated contemplation of the Self. 

**"In the eighth"**: Regarding the phrase "skin and memory appear": although skin and memory exist in the seventh month as well, here it means the skin becomes thick and memory becomes a subject of mental deliberation. One can also infer that the <term>vital essence</term> <note>original: ojas</note> appears. This essence is the refined "sap" of the reproductive fluid. This vital essence resides in the heart; it is "pure," meaning it is not afflicted by corrupted bodily humors like wind (*vayu*). It is described as "yellowish-red," meaning slightly yellow and red in color. The text implies it is the cause or primary reason for "life," or the maintenance of the life-breath.

That vital essence is "restless," meaning it does not stay in one place but runs repeatedly between the mother and the fetus. This was stated by the master <note>original: Vāgbhaṭācārya; an influential ancient Indian physician and author of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayam</note>: "The vital essence circulates in the eighth month, moving between mother and son repeatedly in sequence." 

Because the essence is unstable in the eighth month, a child born then "does not live." This does not refer to the entire duration of the month; rather, it means that if the child is born at the moment the vital essence has left the fetus and moved into the mother, the child dies from being <term>devoid of vital essence</term> <note>original: ojasojjhita</note>. Conversely, if the essence leaves the mother and moves to the fetus, the mother does not survive the birth. If birth occurs exactly during the transit of the essence, neither survives because it is not settled in either.

One might ask: "But in the world, we sometimes see a fetus devoid of vital essence survive for a short time after birth; why is it said they do not live?" To explain this with an analogy, the author says: **"for a brief time."** This is due to <term>residual momentum</term> <note>original: saṃskāra</note>—specifically the momentum left by the circulation of the vital essence. It is like a "severed limb"—when a limb is cut off...

<summary>This page describes the eighth month of pregnancy as a spiritually active but physically precarious period when the vital essence (ojas) fluctuates between mother and child. It explains the ancient medical belief that infants born in the eighth month rarely survive due to this instability of life-force.</summary>
<keywords>Saṅgītaratnākara, embryology, Ojas, vital essence, Vāgbhaṭācārya, eighth month of pregnancy, fetal development, Saṃskāra, liberation</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the sequence on fetal development, describing the physical posture of the child in the womb, the mechanics of labor, and the philosophical argument for the eternity of the soul based on a newborn's instincts.</meta>

### Saṅgītaratnākara [Section on the Origin of the Body]

<header>-igin: 2] Chapter 1: The Descent into the Womb</header>

->The umbilical cord carries the nutrient-rich fluid of the mother's food to the fetus.<-
->With hands joined at its forehead, it remains facing the mother’s back. || 40 ||<-
->It dwells with limbs curled tightly in the womb, resting on the right side.<-
->A female child rests on the left side, while one in the middle is considered neuter. || 41 ||<-
->Driven by the powerful winds of birth, it is then turned head-downward.<-
->The child is pushed out, limbs aching, through the narrow opening of the birth canal. || 42 ||<-
->As soon as it is born, the infant instinctively seeks the mother's breast.<-
->Because of the impressions of knowledge from previous births, the soul’s eternity is proven. || 43 ||<-

---

Regarding the phrase "like that limb": this is a <term>karmadharaya</term> <note>A Sanskrit compound where the two parts refer to the same thing</note> compound. It refers to how a severed limb is seen twitching in the moment after it is cut, due to the residual momentum of the life-force; it means the same thing here regarding a child born in the eighth month. Regarding "from the ninth month onward": the word "onward" is used to show that birth may occur in the ninth month, or sometimes in the tenth or even the eleventh month. || 33–41 ||

**(Commentary by Simhabhupala)** In the fifth month, the consciousness is awakened, meaning the fetus becomes endowed with knowledge. "Distinctness" refers to becoming clearly manifest when separation occurs. "Grown" means having reached development. "Covered by the outer ear": <term>pali</term> <note>original: pāli</note> refers to the earlobe; the fetus covers its ear-holes with its hands, separated by the lobes. "Agitated" means it has attained a state of detachment <note>original: vairāgya</note>. "Focus in the womb" refers to a profound state of meditation and self-investigation. "Agonies" are the pains of the womb. "Thinking of the means to liberation" means contemplating the methods to achieve spiritual freedom. "Devoted to practice" means being established in the investigation of the Self. 

He describes the state of the eighth month with the words "In the eighth." "Hearing" refers here to the act of perceiving external sounds, not the sense organ of hearing itself; because the sense of hearing is composed of space <note>original: ākāśa</note> and is eternal, it cannot be "produced" or "born" in a specific month. <term>Vital essence</term> <note>original: ojas</note> is a specific bodily constituent. It is "pure," meaning free from corruption. It has been stated that this vital essence is the cause of life. He clarifies this further with the phrase "Again to the mother..." 

Regarding how the fetus is nourished, he says: "From the mother." The cord is "connected to her," meaning joined with her systems. "Facing the mother's back" means it is oriented toward the mother's spine. "Resting on the right side": the use of the masculine gender here implies that such a child is male. || 33–41 ||

**(Commentary by Kallinatha)** "By the winds of birth" refers to the downward-moving vital breaths called <term>apana</term> <note>original: apāna</note>. "Through the narrow opening of the machine" refers to the birth canal. "Of that child" refers to the one just born. "Gentle" means possessing the quality of softness.

# Saṅgītaratnākara [The Origin of the Body]

### Page 38

<header>Saṅgītaratnākara [Section on the Origin of the Body]</header>

->There are six types of factors that form the fetus: those derived from the mother, the father,<-
->nutrients, the self, the mind, and the habits of the parents. || 44 ||<-
->The soft parts—blood, fat, marrow, spleen, liver, rectum,<-
->heart, and navel—are known as the factors born of the mother. || 45 ||<-
->Beard, body hair, hair on the head, sinews, veins, arteries, nails,<-
->teeth, and reproductive fluids—the firm parts—originate from the father. || 46 ||<-
->The nourishment of the body, complexion, growth, stability <gloss>1</gloss>, strength, maintenance,<-
->lack of greed, and enthusiasm—these are known as factors born of nutrients. || 47 ||<-

---

The word "spleen" (<term>plīha</term> <note>original: plīha-śabdaḥ</note>) refers to a specific fleshy organ located on the left side, which serves as a foundation [for certain humors]. The "liver" (<term>yakṛt</term>) is a similar fleshy organ located on the right side. Regarding "sinews, veins, and arteries": <term>snāyus</term> (sinews) are fine channels; <term>sirās</term> (veins) are thicker than those; and <term>dhamanīs</term> (arteries) are as thick as the hollow stalk of a castor-oil plant. "Firm" refers to the hard parts of the body. || 42–46 ||

**(Commentary by Simhabhupala)** He explains the method of birth: "It is done," etc. "By the winds of birth" refers to the biological forces that facilitate delivery. "Aching limbs" means the body is pained [by the pressure]. "Through the opening of the machine" <note>The text uses the metaphor of a machine (yantra) to describe the biological structures</note> means through the narrow birth canal. By mentioning the newborn's instinctual drive to seek the breast, he demonstrates the eternity of the soul: "Of the just-born," etc. He then details the different types of factors: "The factors are," etc. "Nutrient" (<term>rasa</term>) refers to the essence of food. "Mind" (<term>sattva</term>) refers to specific internal mental states. "Habit" (<term>sātmya</term>) refers to the specific impressions formed by long-standing familiarity. He explains the factors born from the mother: "The soft ones," etc. These are the regions endowed with softness. The spleen and liver are two specific pieces of flesh located near the heart. "Heart and navel" (<term>hṛn-nābhī</term>) is a compound word; according to the rules of grammar, words denoting limbs of living beings are expressed in the singular. || 42–46 ||

**(Commentary by Kallinatha)** The portion of the text starting with "The nourishment of the body" and ending with "those afraid of excessive detail" is considered self-explanatory and clear as read. || 47–74 ||

---

<header>[The Origin] of the Body | Part 2] First Chapter: Svaragatādhyāya</header>

->Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, merit and demerit, mental impressions,<-

**(Commentary by Simhabhupala)**
He now describes the factors born of the self: "In the body," etc. "Accumulation" <note>upacaya</note> refers to bulk or thickness. "Growth" <note>vṛddhi</note> means exceeding the standard proportions. || 47, 48 ||

He categorizes the organs of perception and their objects: "The organs of perception," etc. "Touch" <note>sparśana</note> refers to the organ of the skin <term>tvagindriya</term>. "Sight" <note>darśana</note> is the eye. "Taste" <note>rasana</note> is the tongue. || 49 ||

He explains the organs of action and their activities: "The voice and hands," etc. || 50 ||

Relying on the views of the Vedantists <note>followers of the Vedanta school of philosophy</note>, he explains the two-fold internal instrument: "Mind and intellect." In the *Vācaspatya* <note>a famous philosophical treatise</note> it is said: "The union of intellect and mind is the foundation for the appearance and manifestation of the 'I' concept." || 51 ||

To distinguish between the intellect and the mind, he explains their specific functions: "Pleasure," etc. Therefore, the distinction is this: the mind is the means for perceiving pleasure and pain, while the intellect is the means for memory, error, doubt, and so on. "Resolution" <note>vyavasiti</note> refers to the act of determination or functioning. || 52 ||

He examines the cause of the senses according to different schools of thought: "The Absolute," etc. The Vedantists say the senses originate from the Absolute <note>Brahman</note>, because the entire universe is a manifestation of the Absolute. Alternatively, the Samkhya philosophers believe the senses have the Absolute as their source but are non-physical <note>arising from the "I-consciousness" rather than the five elements</note>. Others, such as the Vaisheshikas <note>the atomist/naturalist school</note>, argue that the senses are made of physical elements...

->Lucidity, Passion, and Inertia are the three qualities; from the state of Lucidity <note>original: sattva; here referring to the guṇa of purity and light</note>,<-

**(Commentary by Simhabhupala)**

Some say these senses are born from the elements like earth and so on. He now describes the third aspect of the "internal instrument," calling it "the being" <term>sattva</term>. In this context, the term <term>sattvākhyam</term> means "the natural disposition." It varies according to the division of the qualities <term>guṇas</term>: namely Lucidity, Passion, and Inertia <note>original: sattva-rajas-tamas</note>. || 53 ||

Having divided the qualities, he explains them starting with: "Lucidity..." etc. He describes the effects of a Lucid internal instrument: "From Lucidity..." **Faith** <note>original: āstikya</note> is the conviction that "the afterlife exists." A **taste for pure righteousness** means an exclusive affection for stainless duty. By the word "etc.," he implies a turning away from unrighteousness. || 54 ||

He describes the effects of a Passionate internal instrument: "From Passion..." This refers to an internal instrument dominated by the quality of Passion. Next, he describes the effects of an Inertial internal instrument: "Sleep..." etc. **Sleep** <note>original: nidrā</note> is the cessation of the senses' activity regarding external objects, whether it be light sleep or deep sleep. **Laziness** <note>original: ālasya</note> is the lack of effort even toward achieving one's desired goals. **Negligence** <note>original: pramāda</note> is a lack of attentiveness. **Deception** <note>original: vañcana</note> means cheating or misleading others. || 55 ||

He describes the states born of **habituation** <term>sātmya</term>: "Clarity..." etc. **Health** <note>original: ārogya</note> means the state of being free from disease. He then divides the elemental qualities within the body: "The body..." etc. **Composed of elements** <term>bhūtātmaka</term> means it is originated from the five great elements <note>Space, Air, Fire, Water, and Earth</note>. Even though the body might be seen as originating from each element individually, the support and presence of the other elements is always there. || 56 ||

**Hollowness** <note>original: suṣiratā</note> means having pores or small openings. **Distinctness** <note>original: vaiviktya</note> is the state of being separate, which allows the body to achieve its natural disposition through distinct spatial arrangement. **Subtle understanding** <note>original: sūkṣmaboddhṛtā</note> is the ability to thoroughly grasp even difficult concepts without much effort. The distinction between a **cavity** <note>original: bila</note> and **hollowness** <note>original: suṣira</note> is that a cavity is a large opening, while "suṣira" is a small one.

He then describes the qualities of Air in the body: "From Air..." etc. **Touch** is the quality, while the **organ of touch** is the skin...

# The Origin of the Body

## Chapter 1: Section on Sound (Svaragatādhyāya)

### Page 44

<header>Sangeeta Ratnakara: [The Microcosm—</header>

They are considered the boundary-markers of the tissues <term>dhātu; the seven primary elements of the body: plasma, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen</term>, comparable to the heartwood of timber. The first is the flesh-bearer; within the flesh, the veins and arteries, || 77 ||

as well as sinews and channels, grow like the stalks of a lotus in the mud. The others are the bearers of blood, fat, phlegm, waste <note>original: śakṛt; feces</note>, bile, and semen. || 78 ||

> "Thus the body is composed of the elements. Therein, seven layers of skin are produced from blood as it is 'cooked' <note>original: pacyamānāt; refers to the metabolic transformation through internal heat</note>, just as a film forms on the surface of boiling milk.
> The Shining <note>original: bhāsinī</note>, the Red <note>original: lohinī</note>, the White <note>original: śvetā</note>, the Copper-colored <note>original: tāmrā</note>, and the Perceiving <note>original: vedinī</note> skin; 
> then the Healing <note>original: rohiṇī</note>, and the seventh is proclaimed to be the Flesh-bearing <note>original: māṃsadharā</note> layer."

Thus it is said. Regarding the "seven membranes" <term>kalā; internal linings or partitions</term>: The moisture of the essence <note>original: rasa-kledo</note> is a specific refinement of the tissues located in the intervals between the preceding and succeeding tissues. Because it is covered by sinews, phlegm, and the protective casing of the womb, and is matured by the internal fire of the body <term>kośāgni; the metabolic heat within the organs</term>, it is called a "membrane" due to its subtle form, resembling the heartwood of timber. 

As it has been said:

> "The moisture within the receptacles of the tissues, matured by its own heat and covered by phlegm, sinews, and the placenta <note>original: aparā; the afterbirth or fetal membrane</note>, is called a membrane, like the heartwood of timber."

The description of being "covered by sinews, etc." should be understood as a quality common to both the skins and the membranes. These skins and membranes act as "boundary-markers" situated between the tissues; that is, they are located in the midst of the seven tissues—starting with the skin—and their purpose is to prevent the tissues from becoming intermixed. "The first" means the first skin and membrane is named the "flesh-bearer," while the remaining six skins and membranes are the "bearers of blood," and so on. || 75-78 ||

**[Commentary by Simhabhupala]** (Su.) He divides the limbs and minor parts of the body with the words "Of the body" <note>original: piṇḍasya</note>. "Between the tissues" means in the middle of each of the seven tissues. The first skin, the "flesh-bearer," is "like the heartwood of timber," meaning it is firm; the implication is that the others are not as firm. Regarding where the veins and other structures arise, he says: "In the flesh." Arteries <term>dhamani</term> are specific types of veins <term>sirā</term>. A sinew <term>snāyu</term> is a specific type of binding for the flesh, resembling a thread. What do the other skins and membranes hold? He says: "Blood," and so forth. || 75-78 ||

## Chapter 1: Section on Sound (Svaragatādhyāya)

### Page 45

<header>The Origin of the Tissues [2] — Section 1: Sound</header>

Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the seven tissues <term>dhātu; the fundamental biological building blocks that support the body</term>. It is said that the skin is first formed by the "gastric fire" <note>original: jaṭharavahni; the metabolic heat responsible for digestion</note>. || 79 ||

From the essence of food <note>original: annarasa</note> cooked by this fire, blood is produced; and in the same way, the other tissues are generated in a sequence, each refined by its own specific internal heat <note>original: sva-sva-kośāgni; the "fire" within each tissue's own container or stage of development</note>. || 80 ||

There are seven "receptacles" <term>āśaya; internal cavities or organs that house specific substances</term> in succession, designated for: blood, phlegm <note>original: śleṣman</note>, undigested food <note>original: āma</note>, bile <note>original: pitta</note>, wind <note>original: marut</note>, and urine. || 81 ||

Women have an eighth receptacle: the uterus <term>garbhāśaya</term>, located between the bile-receptacle and the digestive-receptacle. From the pure essence of phlegm and blood, the heart is formed, shaped like a lotus. || 82 ||

It is hollow, points downward, and is situated between the liver and the spleen. This is the seat of consciousness <term>cetanasthāna</term>. When this seat is veiled by darkness <note>original: tamas; the quality of inertia or heaviness in Indian philosophy</note>, || 83 ||

the heart closes and the soul <note>original: ātman</note> sleeps; when it expands, the soul wakes. This sleep is of two types: dreaming and deep, dreamless sleep <term>suṣupti</term>. Sleep occurs when the external senses are withdrawn. || 84 ||

**Commentary (by Kallinātha):** Having pointed out the tissues, the author now shows their origin with the verse beginning "Skin, blood..." The phrase "and the skin is said" uses the word "and" to connect it to the previous discussion. The meaning is this: the outer skin, which was categorized here as a tissue, is the very same skin previously defined as the boundary-marker of the tissues. || 79-82 ||

**Commentary (by Siṃhabhūpāla):** He classifies the tissues: "Skin..." etc. He then describes the method of origin for blood and the others: "blood..." etc. "Raw" <note>original: āma</note> refers to undigested essence. He mentions the additional receptacle for women: "the uterus." He then describes the method of the heart's origin, its specific shape, and its location: "From the pure essence..." || 79-82 ||

**Commentary (by Kallinātha):** "This is the seat of consciousness": This refers to the hollow, lotus-shaped heart that points downward. The word "and" here is used to imply a collection of other locations that serve as causes for the manifestation of consciousness. These other locations are mentioned in the revealed scriptures <note>original: śruti</note>, such as "Life-breath <note>original: prāṇa</note> is Brahman, Joy is Brahman, Space is Brahman," and so on...

## Chapter 1: Section on Sound (Svaragatādhyāya)

### Page 46

<header>The Jewel of Music [The Origin of the Body]</header>

> [When the senses] dissolve in the heart, [but] the mind remains awake, that is called a **dream**. If the mind dissolves into the vital breath, then occurs the **deep sleep** of the soul. || 85 ||
> Because the soul is merged in its own self, the Supreme Soul, it is said to "sleep" <note>original: svapiti; the text here uses a traditional etymology where the word for sleep, *svapiti*, is broken down into *svam* (self) and *apita* (merged or entered)</note>.

...and so on. The **seat of consciousness** <term>cetanasthāna</term> is the place of manifestation for the "Unchanging Absolute" <term>kūṭastha-brahman; the eternal, underlying reality that remains constant despite physical changes</term>. Here, the word "conscious" <note>original: cetana</note> does not refer merely to the individual soul <term>jīva</term>. Why? Because that would contradict the Sacred Scriptures <term>śruti</term>. For the Scripture says: "Now, this City of God..." <note>original: atha yadidam brahmapuram; a reference to the Chandogya Upanishad 8.1.1</note> and so on, and "in the shape of a lotus," which describes the lotus of the heart as the dwelling place of the Absolute.

Similarly, in the *Bhamati* <note>a famous 10th-century commentary on the Brahma Sutras by the scholar Vacaspati Misra</note> in the section regarding the "Small Space" <term>daharādhikaraṇa</term>, it begins: "Now, this which is in the City of God is the small, subtle, cave-like dwelling in the shape of a lotus," and then cites the scripture: "All these creatures go day after day to that world of the Absolute, yet they do not find it."

This explains that during sleep, this whole world of living beings—both the wise and the ignorant—reaches the "World of the Absolute" known as the "Small Ether" <term>daharākāśa</term> residing in the heart-lotus. However, because their vision is covered by the veil of darkness from beginningless ignorance <term>avidyā</term>, they do not realize, "I have attained the nature of the Absolute." 

Through this extensive context, and after refuting the idea that the word "Small" <note>original: dahara</note> refers only to the physical sky or the individual soul, it is established as referring to the Absolute. Therefore, here too, one should understand that the "Conscious One" residing in the heart-lotus is indeed the Absolute <term>brahman</term>. 

"In this..." and so on: When this Conscious Absolute is covered or hidden by "darkness"—that is, beginningless ignorance—and when that heart-lotus closes or buds, then the soul sleeps or slumbers. When that lotus blooms, then the soul wakes, becoming aware as "I." The word "also" <note>original: api</note> here carries the sense of "and."

The meaning is this: Even though the individual soul exists due to ignorance of its own true nature, the states of **waking**, **dreaming**, and **deep sleep** occur to the soul. These states are the reasons for the designations of the soul as the "Universal" <term>viśva; the soul in the waking state</term>, the "Luminous" <term>taijasa; the soul in the dream state</term>, and the "Cognitive" <term>prājña; the soul in deep sleep</term>.

"In two ways": Sleep is slumber, and its two specific forms are **dreaming** and **deep sleep**. || 83-85 ||

# 50 Sangītaratnākara: [Origin of the Body]

The downward-going [arteries] are also divided into three types and are located in the receptacle for digested food <note>the intestines and lower abdomen</note>. Among those, the first ten [sets] cause the movement of wind <term>vāta</term> and the other humors, as described previously. || 110 ||

Two arteries carry consumed food from the seat of water <note>original: "ambusamāśrayāt"; likely referring to the stomach or the digestive fire's relationship with fluids</note>. Two each carry water, urine, and strength <note>original: "balam"; here interpreted as semen or vital vigor</note>. In women, these two [arteries] carry the menstrual fluid. || 111 ||

Two [arteries] discharge through the channels <note>the ears or other orifices</note>, and two connected to the large intestine discharge feces. The eight horizontal arteries are considered to have many branches. || 112 ||

Their openings are located in the hair follicles to allow for the release of sweat. They also draw in the essences <term>rasa; fluids or nutrients</term> produced by oil massages, ointments, and similar treatments. || 113 ||

The vital points <term>marman; lethal points where life resides</term> are known to be one hundred and seven. There are thirty-five million <note>three and a half crores</note> hairs on the body, while the beard and head-hair are counted as six hundred thousand. || 114 ||

Including the channels, veins, beards, and head-hair, the total number of body hairs is said to be five hundred forty-six million and seven hundred fifty thousand <note>original: "fifty-four crores and sixty-seven and a half lakhs"</note>. || 115 ||

The measurement for the collection of water and other substances is now stated. Ten handfuls <term>añjali; a measurement formed by joining two hollowed palms</term> of water are known to be in the body; there are nine handfuls of nourishment fluid <term>rasa; plasma</term>. || 116 ||

There are eight handfuls of blood, seven of feces, six of phlegm <term>śleṣman; kapha</term>, five of bile <term>pitta</term>, and four handfuls of urine. || 117 ||

There are three handfuls of muscle-fat <term>vasā</term>, two of fat <term>medas</term>, and one handful of marrow <term>majjan</term> is recognized. || 118 ||

There is a half-handful of brain-marrow, as well as of the essence of phlegm and strength <term>bala; ojas</term>. || 118 <insert>continued</insert> ||

***

He explains: "The downward-going..." (109-). He explains their function: "They cause the movement..." Strength <term>bala</term> means virility/semen (110-111). He explains the specific nature of the horizontal ones: "The horizontal..." (112, 113). He enumerates the vital points: "The vital points..." (114, 115). He explains the measurement of the collections: "With sixty-seven..." A collection <term>saṃhitā</term> refers to the union of hair and other parts.

->**Thus ends the brief summary of the minor limbs. The wise may look for**<-
->**the detailed reality in the *Discernment of the Inner Self*, composed by me. || 119 ||**<-
->**Between the anus and the genitals lies the wheel called the Support, which has four petals.**<-

Regarding the promised measurement of fluids, he says: **"of water, etc."** <note>original: "jalādeḥ"</note>. This refers to the plasma <term>rasa</term> that follows. ¹Regarding **"of the marrow,"** <note>original: "majjñaḥ"</note> it refers to the tissue known as marrow. By saying **"the detail should be seen in the *Discernment of the Inner Self*,"** the author demonstrates his own excellence by pointing out that he has composed that book as well. || 116–119 ||

(Kallinatha's commentary) **Between the anus and the genitals**: From the stay of the individual soul <term>jīva</term> at the time of birth in the four petals—starting from the Northeast—of the **Support Wheel** <term>ādhāra-cakra</term> located between the anus and genitals, various fruits like "Supreme Bliss" <term>paramānanda</term> and others result. **In the Support Lotus**: in that very same Support Wheel. **The Serpent Power** <term>kuṇḍalinī</term>: she is so named meaningfully because she is shaped like a serpent <note>original: "sarparūpiṇī"</note>. She is the **Creative Energy of the Absolute** <term>brahma-śakti</term>; she is the power of Ignorance <term>avidyā-śakti</term> that imposes the form of a "doer" and other qualities upon the Supreme Soul, who is otherwise unattached and indifferent. She is called "the Coiled One" <term>kuṇḍalinī</term> because she possesses a physical form that is curved and coiled. **To the Opening of the Absolute** <term>ā-brahmarandhram</term>: the Opening of the Absolute is the name for the tip of the central channel <term>suṣumṇā</term> located in the center of the thousand-petaled wheel <term>sahasradala-cakra</term> in the head; it means "up to that point." **When led straight**: following the methods taught by a teacher <note>a guru</note> through the sequence of restraints and observances <term>yama-niyama</term>, one blocks the movement of breath in the left and right channels <term>iḍā and piṅgalā</term>. By using that breath combined with the internal fire, one moves aside the "hood" of the Serpent Power which covers the root-opening of the central channel. When the breath is made to enter there, and the "knots" of the Creator, Preserver, and Destroyer <term>brahma-viṣṇu-rudra-granthi</term> are successively pierced, the Serpent Power abandons her own crookedness and attains a straight form. **She grants immortality**: at that time, because of her own straightness, the Serpent Power [reaches] the Opening of the Absolute...

# 52 Sangitaratnakara [Origin of the Body]

**At the root of the genitals is the Self-Abode <term>svādhiṣṭhāna</term>, a wheel of six petals. || 122 ||**
**In its petals, starting from the East, the results are said to be, in order:**
**Humility, Cruelty, the Destruction of Pride, and thereafter Stupor, || 123 ||**
**Disdain, and Distrust. This is the house of the power of desire.**

...Having exited with the tip of her own tail, she <note>the Serpent Power</note> pierces the thousand-petaled wheel <term>sahasradala-cakra</term>, which is the reservoir of nectar, and causes that nectar to flow. Thus it is described. || 120–121 ||

(Simhabhupala's commentary) Having described the major and minor limbs of the physical body, the author now begins to describe the energy wheels <term>cakras</term>: **"Between the anus and the genitals,"** etc. Between the anus and the genitals lies the wheel known as the **Support** <term>ādhāra</term> <note>often called the Muladhara</note>, which has the form of a four-petaled lotus. He describes the results of those four petals: **"Supreme,"** etc. In the Northeast petal is Supreme Bliss; in the Southeast petal is Natural Bliss; in the Southwest petal is the Bliss of Heroes; and in the Northwest petal is the Bliss of Yoga. From this, we understand that the four petals of the Support Lotus are situated in the intermediate directions. **"Existing there"**: the power of the Absolute <term>brahma-śakti</term> known as the **Serpent Power** <term>kuṇḍalinī</term> resides in the Support Lotus, so called because she is the cause for attaining the Absolute <term>brahman</term>. When she is led straight up to the **Opening of the Absolute** <term>brahmarandhra</term> <note>the energy center at the crown of the head</note>, she grants the nectar of immortality, which is liberation. || 120–121 ||

(Kallinatha's commentary) **The Self-Abode**: Above the Support Wheel, at the root of the genitals, is the second wheel named the **Self-Abode** <term>svādhiṣṭhāna</term>, which has six petals. He describes the results like humility and others in the petals starting from the East: **"And of this,"** etc. **"There would be disdain"**: this instruction pertains to the spiritual path. || 122–123 ||

(Simhabhupala's commentary) He describes the wheel named the Self-Abode: **"The Self-Abode."** It has six petals, shaped like a six-petaled lotus. He describes the results of these six petals: **"And of this,"** etc. **Humility** <note>original: "praśrayaḥ"</note> means modesty; it is the result of the petal located in the East. This means the individual soul <term>ātman</term> residing there becomes humble. **Cruelty** <note>original: "krūratā"</note> means an obsession with wicked deeds. **Pride** is the feeling of self-importance; its **destruction** <note>original: "garva-nāśo"</note> is the third result. **Stupor** <note>original: "mūrcchā"</note> means an excess of delusion. **Disdain** <note>original: "avajñā"</note> means contempt or looking down on others. **Distrust** <note>original: "aviśvāsaḥ"</note> means being suspicious of everything or a lack of confidence. This Self-Abode wheel is the **house**—the shelter—of the power that generates desire <term>kāma</term>. || 122–123 ||

# 53 First Chapter on Sound

### [Origin of the Body, Part 2]

**At the navel is a ten-petaled wheel called the Jewel-City <term>maṇipūraka</term>. || 124 ||**
**Deep sleep, thirst, envy, and treachery;**
**Shame, fear, disgust, delusion, impurity, and sadness— || 125 ||**
**These occur in the petals starting from the East. This center is also the abode of the Sun.**
**In the heart is the Unstruck <term>anāhata</term> wheel, the seat of worship for Shiva, who takes the form of the Sacred Sound <term>praṇava</term> <note>The syllable 'Om'</note>. || 126 ||**
**Tradition holds it to have twelve petals.**
**The ending of fickleness, clarity, reasoning, remorse, || 127 ||**
**Hope, radiance, anxiety, effort, and equanimity;**
**Then deceit, distress, discernment, and ego— || 128 ||**
**These are said to be the fruits for the Self residing in the petals, starting from the East.**

(Kallinatha) Then, moving upward through the eight locations—the navel, heart, throat, uvula, mid-brow, forehead, hair-root, and the opening of the Absolute <term>brahmarandhra</term>—he describes the results for each petal of the eight wheels: the Jewel-City <term>maṇipūraka</term>, the Unstruck <term>anāhata</term>, the Pure <term>viśuddhi</term>, the Playful <term>lalanā</term>, the Command <term>ājñā</term>, the Mind <term>manas</term>, the Moon <term>soma</term>, and the Thousand-Petaled <term>sahasra-patra</term>. He begins with the navel: **"At the navel is a ten-petaled wheel..."** etc. || 124–128 ||

(Simhabhupala) He describes the Jewel-City wheel: **"At the navel."** He explains the results of its petals from the East onward: **"Deep sleep,"** etc. Deep sleep <term>suṣupti</term> is the state where the external senses and the mind cease their activity. Thirst <term>tṛṣṇā</term> is desire. Envy <term>īrṣyā</term> is the inability to tolerate the good qualities of others. Treachery <term>piśunatā</term> is pointing out the faults of others, whether they exist or not. Shame and Fear are well-known. Disgust <term>ghṛṇā</term> is the desire to avoid the suffering of others <note>often interpreted here as a sensitive or over-averse nature</note>. Delusion <term>moha</term> is the lack of awareness of objects even while in the waking state. Impurity <term>kaṣāya</term> is having a clouded or stained heart. Sadness <term>viṣāda</term> is sorrow accompanied by worry. That Jewel-City wheel is the "abode of the Sun," meaning it is the location of the life-breath <term>prāṇa</term> associated with the sun. || 125, 126 ||

He describes the Unstruck wheel: **"In the heart."** He calls it the seat of worship for Shiva who has the form of the Sacred Sound <term>praṇava</term> <note>original: "oṃkārākṛteḥ"</note>. This means one should worship the Supreme Lord by meditating on him while he resides there. He describes the results of the Self residing in the twelve petals starting from the East: **"Fickleness,"** etc. The state of being unsteady is fickleness <term>laulya</term>.

# 54 Sangita Ratnakara [Origin of the Body]
