# The Ocean of Music <note>original: *Saṅgītaratnākara*</note>
<page-num>80</page-num>
<header>Section 3: Chapter 1: On the Notes <note>original: *svara-*</note></header>

Because it generates or reveals the [other] six notes, the term **Şaḍja** <note>literally "Six-born"</note> is formed from the root *jan* (to give birth) with an internal causative sense, using the grammatical suffix *ḍa* and the dropping of the final syllable. Alternatively, it is called **Şaḍja** because it is generated or revealed by the other six notes entering into it as subordinate parts. The word is formed as before. Or, it is called **Şaḍja** because it is born from the six locations of the nose, throat, chest, palate, tongue, and teeth, according to the grammatical rule "born from a fifth-case noun."

> “It reaches the heart more quickly than any other; thus it is known as **Ṛṣabha** <note>The Bull</note>.
> Just as a great bull appears magnificent standing among cows, 
> So does this note shine, having arisen within the scale of notes.”

It is called **Ṛṣabha** from the root *ṛṣ* (to go or reach), with the suffix *abhac*, because it "reaches" the heart faster than other notes. Just as a bull is the leader among a herd of cattle, so is this note the second strong power in the collection of notes. Or, it is called **Ṛṣabha** because it bellows like a bull.

> “Because it holds the voice which consists of song, it is named **Gāndhāra**.”

It holds the voice (*gā*) which is the essence of song; thus, from the root *dhṛ* (to hold or support) with the word "voice" as the preceding object, the form **Gāndhāra** is derived by adding the suffix *aṇ* and applying grammatical variations. Or, it is called **Gāndhāra** because it is the cause of the pleasure of the <term>Gandharvas; celestial musicians</term>.

> “Because of its position in the middle of the notes, the **Madhyama** <note>The Middle</note> note is so desired.”

Because it is the fourth note among the seven, and thus stands in the center, the form **Madhyama** is derived by adding the suffix *ma* to the word for "middle." Alternatively, it is *mad-dhvama*, meaning "the disease (*ama*) of my intellect (*dhi*)." That is to say, because of its extreme beauty, the sound of this note among the seven "pains" or overwhelms the listener by creating a doubt of its own loveliness <note>this is a poetic play on words common in Sanskrit etymology to show the note's captivating power</note>.

> “He who measures the extension of the other notes is **Pañcama** <note>The Fifth</note>.
> Or, by counting according to the order of recitation, it is the fifth by number.”

# The Ocean of Music <note>original: *Saṅgītaratnākara*</note>

The name **Pañcama** <note>The Fifth</note> is derived from the root *pac* (to expand). By adding the grammatical suffix *ghañ*, we get the sense of "measuring a five-fold expansion." Following the rule "a suffix *ka* is added when there is no preceding prefix," the form **Pañcama** is established. Certain technical phonetic variations are set aside here because the word is a proper name. Alternatively, it is called **Pañcama** simply because it is the fifth in the sequence when counting the notes, or because it is produced from the fifth anatomical location.

->“The one who possesses steady wisdom is called *Dhīvān*; that which belongs to him is known as **Dhaivata**.”<-
->Alternatively, “Because it is held in the sixth location, it is considered **Dhaivata**.”<-

*Dhīvān* means one who possesses *dhī* <note>wisdom or steady intellect</note>. The form **Dhaivata** is derived by adding a suffix to indicate "that which belongs to him." This relationship can be understood in several ways: as the thing to be described and its describer, as the flavor to be tasted and its taster, or as the effect and its cause. In this context, because this note’s microtones <term>śruti: the smallest audible intervals of pitch</term> touch the succeeding note, they are difficult for those with unrefined minds to distinguish. Thus, it is the **Dhaivata** because it is only fully perceivable by the wise, who possess subtle intellect. Alternatively, it is called **Dhaivata** because it is "held" in the sixth anatomical position, the forehead.

->“All the notes sink or settle into it; therefore it is called **Niṣāda**.”<-

Derived from the root *ṣadlṛ* (to settle or disintegrate), **Niṣāda** <note>The Settled One</note> is the note where the other notes find their conclusion or "sink" into, according to the grammatical rule for nouns indicating a location of action. Following this logic, these notes are exactly seven in number. This numerical limit is based on their correspondence with the seven bodily tissues <term>dhātus: the fundamental biological layers of the body like blood and bone</term> or the seven energy centers <term>cakras: spiritual focal points in the body</term>, as taught by the sage Matanga.

To make practical performance easier, the first letters of these notes are extracted to create shorthand names. Matanga’s method for this extraction is as follows: consider the eight groups <term>vargas: the categorized groups of the Sanskrit alphabet</term> of the alphabet (a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa). 

From the eighth group <note>the śa-group: ś, ṣ, s, h</note>, take the third letter <note>s</note> and join it with the "Seed of Hari" <note>the vowel 'a'</note> to extract the first note: **Sa**. 

From the seventh group <note>the ya-group: y, r, l, v</note>, take the second letter <note>r</note> and join it with the "Seed of Desire" <note>the vowel 'i'</note> to extract the second note: **Ri**. 

From the second group <note>the ka-group: k, kh, g, gh, ṅ</note>, take the third letter <note>g</note> and join it with the "Seed of Hari" <note>a</note> to extract the third note: **Ga**. 

From the sixth group <note>the pa-group: p, ph, b, bh, m</note>, take the fifth letter <note>m</note> joined with the vowel 'a' to extract the ¹fourth note.

# The Ocean of Music <note>original: *Saṅgītaratnākara*</note>
<page-num>82</page-num>
<header>The Ocean of Music &emsp;&emsp; [Section on Notes]</header>

### ### That which arises immediately after the microtone, which is smooth and resonant; ###
### which by itself delights the listener's heart—that is called a Note. <note>Verse 24</note> ###

...one should extract the fifth note <term>Pañcama: the fifth note of the scale, equivalent to 'So' or 'G'</term> joined with the syllable *ka*. From the fifth, one should extract the sixth note joined with the fourth *a* vowel. From the fifth, one should extract the seventh note joined with the fifth "seed-syllable of desire" <note>original: *kāmabīja*, a mystical syllable used in tantric practice</note>. Regarding the shorthand names like Sa, Ri, Ga, and so on: Matanga <note>an ancient sage and musicologist</note> addresses the objection that because these are initial consonants, they cannot technically be "vowels" or "notes" by themselves. He replies that this is simply a technical convention <note>original: *saṃketa*</note> established by the authority of the ancient teachers.

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** Having thus defined the microtones <term>śruti: the 22 smallest audible intervals of pitch in an octave</term>, the author now defines the notes. To facilitate practical use, he provides alternative names for the notes such as **Shadja** and **Rishabha** by using their first syllables. These shorthand names—**Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni**—are chosen as the primary designations because they are extracted from the full names. Although the pronunciation *Ṣa-Ṛ-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni* would be more grammatically accurate based on the full names, the common reading *Sa-Ri-Ga* is accepted even if it is technically a linguistic corruption <note>original: *apabhraṃśa*</note>.

**(Kalanidhi Commentary)** The author provides the general definition and the etymological explanation of the word **Svara** <note>Note</note>. 

"Arising immediately after the microtone" means it appears after the initial microtone, which is the first sound produced by the striking of the internal breath against the anatomical centers. 

"Smooth" <note>original: *snigdha*</note> means it is not harsh and can be clearly heard from a distance. 

"Resonant" <note>original: *anuraṇātmaka*</note> means it has the nature of an after-sound or an echo. 

"Delights the listener's heart by itself" means it creates an emotional coloring <note>original: *rañjayati*</note> without needing any auxiliary causes. 

The word **Svara** is grammatically derived from the root *rañj* (to color or delight). By applying grammatical rules—specifically the *ḍa* suffix, the dropping of certain letters, and phonetic transformations—the form **Svara** is established to describe that which shines or delights on its own.

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** He explains the definition and derivation of a Note: it "arises after the microtone." When a string is first struck, the initial sound produced that lacks resonance is the **microtone** <note>śruti</note>. The sound that is heard immediately afterward, which possesses the quality of resonance, is the **Note** <note>svara</note>. Why is it called a Note? He says: "by itself." Because it delights the listener's mind independently, without needing anything else, it is called a Note. How does it possess this power to delight? This is inherent in its nature...

<summary>This page defines the musical Note (Svara) as a resonant sound that arises from a Microtone (Śruti) and possesses the inherent power to delight the listener. It also justifies the use of shorthand notation (Sa, Ri, Ga, etc.) as a necessary practical convention in musicology.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from page 82, which defined a "Note" (Svara) as a smooth, resonant sound that arises after a microtone and delights the heart, this page provides a philosophical commentary on the quality of "smoothness" and debates the ontological relationship between the microtone (Śruti) and the musical note (Svara).</meta>

# The Ocean of Music <note>original: *Saṅgītaratnākara*</note>
<page-num>83</page-num>
<header>Section 3: Notes] First Chapter on Notes</header>

**(Sudhākara Commentary continued)**

The adjective used in the definition is **smooth** <note>original: *snigdha*</note>. Although "smoothness" or viscosity is technically a property only of water—as the philosophical schools state, "viscosity is the specific quality of water"—it is not something that can be perceived by the sense of hearing. Nevertheless, the term "smoothness" is used metaphorically <note>original: *aupacārikaṃ*</note> to describe the pleasing, fluid quality of musical notes.

Regarding the relationship between the microtone <term>śruti: the subtle intervals of sound</term> and the note <term>svara: the musical note that emerges from these intervals</term>, there are many conflicting views:

Some describe an **essential identity** <note>original: *tādātmya*</note> between the microtone and the note. They have said:

-> "Because both are perceived by the sense of hearing and lack any distinct tactile quality, the relationship between the microtone and the note is one of essential identity, like that between a universal class and a specific individual." <-

Others speak of the notes as a **reflection** or **illusory appearance** <note>original: *vivarta*</note> of the microtones. They have said:

-> "Just as the faces of men are reflected in mirrors, so do the notes appear as reflections dwelling within the microtones themselves." <-

Some describe it as a **cause-and-effect** relationship. They have said:

-> "Some indeed say that notes are the effect produced by microtones, just as a clay pot is the effect produced here by the lump of clay and the potter's staff." <-

Others favor the theory of **transformation** <note>original: *pariṇāma*</note>. They have said:

-> "Microtones indeed undergo a transformation into the form of notes, entirely in the same way that milk turns into the form of curd." <-

Still others accept the theory of **manifestation** <note>original: *abhivyakti*</note>. They have said:

-> "The seven notes, Shadja and the rest, are always manifested by the microtones, just as a lamp reveals objects like pots that are sitting in the dark." <-

Among these various views, the theories of **transformation** and **manifestation** are the ones accepted by Matanga <note>a legendary sage and author of the *Bṛhaddeśī*, a foundational text on Indian musicology</note>. As he said:

-> "The difference between the distinct characteristics of these sounds is established, just as it is between different objects. Indeed, a thing devoid of specific characteristics would be like a 'flower in the sky' <note>a Sanskrit idiom for something that is impossible or non-existent</note>. Because they are grasped by different perceptions, there is a distinctness between the note and the microtone. Furthermore, because they differ as that which is supported and the support itself, how can an absolute identity be established?" <-

<summary>This page explores the metaphorical use of "smoothness" in music and presents five philosophical theories on how musical notes relate to microtones, ultimately favoring the views of transformation and manifestation.</summary>

> "That which was claimed—that notes are an **illusory transformation** <note>original: *vivartatvaṃ*</note> of microtones—is inconsistent. For if the notes were merely an illusion, it would result in a state of confused or false knowledge. Furthermore, the microtones could not then be considered the 'cause' of the notes. We know this because in the world of physical objects, once the effect is fully present, the original form of the cause is no longer perceived. For instance, when a clay pot exists, the original **lump of clay** <note>original: *mṛtpiṇḍo*</note> is no longer seen. Therefore, the wise consider the correct view to be either **transformation** <note>original: *pariṇāmo*</note> or **manifestation** <note>original: *abhivyakti*</note>."

As for the master Matanga, he derived the word **Note** <term>Svara: the basic unit of a melody</term> in a different way. As he said:

> "The word is derived from the verbal root **rājṛ**, meaning 'to shine' or 'to be brilliant,' preceded by the prefix **sva** (self). Because a note shines by itself, it is known as a **Svara** <note>literally, 'self-shining'</note>."

The etymologies <note>original: *nirukti*</note> of the seven notes, starting with the first note, **Ṣaḍja**, were described by the author of *The Essence of Musical Time* <note>original: *Saṅgītasamayasārakāreṇa*, referring to the scholar Pārśvadeva</note>:

> "Because it is produced from **six** parts of the body—the nose, throat, chest, palate, tongue, and teeth—it is known as **Ṣaḍja** <term>Ṣaḍja: literally 'born of six'; the tonic or first note, abbreviated as 'Sa'</term>."
>
> "The air rising from the navel, striking the throat and the head, bellows like a **bull** <note>original: *ṛṣabha*</note>; for this reason, it is called **Ṛṣabha** <term>Ṛṣabha: the second note, abbreviated as 'Ri'</term>."
>
> "The air rising from the navel and striking the throat and head becomes the cause of delight for the **Gandharvas** <note>celestial musicians in Hindu mythology</note>; for that reason, it is called **Gāndhāra** <term>Gāndhāra: the third note, abbreviated as 'Ga'</term>."
>
> "The air rising from the navel and striking the heart is called the **Middle One**, because it originates from the middle position of the body." <term>Madhyama: the fourth note, abbreviated as 'Ma'; literally 'Middle'</term>."
>
> "The air rising from the navel and striking the lips, throat, head, and heart is produced from **five** places; for this reason, it is called **Pañcama** <term>Pañcama: the fifth note, abbreviated as 'Pa'; literally 'the Fifth'</term>."
>
> "The air rising from the navel and striking the throat, palate, head, and heart is held in those various places; therefore it is considered **Dhaivata** <term>Dhaivata: the sixth note, abbreviated as 'Dha'</term>."
>

# The Ocean of Music <note>original: *Saṅgītaratnākara*</note>
<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>Section 3: Microtones | First Chapter: On Notes | 85</header>

Now, an objection is raised: if the **note** <term>Svara: the fundamental musical pitch</term> is caused by the fourth **microtone** <term>Śruti: the smallest audible interval of sound</term> and others like it, then how can the preceding three microtones be considered its cause? || 25 ||

We reply: the fourth, third, and subsequent microtones are determined by their **expectation of what precedes them** <note>original: *pūrvābhikāṅkṣayā*; implying that a higher pitch is only defined by its relationship to the lower pitches before it</note>. Therefore, the preceding microtones are indeed causes in this context. There are five **classes** <note>original: *jātayaḥ*; categories based on the emotional or aesthetic quality of the sound</note> of microtones: **Brilliant** <note>original: *Dīptā*</note>, **Extended** <note>original: *Āyatā*</note>, **Compassionate** <note>original: *Karuṇā*</note>, **Soft** <note>original: *Mṛdu*</note>, and **Moderate** <note>original: *Madhyā*</note>. || 26–27 ||

Their arrangement within the notes is as follows: In **Ṣaḍja** <term>the 1st note, "C"</term>, the microtones are Brilliant, Extended, Soft, and Moderate. In **Ṛṣabha** <term>the 2nd note, "D"</term>, they are Compassionate and Moderate. || 28 ||

In **Gāndhāra** <term>the 3rd note, "E-flat"</term>, the microtone is Soft. In **Madhyama** <term>the 4th note, "F"</term>, they are Brilliant, Extended, Soft, and Moderate. || 29 ||

In **Pañcama** <term>the 5th note, "G"</term>, the microtones are Soft, Moderate, Extended, and Compassionate. In **Dhaivata** <term>the 6th note, "A"</term>, they are Compassionate, Extended, and Moderate. In the seventh note, **Niṣāda** <term>the 7th note, "B-flat"</term>, they are Brilliant and Moderate. || 30 ||

We shall now describe the internal divisions of these classes. The **Brilliant** <note>original: *Dīptā*</note> class is said to be of four types: **Sharp** <note>original: *Tīvrā*</note>, **Terrible** <note>original: *Raudrī*</note>, **Thunderbolt-like** <note>original: *Vajrikā*</note>, and **Fierce** <note>original: *Ugrā*</note>. || 31 ||

The **Extended** <note>original: *Āyatā*</note> class is celebrated for having five varieties: **Lily-like** <note>original: *Kumudvatī*</note>, **Angry** <note>original: *Krodhā*</note>, **Expanding** <note>original: *Prasāriṇī*</note>, **Kindling** <note>original: *Sandīpanī*</note>, and **Rising** <note>original: *Rohiṇī*</note>. || 32 ||

### The Moonlight of Art <note>original: *Kalānidhi*, the commentary by Kallinātha</note>

(Kallinātha): If it is argued that only the fourth microtone (and its equivalents in other notes) should be the cause of a note, and not the ones preceding it, the author raises an objection: *“Now, if...”* Regarding the phrase *“of the three, etc.”*: this refers to the third microtone and those before it. In this commentary, the use of the term *“three, etc.”* is justified by the grammatical rule where a suffix is dropped but the meaning is retained.

The author resolves this by saying: *“We reply...”* The “fourth” refers to the final microtone of **Ṣaḍja**, **Madhyama**, and **Pañcama** (the 4-microtone notes). The “third” refers to **Ṛṣabha** and **Dhaivata** (the 3-microtone notes). By the word “and others,” the “second” microtone is included for **Gāndhāra** and **Niṣāda** (the 2-microtone notes). These are determined by their *“expectation of what precedes them.”* Through the power of the word “and others,” a repetition should be understood: it is determined by the expectation of each and every preceding microtone. In defining their own nature as successive steps, they achieve their manifestation as...

# The Ocean of Music <note>original: *Saṅgītaratnākara*</note>
<page-num>86</page-num>
<header>The Ocean of Music: [Chapter on the Classes of Notes]—</header>

**Dayāvatī**, **Ālāpinī**, and **Madantikā** are thus declared; these three are the varieties of the **Compassionate** <note>original: *Karuṇā*; refers to the class of microtones with a pathetic or tender quality</note> class. The **Soft** <note>original: *Mṛdu*</note> class has a fourfold division: || 33 ||

**Mandā**, **Ratikā**, **Prīti**, and **Kṣiti**. The **Moderate** <note>original: *Madhyā*</note> class is of six types: **Chandovatī**, **Rañjanī**, **Mārjanī**, **Raktikā**, || 34 ||

**Ramyā**, and **Kṣobhiṇī**. Now, we shall describe the placement of the notes within these. **Tīvrā**, **Kumudvatī**, **Mandā**, and **Chandovatī** reside in **Ṣaḍja** <term>the 1st note, "C"</term>. || 35 ||

**Dayāvatī**, **Rañjanī**, and **Raktika** are located in **Ṛṣabha** <term>the 2nd note, "D"</term>. **Raudrī** and **Krodhā** are in **Gāndhāra** <term>the 3rd note, "E-flat"</term>. Then **Vajrikā**, **Prasāriṇī**, || 36 ||

**Prīti**, and **Mārjanī**—these microtones are dependent on **Madhyama** <term>the 4th note, "F"</term>. **Kṣiti**, **Raktā**, **Sandīpanī**, and **Ālāpinī** are in **Pañcama** <term>the 5th note, "G"</term>. || 37 ||

**Madantī**, **Rohiṇī**, and **Ramyā**—these three reside in **Dhaivata** <term>the 6th note, "A"</term>. **Ugrā** and **Kṣobhiṇī** are the two microtones that dwell in **Niṣāda** <term>the 7th note, "B-flat"</term>. || 38 ||

->**Commentary**<-

The meaning is this: since the designation of the "fourth" and subsequent microtones is determined by the expectation of the ones preceding them, the sequence is defined accordingly. In order to clearly understand the distinct nature of the microtones without confusing them with one another, and to achieve aesthetic beauty <note>original: *rakti*; the power of music to "color" or affect the mind</note> through their proper harmonic association, the author demonstrates the arrangement of these classes—along with their internal divisions—within the notes, starting with the phrase "Brilliant, Extended..." <note>original: *dīptā āyatā ityādinā*</note>. The description of these microtone classes after the application of the notes is appropriate, as it follows the logical connection of distinguishing between microtones and notes. The mention of them in a different order elsewhere is intended to show that, in some contexts, the specific sequence is not strictly mandatory. By this, one should understand that the order mentioned in verses such as "The families and classes..." is not fixed for every application. || 25–38 ||

->**The Subodhini Commentary**<- <note>original: *Su-bodhinī*; a famous commentary on the text by Simhabhūpāla</note>

Regarding the statement "From microtones, notes are produced": the use of the fifth case <note>the ablative case in Sanskrit grammar, used here for 'śrutibhyaḥ'</note> according to the grammatical rule "The source of the producer is the prime cause" <note>original: *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*; a rule from Panini's grammar explaining the origin of a thing</note> indicates that the microtones are the cause of the notes. Furthermore, because it is said that "this note has four microtones," "this note has three," and "this note has two," it is understood that all microtones act as causes...

# First Chapter: On Notes
<page-num>87</page-num>
<header>First Chapter: On Notes</header>
<meta>[-Sentiments: 3]</meta>

is perceived; now, an objection is raised: **"Now, an objection"** <note>original: *nanu*; a standard way to introduce a counter-argument in Sanskrit philosophy</note>. If a note <term>Svara</term> is established on a specific microtone <term>Śruti</term>—such as the fourth—then the fourth, seventh, ninth, thirteenth, seventeenth, twentieth, and twenty-second microtones may well be the cause of the notes **Ṣaḍja** and the rest, whether by manifesting them or transforming into them. But what is the cause or purpose of the preceding microtones, such as the first, second, and third, in relation to the note? By the phrase "the third and others," we mean to ask: what is the use of the three preceding microtones for **Ṣaḍja**, **Madhyama**, and **Pañcama**; the two preceding for **Ṛṣabha** and **Dhaivata**; and the single preceding one for **Gāndhāra** and **Niṣāda**? 

The author resolves this: **"We say"** <note>original: *brūmaḥ*; the author's reply to the objection</note>. The designation of a microtone as the "fourth," "third," or otherwise is determined only in relation to the preceding ones. This convention—calling this the fourth, this the third, and this the second—depends entirely on the microtones that come before. If the preceding microtones did not exist, in relation to what would the status of being the "fourth" be established? Therefore, even the preceding microtones are established as causes, as they are necessary to determine the identity of the fourth microtone and the others.

Now, he divides the microtones into their families: **"Brilliant, Extended..."** <note>original: *Dīptā-āyatā*</note>. There are five families <term>Jātis</term> of microtones: **Brilliant** <note>original: *Dīptā*</note>, **Extended** <note>original: *Āyatā*</note>, **Compassionate** <note>original: *Karuṇā*</note>, **Soft** <note>original: *Mṛdu*</note>, and **Moderate** <note>original: *Madhyā*</note>. 

Regarding the question of which family resides in which note, he says: **"And of those..."** In **Ṣaḍja** <term>the 1st note, "C"</term>, there are four microtone families beginning with the **Brilliant**: the first microtone is **Brilliant**, the second is **Extended**, the third is **Soft**, and the fourth is **Moderate**. 

In **Ṛṣabha** <term>the 2nd note, "D"</term>, the first microtone is **Compassionate**, the second is **Moderate**, and the third is **Soft**. 

In **Gāndhāra** <term>the 3rd note, "Eb"</term>, the first microtone is **Brilliant** and the second is **Extended**. 

In **Madhyama** <term>the 4th note, "F"</term>, they are situated as **Brilliant**, **Extended**, **Soft**, and **Moderate**. Thus, for **Madhyama**, the first microtone is **Brilliant**, the second is **Extended**, the third is **Soft**, and the fourth is **Moderate**. 

In **Pañcama** <term>the 5th note, "G"</term>, the first microtone is **Soft**, the second is **Moderate**, the third is **Extended**, and the fourth is **Compassionate**. 

In **Dhaivata** <term>the 6th note, "A"</term>, the first microtone is **Compassionate**, the second is **Extended**, and the third is **Moderate**. 

In the seventh note, **Niṣāda** <term>the 7th note, "Bb"</term>, the first microtone is **Brilliant** and the second is **Moderate**.

Having promised to explain the sub-varieties of these families, he states: **"And of those..."** 

The **Brilliant** class is fourfold: **Sharp** <note>original: *Tīvrā*</note>, **Terrible** <note>original: *Raudrī*</note>, **Thunderbolt-like** <note>original: *Vajrikā*</note>, and **Fierce** <note>original: *Ugrā*</note>. 

The **Extended** class has five divisions: **Water-Lily-like** <note>original: *Kumudvatī*</note>, **Angry** <note>original: *Krodhā*</note>, **Spreading** <note>original: *Prasāriṇī*</note>, **Illuminating** <note>original: *Sandīpanī*</note>, and **Growing** <note>original: *Rohiṇī*</note>. 

The **Compassionate** class has a triad of divisions: **Merciful** <note>original: *Dayāvatī*</note>, **Conversing** <note>original: *Ālāpinī*</note>, and **Intoxicating** <note>original: *Madantikā*</note>. 

The **Soft** class has four divisions: **Low** <note>original: *Mandā*</note>, **Delight** <note>original: *Rati*</note>, **Affection** <note>original: *Prīti*</note>, and **Earth** <note>original: *Kṣiti*</note>. 

The **Moderate** class is of six types: **Metrical** <note>original: *Chandovatī*</note>, **Coloring** <note>original: *Rañjanī*</note>, **Cleansing** <note>original: *Mārjanī*</note>, **Reddened** <note>original: *Raktikā*</note>, **Beautiful** <note>original: *Ramyā*</note>, and **Agitating** <note>original: *Kṣobhiṇī*</note>. 

The word **"but"** <note>original: *tu*</note> indicates that this class has more varieties than the previous ones. Having promised the placement of these within the notes, he says: **"Now, of these..."** Of these microtone families, those existing in **Ṣaḍja** are the four classes beginning with **Sharp** <note>original: *Tīvrā*</note> and the others. Thus, in **Ṣaḍja**, the first microtone is **Brilliant**, pervaded by the **Sharp** variety; the second is **Extended**, of the **Water-Lily** variety; the third is **Soft**, of the **Low** variety; and the fourth is **Moderate**, of the **Metrical** variety. In **Ṛṣabha**, the first microtone is of the **Merciful** variety...

->These notes are considered threefold based on the distinction of register—lower, middle, and upper.<-
->Their twelve modified states are likewise presented. || 39 ||<-
->The note **Ṣaḍja** <note>The first note of the scale, abbreviated as 'Sa'</note> becomes modified as a two-microtone note in two ways: "shifted" and "non-shifted."<-
->This occurs when the note **Niṣāda** <note>The seventh note, 'Ni'</note> is seen in its "common" and "sharp" <note>original: *kākalī*; a specifically raised version of the seventh note</note> states. || 40 ||<-
->When the note **Ṛṣabha** <note>The second note, 'Ri'</note> relies on the microtone of **Ṣaḍja** during a "common" <note>original: *sādhāraṇa*</note> state,<-
->it attains a four-microtone value; thus, one modified form occurs. || 41 ||<-

...is **compassionate** <note>original: *karuṇā*; the aesthetic quality of the microtone</note>; the second is of the **pleasing** family <note>original: *rañjanī-jāti*</note> and is "middle"; the third is of the **delightful** family and is "soft." In **Gāndhāra** <note>the third note, 'Ga'</note>, the first microtone is of the **fierce** family and is "brilliant"; the second is of the **angry** family and is "expansive." In **Madhyama** <note>the fourth note, 'Ma'</note>, the first microtone is of the **thunderbolt** family and is "brilliant"; the second is of the **spreading** family and is "expansive"; the third is of the **affectionate** family and is "soft"; the fourth is of the **cleansing** family and is "middle." In **Pañcama** <note>the fifth note, 'Pa'</note>, the first microtone is of the **earthly** family and is "soft"; the second is of the **impassioned** family and is "middle"; the third is of the **enkindling** family and is "expansive"; the fourth is of the **conversational** family and is "compassionate." In **Dhaivata** <note>the sixth note, 'Dha'</note>, the first microtone is of the **intoxicating** family and is "compassionate"; the second is of the **ascending** family and is "expansive"; the third is of the **beautiful** family and is "middle." In **Niṣāda** <note>the seventh note, 'Ni'</note>, the first microtone is of the **terrible** family and is "brilliant"; the second is of the **agitating** family and is "middle." 

Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of defining these classes of microtones <term>Śruti-jāti</term>? It is said: this definition is provided to indicate that upon hearing a microtone of a certain class, a corresponding transformation or "coloring" arises in the mind, matching the name of that class. Therefore, by hearing a "brilliant" <note>original: *dīptā*</note> microtone, the mind itself becomes brilliant; by hearing an "expansive" <note>original: *āyatā*</note> microtone, the mind feels expanded; and the same should be understood for "compassionate" and the other qualities. || 25-38 ||

<note>Commentary by Kallinātha</note> Having spoken of the classes of microtones in the preceding context, the author now speaks of the threefold nature of notes based on the difference of register <term>Sthāna</term>, while referring back to the primary notes: **"These notes are in the lower register..."** etc. But one might object: should not the "shifted" notes and others be considered separate notes entirely? Why categorize them as **Ṣaḍja** and the rest in an altered state? To this, the author says: **"Their twelve..."** He defines the twelve modified notes <term>Vikṛta-svara</term> in the order they occur, with reference to the two primary scales <note>original: *grāma*; the Sa-grama and Ma-grama systems</note>, starting with: **"The shifted and non-shifted..."** The four-microtone **Ṣaḍja** becomes a two-microtone modified note in two ways, termed "shifted" and "non-shifted." It is "shifted" in the "common" state, and also when **Niṣāda** takes the "sharp" state...

**Gāndhāra** <note>the third note, 'Ga'</note> is three-microtone in its "common" state and four-microtone in its "intermediate" state. These two variations of it have been proclaimed by **Niḥśaṅka** <note>original: *niḥśaṅkena*; "The Fearless One," an epithet for the author Śārṅgadeva</note>. || 42 ||

**Madhyama** <note>the fourth note, 'Ma'</note>, like **Ṣaḍja** <note>the first note, 'Sa'</note>, is of two types based on its reliance on the "intermediate" and "common" states. **Pañcama** <note>the fifth note, 'Pa'</note> in the "Middle Scale" <note>original: *madhyama-grāma*</note> is three-microtone; however, in the "overlapping" <note>original: *kaiśika*</note> state, || 43 ||

by taking a microtone from **Madhyama**, it becomes four-microtone. Thus, it has two forms. In the Middle Scale, **Dhaivata** <note>the sixth note, 'Dha'</note> becomes modified as a four-microtone note. || 44 ||

In the "overlapping" state and the "sharp" <note>original: *kākalī*</note> state, **Niṣāda** <note>the seventh note, 'Ni'</note> becomes three-microtone and four-microtone respectively. Having obtained these two modified forms, twelve [modified notes] are remembered. || 45 ||

Together with the seven "pure" <note>original: *śuddha*</note> notes, they become nineteen.

...is seen as "non-shifted." <gloss>Regarding the phrase "three-microtone in commonality," it means in the "commonality of Madhyama." Regarding "four-microtone in the intermediate state," it should be specified as "in its own intermediate state."</gloss> 
<gloss>"Madhyama is like Ṣaḍja": Here, "like Ṣaḍja" means that just as Ṣaḍja is two-microtone and modified by the distinction of being "shifted" or "non-shifted," so too is Madhyama—this is the meaning of the comparison.</gloss> 
<gloss>Regarding "in the overlapping and sharp states": in the "overlapping" state of Ṣaḍja, it is three-microtone; in its own "sharp" state, it is four-microtone. || 39–45 ||</gloss>

(Su. <note>Refers to the *Sudhākara* commentary by King Siṃhabhūpāla</note>) Having thus described the microtones, the classes of microtones, and the manifestation of notes from those classes, he now defines the distinctions between the notes with the phrase "They [are...]." Those notes, beginning with **Ṣaḍja**, are of three types. Why are there three types? He answers: "Due to the distinction of register <note>original: *sthāna*</note> known as lower, middle, and upper." Therefore, there is no fundamental difference in their essence, but rather a distinction conceived by their position. Just as a single man named Devadatta <note>A traditional placeholder name in Sanskrit logic, similar to "John Doe"</note> appears to be different while staying on the first, second, or third floor of a palace, so too do the notes appear different based on their specific register. # The Jewel Mine of Music: On Notes
<page-num>90</page-num>
<header>The Jewel Mine of Music [Section on Notes—</header>

A distinct, fundamental difference is perceived [between different notes], and the same is true for **Ṣaḍja** <note>the first note, 'Sa'</note> and the others when they are situated in the lower, middle, and upper registers. Why, then, is a "conceptual" or "imaginary" unity accepted here? We reply: because of **recognition** <term>pratyabhijñā; the cognitive process of identifying a present object as the same one encountered before</term>. In all three registers, we recognize them as the same notes. The **Ṣaḍja** in the lower register is perceived as the very same note in the middle and upper registers; this recognition, witnessed by all people, cannot be ignored. There is a great distinction here: among the seven notes—**Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha,** and the rest—there is not even a trace of such "recognition" between one note and another (e.g., between Sa and Ri).

Having thus defined the seven **pure** <note>original: *śuddha*</note> notes, the author now defines the twelve **modified** <note>original: *vikṛta*</note> notes by dividing them: *“They themselves...”* etc. These seven pure notes themselves, when they reach a state of modification or change, become twelve in number. || 39 ||

He demonstrates that very modification: *“Shifted...”* etc. **Ṣaḍja**, which possesses four **microtones** <term>śruti; the smallest audible pitch intervals</term>, becomes modified in two ways: it is called **shifted** <note>original: *cyuta*</note> and **un-shifted** <note>original: *acyuta*</note>. Among these, "shifted" refers to when it has moved down from the fourth microtone where it was originally established. "Un-shifted," however, refers to when it remains on that same microtone but becomes modified due to the loss of its preceding microtones. When does it undergo such modification? He says: *“In commonality...”* In the state of "commonality" and when **Niṣāda** <note>the seventh note, 'Ni'</note> becomes **sharp** <note>original: *kākalī*</note>, both types of modification occur.

> "If **Niṣāda** should take refuge in the first microtone of **Ṣaḍja**,
> and **Ṛṣabha** takes the last, that is called the 'overlapping' of **Ṣaḍja**."

In this "overlapping" state of **Ṣaḍja** <note>original: *ṣaḍja-sādhāraṇa*</note> which will be described later, **Ṣaḍja** is shifted from its own place on the fourth microtone and stays on the third microtone, thus becoming modified.

> "If **Niṣāda** should resort to two microtones of **Ṣaḍja**,
> that is **Kākalī**; if **Gāndhāra** takes two from **Madhyama**, it is **Antara**."

As will be explained, when **Niṣāda** becomes **Kākalī** <note>a "sharp" seventh note</note>, **Ṣaḍja** is considered "un-shifted" because it remains in its own place on the fourth microtone, yet it is modified because it has lost its first two microtones [to the note below it]. Now, one might ask: if it stays in its own place, even if it loses its first two microtones, how can it be modified if there is no change in its sound? It is replied: although there is no change in the sound itself because it stays in that position, when **Niṣāda** is in its own place, **Ṣaḍja** has four microtones and thus possesses **extension** <term>āyatatva; a state of full melodic tension or reach</term>. When **Niṣāda** becomes **Kākalī** and stands on the second microtone of **Ṣaḍja**, then **Ṣaḍja** is perceived as **un-extended** <note>original: *anāyata*</note> because it only possesses two microtones. Therefore, it is indeed modified. || 40 ||

He explains the modification of **Ṛṣabha** <note>the second note, 'Ri'</note>: *“In commonality...”* In the "overlapping" of **Ṣaḍja**, **Ṛṣabha** takes the last microtone of **Ṣaḍja**; at that time, having become a four-microtone note, it is modified. || 41 ||

He explains the two types of modification for **Gāndhāra** <note>the third note, 'Ga'</note>: *“In commonality...”* In the "overlapping" of **Madhyama** <note>the fourth note, 'Ma'</note>...

## The peacock, the rain-bird, the goat, the heron, the cuckoo, and the frog, ॥ 46 ॥
## And the elephant—these seven produce the seven notes beginning with Shadja in succession.

**Gandhara** <note>the third note, 'Ga'</note> takes the first microtone of **Madhyama** <note>the fourth note, 'Ma'</note>. At that time, it becomes a modified note consisting of three microtones. <note>1. Regarding the 'intervening' note.</note> The "intervening" **Gandhara** <note>original: *antara-gāndhāra*</note> takes the first two microtones of **Madhyama**. In that case, it becomes a modified note consisting of four microtones. || 42 ||

The author now describes the two modified variations of **Madhyama**: [beginning with the word] "Madhyama." Just as **Shadja** <note>the first note, 'Sa'</note> was described as having two modifications—as "shifted" and "un-shifted"—in the context of its overlap with **Nishada** <note>the seventh note, 'Ni'</note> becoming "sharp" <note>original: *kākalī*</note>, so too **Madhyama** becomes modified in two ways during its overlap with **Gandhara** when it becomes "intervening" <note>original: *antara*</note>.

> "Such is the overlap of Madhyama regarding Ga and Pa," as it is said;
> ". . . for Madhyama, Gandhara is the intervening note."

Thus, the overlap of Madhyama and the "intervening" nature of Gandhara will be discussed further. || 42- || He now explains the two-fold modification of **Panchama** <note>the fifth note, 'Pa'</note>: [beginning with] "Panchama." When **Panchama** is situated on its third microtone, it is said to belong to the **middle scale** <term>madhyama-grāma; one of the two fundamental scales in ancient Indian music</term>. In that middle scale, **Panchama** becomes a modified note of three microtones. Furthermore, in the "hair-fine" overlap <note>original: *kaiśika-sādhāraṇa*</note> with Madhyama, it reaches the final microtone of Madhyama and becomes a modified note of four microtones. || 43, 43- || 

He explains the single modification of **Dhaivata** <note>the sixth note, 'Dha'</note>: [beginning with] "Dhaivata." In the middle scale, because **Panchama** is positioned on its third microtone, the final microtone of **Panchama** enters into **Dhaivata**. It then becomes a modified note of four microtones. || 44 || 

He explains the two-fold modification of **Nishada**: [beginning with] "Kaisika." In the hair-fine overlap with Shadja, when **Nishada** stands on the first microtone of Shadja, it becomes a modified note of three microtones. However, when it becomes "sharp" <note>original: *kākalī*</note> and takes two microtones of Shadja to become a note of four microtones, it is also considered modified. Thus, there are twelve modified variations. Including the pure notes, there are nineteen variations in total, as he says: "By these..." || 45, 45- ||

---

(Commentary by Kallinatha) To help understand the nature of Shadja and the other notes from common experience, the author mentions the sounds of specific animals like the peacock as examples, saying: "The peacock..." Having described the differences in nature between the notes, he now demonstrates their fourfold classification according to their usage in practice—

# The Jewel Mine of Music: On Notes
<page-num>92</page-num>
<header>First Chapter: On Notes</header>

### Notes are of four kinds: the sonant, the consonant, the dissonant, ॥ 47 ॥
### and the assonant. The sonant note is that which is frequent in performance.
### When the interval between two notes contains twelve or eight ॥ 48 ॥
### microtones, those two are mutually consonant. Ni and Ga are dissonant to others; ॥ 49 ॥
### or [dissonance] may exist between Ri and Dha, or between Ri and Dha individually.

**Regarding "four kinds":** The **sonant** <note>original: *vādī*; literally "the speaker"</note> is so called from "speaking." One might object: "Speaking and similar actions are characteristics of living beings; how can they belong to inanimate notes?" This is true; however, by "speaking," we mean the capacity to manifest the melody <note>original: *rāga-pratipādakatvaṃ*</note> that is intended, not literal speech; thus, there is no error. 

The **consonant** <note>original: *saṃvādī*; literally "speaking together"</note> is so called from "speaking with." "Speaking with" refers to the capacity to sustain the melodic character of a melody that was generated by the sonant note. 

The **dissonant** <note>original: *vivādī*; literally "disputing"</note> is so called from "disputing." "Disputing" refers to the destruction of the pleasing quality <note>original: *rakti*</note> produced by the sonant and other notes. 

The **assonant** <note>original: *anuvādī*; literally "speaking after"</note> is so called from "speaking after." "Speaking after" refers to following or conforming to the pleasing quality established by the sonant and consonant notes. 

The author defines these in order, beginning with: **"The sonant, however..."** In performance—such as in the ancient melodic frameworks <note>original: *jāti*</note>—it is **frequent** <note>original: *bahulaḥ*</note>, meaning it is repeated again and again through its various functions such as being the predominant note <note>original: *mahattva*</note> or the final note <note>original: *nyāsa*</note>.

In order to understand the definition of consonance, one should first draw a **circular diagram** <note>original: *maṇḍala-prastāra*</note> or a **lute diagram** <note>original: *vīṇā-prastāra*</note>. 

The circular diagram is made as follows: Draw six vertical lines, and leaving a little space at the top and bottom, draw five horizontal lines in the middle. Then, the points where the lines end around the perimeter will be twenty-two. 

As for the lute diagram: simply draw twenty-two horizontal lines. In that case, there will be twenty-two line-ends on either the left or right side. 

In one of these microtonal circles <note>original: *śruti-maṇḍala*</note>, one should write the pure or modified notes—**Shadja** <note>the 1st note, 'Sa'</note> and the others—according to their respective microtone counts. Among these, it should be understood that when the microtones falling in the interval between two notes—excluding their own base microtones—are seen to be **twelve or eight**, those two notes are **mutually consonant**. 

Regarding **"Ni and Ga are dissonant to others"**: This means **Nishada** <note>the 7th note, 'Ni'</note> and **Gandhara** <note>the 3rd note, 'Ga'</note> are dissonant (opposing) to the other five notes. One might object: "It is said that Ni and Ga are dissonant to all five other notes; but this is incorrect, because pure **Madhyama** <note>the 4th note, 'Ma'</note> and **Nishada** are observed to be mutually consonant." Due to this dissatisfaction...

# The Jewel Mine of Music: On Notes
<page-num>93</page-num>
<header>Section on Moods: 3 | First Chapter: On Notes</header>

->The remaining notes are termed assonant; the sonant note is sung here as the King.<-
->The consonant note, because it follows the sonant, is called the Minister. ॥ 50 ॥<-
->The dissonant note, because of its contrary nature, is called the Enemy by the wise.<-

Regarding the alternative view: specifically, Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata <note>original: *ri-dha*</note>. The initial general statement that "these two are dissonant to others" follows the opinion that consonance only occurs between notes of equal microtonal <note>term: *śruti* | the smallest audible unit of pitch in Indian music theory</note> value. Thus, the definition of consonance is established as an interval of either twelve or eight microtones. Regarding the phrase "between those two": this means Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata are dissonant to Niṣāda and Gāndhāra. By this, the definition is suggested that notes separated by only a single microtonal interval are mutually dissonant. Even when experts mention dissonance as being "two intervals apart," they mean a separation of one microtone when including the base microtone of the note itself; the meaning remains the same. Similarly, when experts define consonance as an interval of "thirteen or nine," it is effectively the same as twelve or eight microtones. 

Therefore, just as Ṛṣabha and Gāndhāra, or Dhaivata and Niṣāda, are mutually dissonant in their natural state, one must observe the same dissonance between Gāndhāra and Madhyama, or Niṣāda and Ṣaḍja, in their modified <note>original: *vikṛta*</note> states. The core idea is this: even if the sonant, consonant, and assonant notes are swapped in their positions during a performance, the essential character of the melodic mode <note>term: *jāti-rāga* | the ancient classification of melodic frameworks</note> is not destroyed. However, the use of a dissonant note would indeed destroy the melody. "The remaining" refers to those notes lacking the characteristics of sonant and the others. Now, the author illustrates the hierarchy of the sonant and others in practice, using an analogy: "The sonant is the King," and so on. ॥ 46-51 ॥

**Sudhakara’s Commentary:** To help identify the nature of these notes, the author describes their unique "singers" from the natural world: the **Peacock** cries the note Ṣaḍja; the **Chataka bird** cries Ṛṣabha; the **Goat** bleats Gāndhāra; the **Heron** <note>original: *krauñca*</note> calls Madhyama; the **Indian Cuckoo** <note>original: *kokila*</note> sings Pañcama; the **Frog** croaks Dhaivata; and the **Elephant** trumpets Niṣāda. ॥ 46, 46- ॥

The author then describes the fourfold nature of notes: "Of four kinds..." He defines the sonant note: "The sonant is..." In performance, such as in melodic modes, the note that is uttered most frequently is the sonant <note>original: *vādī*</note>, which is another term for the "ruling note" <note>term: *aṃśa* | the primary note upon which a melody is built</note>. Now, one might ask: "The word *vādī* literally means 'one who speaks'; but speaking is a property of living beings—how can it apply to inanimate notes?" This is true; however, by "speaking," we specifically mean the capacity to manifest or explain the melody. Thus, they are called "sonant" because they "speak" or establish the melodic identity of the songs. ॥ 47, 47- ॥ Consonant...

# The Jewel Mine of Music: Section on the Family of Notes
<page-num>94</page-num>
<header>The Jewel Mine of Music: [Section on the Family of Notes]</header>

He explains the definition [of consonance] with the phrase: "The microtones" <note>original: *śrutaya iti*</note>. When there are twelve or eight microtones situated between two notes, those two become mutually consonant <note>term: *saṃvādī* | a harmonious relationship similar to a perfect fifth or perfect fourth</note>. 

But one might ask: Has not Mataṅga stated that consonance consists of an interval of thirteen and nine microtones? As he said:

> "Consonant notes, moreover, being of equal microtonal value, are to be understood as having an interval of thirteen or nine between each other."

Dattila has also said:

-> "Mutual consonants are to be known by an interval of thirteen and nine." <-

So why is it said here: "those whose range contains twelve or eight microtones"? 

This is explained as follows: if one excludes the two microtones upon which the two notes themselves are placed, and there are twelve or eight microtones remaining in the middle, then those two are consonant. This is the intended meaning of the statement. Mataṅga and others, however, arrived at the interval of thirteen and nine by counting the microtone of the note's own position as well. Thus, there is no contradiction. 

Therefore:
* The consonants of **Ṣaḍja** <note>the 1st note, 'Sa'</note> are **Madhyama** <note>the 4th note, 'Ma'</note> and **Pañcama** <note>the 5th note, 'Pa'</note>.
* The consonant of **Ṛṣabha** <note>the 2nd note, 'Ri'</note> is **Dhaivata** <note>the 6th note, 'Dha'</note>.
* The consonant of **Gāndhāra** <note>the 3rd note, 'Ga'</note> is **Niṣāda** <note>the 7th note, 'Ni'</note>.
* The consonant of **Madhyama** is **Ṣaḍja**.
* The consonant of **Pañcama** is **Ṣaḍja**.
* The consonant of **Dhaivata** is **Ṛṣabha**.
* The consonant of **Niṣāda** is **Gāndhāra**.

One might ask: what is the practical use of this consonance? 

We reply: In a given song, if **Ṣaḍja** is designated as the primary note <note>term: *aṃśa* | the predominant melodic center</note>, substituting **Madhyama** in its place will not destroy the melodic character of the mode <note>term: *jātirāga* | ancient melodic classifications</note>. Or, if **Madhyama** is used as the primary note according to the scales <note>term: *mūrcchanā*</note>, using **Ṣaḍja** in its place will not destroy the mode. Using **Pañcama** and **Ṣaḍja** in each other's place does not cause the loss of the melodic mode. Similarly, using **Dhaivata** and **Ṛṣabha** in each other's place does not destroy the mode, and using **Niṣāda** and **Gāndhāra** in each other's place does not harm the melody.

He now gives the definition of dissonance <note>term: *vivādī* | a discordant or 'enemy' relationship</note> with the phrase: "**Ni** and **Ga**." **Niṣāda** and **Gāndhāra** are dissonant to all other notes. 

He mentions an alternative view: "Of **Ri** and **Dha**" <note>original: *ri-dhayor-iti*</note>. This suggests those two (**Ni** and **Ga**) are dissonant specifically to **Ṛṣabha** and **Dhaivata**. 

He mentions a third view: "Of those two" <note>original: *tayor-iti*</note>. This means **Ṛṣabha** and **Dhaivata** are dissonant to those two, **Niṣāda** and **Gāndhāra**. 

Mataṅga, however, defined dissonance as having an interval of two microtones; as he said, "Two notes with an interval of two [microtones] are dissonant." 

Now, what is this "dissonance"? 

We reply: Dissonance is the quality of being a "destroyer"—it destroys the sonance, consonance, or assonance that a mode receives from the sonant note <note>term: *vādī* | the melodic "ruler" or tonic</note> and others. Thus, when **Gāndhāra** is used in the place of **Ṛṣabha**, or **Ṛṣabha** in the place of **Gāndhāra**, the melodic mode is ruined.

He explains the definition of assonance <note>term: *anuvādī* | notes that are neutral followers</note> with the phrase: "Of the remaining" <note>original: *śeṣāṇām-iti*</note>. Those notes that have neither mutual consonance nor dissonance are called assonant. Mataṅga, however, defined assonance by the absence of a single microtonal interval...

<summary>This page defines the mathematical and functional relationships between musical notes, explaining how consonant notes (12/8 microtones apart) can substitute for one another without ruining a melody, while dissonant notes act as "destroyers" of the musical logic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of musical intervals and the hierarchical roles of musical notes. <page-num>95</page-num>
<header>— Flavors 3] First Chapter: On Musical Notes</header>

->Because it follows the King and the Minister, the Assonant note is like a servant. || 51 ||<-
->Born of the lineage of the gods are the notes Shadja, Gandhara, and Madhyama.<-

The nature of the **Sonant** <note>term: *Vadi* | The dominant or "King" note that defines the melody</note> has been stated. Now, one might ask: what does the **Assonant** <note>term: *Anuvadi* | A neutral note that follows the others</note> note "repeat" or "follow"? When the "Raga-ness" <note>the unique melodic character</note> of a musical mode is established by the Sonant note, the Assonant note is that which supports it. 

Because of this, if the note **Rishabha** <note>the 2nd note, 'Ri'</note> is used in the place of **Shadja** <note>the 1st note, 'Sa'</note>, or if Shadja is used in the place of Rishabha, it does not destroy the character of the melody. Similarly:
* If **Dhaivata** <note>the 6th note, 'Dha'</note> is used in the place of **Panchama** <note>the 5th note, 'Pa'</note>, or vice versa, the melody is not destroyed.
* If Dhaivata is used in the place of Shadja, or vice versa, the melody is not destroyed.
* If Panchama is used in the place of Rishabha, or vice versa, the melody is not destroyed.
* If Rishabha or Dhaivata is used in the place of **Madhyama** <note>the 4th note, 'Ma'</note>, or vice versa, the melody remains intact.

In the case of Rishabha and **Gandhara** <note>the 3rd note, 'Ga'</note>, one might expect them to be Assonant because they are separated by only one microtone; however, they are actually considered **Dissonant** <note>term: *Vivadi* | A note that creates tension or "clashes"</note> because they are separated by two microtones. 

This is the analysis of the Sonant, Consonant, Dissonant, and Assonant notes in the **Shadja-grama** <note>term: *Ṣaḍja-grāma* | The primary system or "scale" of notes</note>. A similar logic applies to the **Madhyama-grama** <note>term: *Madhyama-grāma* | The secondary scale system</note>, though this analysis is slightly modified because the note Panchama is shifted to the third microtone position. 

In that system (Madhyama-grama):
* The Consonant of **Shadja** is Madhyama.
* The Consonants of **Rishabha** are Dhaivata and Panchama.
* The Consonant of **Gandhara** is **Nishada** <note>the 7th note, 'Ni'</note>.
* The Consonants of **Madhyama** are Shadja and Nishada.
* The Consonant of **Panchama** is Rishabha.
* The Consonant of **Dhaivata** is Rishabha.
* The Consonants of **Nishada** are Gandhara and Madhyama.

The Dissonant relationship is the same in both scale systems. Regarding the Assonants:
* The Assonants of **Shadja** are Panchama, Dhaivata, and Rishabha.
* The Assonants of **Rishabha** are Shadja and Madhyama.
* For **Gandhara** and **Nishada**, there is no Assonant relationship because they are dissonant with all other notes.
* The Assonants of **Madhyama** are Rishabha and Dhaivata.
* The Assonants of **Panchama** are Madhyama and Dhaivata.
* The Assonants of **Dhaivata** are Madhyama and Panchama.

He explains the primary and secondary roles of these notes: "The **Sonant** is the King." Just as a King is the chief figure, so is the Sonant note, because all others follow it. The **Consonant** <note>term: *Samvadi*</note> is like the King's chief minister. Why? Because it follows and acts in harmony with him; hence the word *Amatya* <note>original: 'अमात्य' | minister</note> is used, meaning "one who sits/stays near." The **Dissonant** <note>term: *Vivadi*</note> is like an enemy, because it is the opposite and does not comply. The **Assonant** <note>term: *Anuvadi*</note> is like a servant; if the Sonant is the King and the Consonant is the Minister, the servant follows them both. || 46–51 ||

(Ka.) Understanding that there is also a spiritual merit <note>original: *adṛṣṭa* | "unseen" fruit of action</note> in the correct practice of music, he now describes the families and origins of the notes in the following order: "Born of the lineage of the gods," and so on. || 52–59 ||

<header>Sangitaratnakara: [On Lineages, Rishis, and Meters]</header>

**Panchama** <note>the 5th note, 'Pa'</note> is born of the lineage of the Ancestors. **Rishabha** <note>the 2nd note, 'Ri'</note> and **Dhaivata** <note>the 6th note, 'Dha'</note> are born of the lineage of the Sages. || 52 ||

**Nishada** <note>the 7th note, 'Ni'</note> is born of the lineage of the Demons. **Shadja** <note>1st</note>, **Madhyama** <note>4th</note>, and **Panchama** <note>5th</note> are of the Priest class <note>term: *Brahmin*</note>. **Rishabha** and **Dhaivata** should be known as the Warrior class <note>term: *Kshatriya*</note>; **Nishada** and **Gandhara** <note>3rd</note> are considered the Merchant class <note>term: *Vaishya*</note>. || 53 ||

The two transitional notes—**Antara** <note>the sharp 3rd</note> and **Kakali** <note>the sharp 7th</note>—are of the Laborer class <note>term: *Shudra*</note>. Now I describe the colors of these notes in order: the hue of a lotus <note>red</note>, tawny <note>reddish-yellow</note>, gold-colored, the brightness of jasmine <note>white</note>, and black. || 54 ||

[Then] yellow and variegated <note>multi-colored</note>. Next, I shall speak of their birthplaces. In the islands of **Jambu**, **Shaka**, **Kusha**, **Krauncha**, **Shalmali**, **Shveta**, and **Pushkara** <note>these are the seven mythical continents of Hindu cosmology</note>, || 55 ||

these notes, beginning with **Shadja**, were born respectively. The Sages Fire <note>Agni</note>, the Creator <note>Brahma</note>, the Moon <note>Chandra</note>, the Beloved of Lakshmi <note>Vishnu</note>, and Narada || 56 ||

perceived the five notes starting with **Shadja**; Tumburu <note>a celestial musician</note> is the seer of the seventh. Fire, Brahma, Saraswati <note>Goddess of Learning</note>, Shiva, the Lord of Shri <note>Vishnu</note>, Ganesha, || 57 ||

and the "Thousand-Rayed One" <note>the Sun</note> are said to be the presiding deities of the notes beginning with **Shadja**, in order. The poetic meters **Anushtubh**, **Gayatri**, **Trishtubh**, **Brihati**, || 58 ||

**Pankti**, **Ushnik**, and **Jagati** are assigned to the notes starting with **Shadja**. **Shadja** and **Rishabha** should be used in the Heroic, Wondrous, and Furious moods. **Dhaivata** is used in the Odious and the Terrible. || 59 ||

**Gandhara** and **Nishada** are for the Compassionate mood; **Madhyama** and **Panchama** are for the Humorous and the Erotic moods.

<page-num>97</page-num>
<header>Chapter 1: On Musical Notes (Svaragatadhyaya)</header>

**Dhaivata** <note>the 6th note, 'Dha'</note> is yellow; **Nishada** <note>the 7th note, 'Ni'</note> is variegated <note>original: *karbura*</note> or multi-colored. || 54 ||

Now, having promised to do so, the author describes the birthplaces of these notes: "The birthplace of these..." **Shadja** <note>1st</note> is born in **Jambu** island; **Rishabha** <note>2nd</note> in **Shaka** island; **Gandhara** <note>3rd</note> in **Kusha** island; **Madhyama** <note>4th</note> in **Krauncha** island; **Panchama** <note>5th</note> in **Shalmali** island; **Dhaivata** <note>6th</note> in **Shveta** island; and **Nishada** <note>7th</note> in **Pushkara** island. 

One might ask: what is the use of describing these continental origins? We say: it is to determine the true essence <note>original: *sattva*</note> of the notes. As was said by **Matanga** <note>an early authority on musicology</note>—"Why is there a rule that there are only seven notes?" It is said: just as there are only seven tissues <note>term: *dhatus* — the fundamental biological elements of the body</note> known in the body, such as lymph and others, because they are based on seven foundations; as **Sushruta** <note>the famous ancient physician and author of the *Sushruta Samhita*</note> says:

> "Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and reproductive fluid <note>original: *shukla*</note> are the seven tissues."

So too, because they are based on the seven energy centers <note>term: *chakras*</note> or the seven continents, there are exactly seven notes. 

One might object: since **Kakali** <note>sharp 7th</note> and **Antara** <note>sharp 3rd</note> also exist as distinct notes, how is the rule of "only seven" established? Should one not say there are nine notes? Not so; because these two lack the status of a primary note <note>original: *ananshatvat* — they cannot serve as the fundamental or "soul" of a melody</note>, they are not considered independent notes. **Kakali** is simply a modified form of **Nishada**, and **Antara** is a modified form of **Gandhara**. As was said by **Dattila** <note>an ancient sage of music</note>:

> "**Nishada** is called **Kakali** when it is raised by two microtones <note>term: *shrutis*</note>.
> **Gandhara** is similarly named the **Intermediary note** <note>term: *Antara-svara*</note>.
> Because they cannot serve as the primary note <note>original: *ansha*</note>, they are not called independent notes.
> Therefore, these two were described by the ancients as [forms of] **Nishada** and **Gandhara**."

|| 55, 55½ ||

Next, he speaks of the Seers <note>term: *Rishis*</note> who "saw" or realized the notes: The seer of **Shadja** is **Fire** <note>Agni</note>; of **Rishabha**, **Brahma**; of **Gandhara**, the **Moon** <note>Chandra</note>; of **Madhyama**, **Vishnu**; of **Panchama**, **Narada**; and for **Dhaivata** and **Nishada**, it is **Tumburu** <note>a celestial musician</note>. || 56, 56½ ||

He then describes the presiding Deities: Fire... || 57, 57½ ||

He describes the poetic meters: In order, **Anushtubh** <note>an eight-syllable meter</note>... 

One might ask: what is the use of defining the notes through descriptions like "lotus-colored," and identifying their seers, deities, and meters? It is for the purpose of **Note Meditation** <note>term: *Svaropasana*</note>. When the notes beginning with **Shadja** are meditated upon using their "seed syllables" <note>term: *bijas* — mystical sounds used in mantra practice</note>, then their respective seers, deities, and meters must be remembered, and their colors should be visualized. For this reason, the seed syllables of the notes were spoken of by **Matanga**, as follows:

> "By taking the eight groups of the alphabet starting with 'A' and ending with 'Ya/Sha,' 
> and combining them with the vowel measures, one should derive the seven notes."

<header>First Chapter: On Notes <note>original: *Svaragatadhyaya*</note></header>

# Now begins Section Four: On Gamuts, Scales, Sequences, and Tones

->A Gamut <note>term: *Grama* — literally a "village"; here, a collection of notes forming a fundamental scale.</note> is a collection of notes that serves as the basis for Scales <note>term: *Murchhana* — the ascending and descending sequence of the seven notes.</note> and so on. <gloss>1</gloss><-
->There are two of these on this earth; of those, the Shadja-grama is the first. || 1 ||<-
->The second is the Madhyama-grama; their definitions are now stated.<-
->The Shadja-grama occurs when the fifth note <note>**Panchama**, or 'Pa'</note> is established on its fourth microtone <note>term: *Shruti* — the smallest audible interval of sound.</note>. || 2 ||<-

(Ka.) <note>The commentary of Kallinatha.</note> Having thus defined the individual notes, [the author recognizes] that when they are scattered or isolated, they do not serve any practical or spiritual purpose. To achieve that purpose, he intends to describe the Scales <note>Murchhanas</note> and other structures which consist of the fixed arrangement of all the notes together. Since these structures depend upon and are regulated by the Gamuts <note>Gramas</note>, he first provides the general definition of a Gamut: **"A Gamut is..."**

A Gamut is so called because it is like a village. Just as in common usage a group of people is called a village, in this context, a group of notes is intended by the term "Grama." If one were to say only that "a group of notes is a Grama," the definition would be too broad <note>term: *ativyapti* — a logical fallacy where a definition applies to things outside its scope.</note>, because groups of notes also occur in ordinary secular speech and Vedic chanting. To exclude those, the qualification "the support for Scales <note>Murchhanas</note>, etc." is added. Here, the word "etc." includes Sequences <note>Krama</note>, Tones <note>Tana</note>, Melodic Movements <note>Varna</note>, Ornaments <note>Alamkara</note>, and Melodic Types <note>Jati</note>.

In the general definition, the word "Grama" is used as a singular category. While it might seem that any of the seven notes could serve as the primary identifier for a Gamut, [the author] explains the specific characteristics of the Gamuts through worldly convention, starting with: **"There are two of these..."**

One might ask: If any group of seven notes can technically be called a Gamut, why limit it by saying there are only "two on earth"? To this, it is said: This is due to the dual application of notes in their pure and modified forms, and also because of the Sage's <note>Refers to the sage **Bharata**, author of the *Natyashastra*.</note> words:

> "Two gamuts are famous in the world, known as the Shadja and the Madhyama."

Because it is based on the pure <note>shuddha</note> notes, the Shadja-grama is the first; because it involves modifications, the second is the Madhyama-grama. Regarding the phrase "established on its own fourth microtone": this refers to its [the fifth note's] own...

<header>### *The Ocean of Music* <note>original: *Sangita Ratnakara*</note>: [Gamuts and Scales]</header>

->When this [Panchama] is established on its penultimate microtone <note>term: *shruti* — the smallest audible interval of sound</note>, it is considered the **Madhyama-grama**. Or alternatively, Dhaivata has three microtones in the Shadja-grama, but four in the Madhyama-grama. || 3 ||<-

->If Gandhara takes one microtone each from Rishabha and Madhyama; and if Dhaivata takes a microtone from Panchama, while Nishada takes one microtone from Dhaivata and one from Shadja... || 4 ||<-

->...then the Sage Narada called that the **Gandhara-grama**. This gamut exists in the heavenly world <note>Swarga-loka</note>, not on the surface of the earth. || 5 ||<-

The **Shadja-grama** occurs when the note Panchama <note>the fifth note, 'Pa'</note> is situated on the 17th microtone from the beginning, called *Alapini* (which is of the *Karuna* class). The phrase **"established on its penultimate microtone"** means it resides on the 16th microtone, *Sandipani* (of the *Ayata* class). 

In this context, the author uses the word "its own" <note>original: *svashabda*</note> to provide a precise definition. If he had simply said "situated on the penultimate microtone" without the qualifier, then in the Madhyama-grama (specifically during the overlapping of the note Madhyama), the note Panchama—which possesses four microtones—could be confused with other positions. By specifying "its own," the author ensures we understand the note is shifting one microtone lower within its own allocated space. 

The phrase **"Or alternatively"** indicates an additional way to recognize the gamuts. Why is this necessary? Because while the difference between gamuts is primarily determined by the shift in the note Panchama, the text also describes the variation in the note Dhaivata. Since the variation in Dhaivata is not perceived without its proximity to Panchama, Dhaivata does not create a gamut on its own. However, mentioning Dhaivata serves as a secondary indicator <note>term: *upalakshana*</note>; when Dhaivata gains the final microtone of Panchama, it becomes "modified" <note>term: *vikrita*</note> with four microtones. When it does not, it is "pure" <note>term: *shuddha*</note> with three. These changes help us identify which of the two gamuts is being used. || 1-5 ||

(Su.) <note>The *Sudhakara* commentary by Simhabhupala.</note> To define the Gamut, he says: **"A Gamut is a collection of notes."** A collection of notes is called a "Grama" (village). But why is a group of notes called a "village"? It is explained: because it serves as the foundation or "abode" for Scales <note>term: *murchhana* — the sequential arrangement of notes</note> and other musical structures; therefore, a collection of notes is a Gamut. In ordinary life, a group of people is called a village. As stated by Matanga—

<header>### Chapter One: The Chapter on Notes</header>
<sig>—Successive Tones 4]</sig>

> ‘Just as all family members live together as one, 
> <gloss>¹</gloss> so too is that a "village" <note>original: *grama* — here meaning a musical gamut</note> of the whole world where there is a constant arrangement.’

Thus it is said. Alternatively, if any group of notes were called a "village" without order, then even a randomly uttered collection of sounds would be a gamut. To prevent this, the text states it is "the basis for scales <note>term: *murchana* — the structured ascent and descent of notes</note> and so on." This means that only a group of notes which serves as the foundation for scales is called a Gamut, not a randomly uttered collection. This is also stated by the author of the *Sangita Samayasara* <note>A classic 13th-century musical treatise by Parshvadeva</note>:

> ‘A collection of notes which possess fixed microtones <note>term: *shruti*</note> 
> and which manifest as scales, melodic fragments, and modes, 
> is considered a **Gamut** <note>original: *grama*</note>.’

He then describes its divisions by saying, "Those are two." Now, it is well known that there are *three* gamuts; why then does he say there are "two"? To answer this, he adds, "On the surface of the earth." Between those two, the **Shadja-grama** <note>the gamut starting on the tonic 'Sa'</note> is the first and primary one. The second is the **Madhyama-grama** <note>the gamut starting on the fourth note 'Ma'</note>. For this reason, the Sage Matanga said:

> ‘Between the two gamuts, which one is considered primary? 
> The primacy of the **Shadja** gamut is <gloss>²</gloss> understood from the words of the Sage.’

Having pledged to define them, he describes them: "Of those two..." The **Shadja-grama** exists when the note **Panchama** <note>the 5th note, 'Pa'</note> is established on its own fourth microtone, remaining in its natural, unaltered state. Although in the Shadja-grama the other notes like Shadja are also in their natural states, the text specifically mentions the natural state of Panchama to distinguish it from the Madhyama-grama, where Panchama becomes altered. 

He then gives the definition of the **Madhyama-grama**: "On its penultimate..." This means the Madhyama-grama occurs when this same Panchama is situated on its third microtone—the one positioned near its penultimate/final microtone. 

Although the first microtone of **Dhaivata** <note>the 6th note, 'Dha'</note> is also near the final microtone of Panchama, the text uses the word "its own" <note>original: *sva*</note> to clarify that the microtone belongs to Panchama itself, not to the next note. He expresses this same definition in another way: "Or alternatively..." The note Dhaivata has three microtones in the Shadja-grama, but in the Madhyama-grama, by taking the final microtone of Panchama, it becomes a note of four microtones. The meaning remains the same. However, previously the definition of both gamuts was given by focusing on the note Panchama...

Regarding the phrase "because it is never omitted": the non-omission of the **Madhyama** note is explained by some as follows: according to the view that "consonance" <note>original: *samvada*</note> is the echoing on a single string of the lower notes (Sa, Ri, Ga) and the higher notes (Pa, Dha, Ni) respectively, the isolated **Madhyama** has no consonant partner. Therefore, as it stands as a boundary, its omission is not desired. According to others, however, in the pure melodic sequences...

<header>First Chapter on Notes | [Sequential Tanas 4]</header>

## The sequential ascent and descent of the seven notes [is a Murchana]. ##

In the section on definitions, Bharata <note>original: *Bharata* — the legendary sage and author of the *Natyashastra*</note> and others establish that notes such as **Shadja**, **Rishabha**, **Nishada**, and **Panchama** can be omitted to create hexatonic <term>shadava — a six-note scale</term> and pentatonic <term>auduva — a five-note scale</term> patterns. However, they exclude the **Madhyama** from this rule of omission. Thus, the **Madhyama** is considered "indestructible" <note>meaning it is the permanent anchor of the scale</note>. ॥ 6—8 ॥

(Simhabhupala) Now, one might ask: why are the designations of "gamut" <term>grama — the fundamental collection of notes</term> only applied to **Shadja**, **Madhyama**, and **Gandhara**, and not to the other notes? To this, the author says: "Shadja..." The **Shadja** is the first of all notes; therefore, it is the principal or chief. He provides another reason for its importance: "because of the abundance of its ministers." The "ministers" are the consonant notes <term>samvadi — notes that share a harmonious relationship</term>. These are more numerous for **Shadja** than for other notes. For other notes, there is only one consonant note; however, for **Shadja**, both **Madhyama** and **Panchama** act as consonants. The **Madhyama** is also a leader in its gamut. The reason given is its "non-omissibility." When forming six-note or five-note scales, the **Madhyama** is never deleted. Therefore, it too is principal. Because the **Gandhara** belongs to the same "divine family" <note>original: *deva-kula*</note> as **Shadja** and **Madhyama**, it is the leader of the notes in the heavens and also receives the designation of a gamut. Thus, Matanga <note>original: *Matanga* — a pivotal medieval musicologist and author of *Brihaddeshi*</note> stated: "How are the gamuts named after the **Shadja** and **Madhyama** notes? It is said: they are named so because of their uniqueness. Their uniqueness comes from being born of a divine family." The non-omissibility of **Madhyama** was also stated by Dattila <note>original: *Dattila* — an ancient authority on musical theory</note>:

> "One should know that **Panchama** is non-omissible in the **Madhyama-grama**, while **Dhaivata** is non-omissible in the **Shadja-grama**. However, the **Madhyama** is non-omissible in all cases."

He names the presiding deities for all three gamuts with the word "In sequence..." <note>Referring to Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva mentioned on the previous page</note>. He describes the seasonal rules for singing with "In winter..." He further regulates the specific times for singing within those seasons, such as "in the forenoon," etc. Since it is stated that these rules are for those "seeking prosperity," the reward follows the rule; however, there is no sin in not following them <note>suggesting these are optional auspicious practices rather than strict ritual laws</note>. The purpose of defining the gamuts was stated by Matanga: "The purpose is to establish the system for notes, microtones, scales, melodic fragments, melodic types, and ragas." ॥ 6--8 ॥ This concludes the section on Gamuts.

(Kallinatha) Regarding the definition of a gamut, the author now provides the general definition of the **Murchanas** <term>murchana — the expansion of a gamut into a full scale</term>, which were the first things mentioned as being contained within a gamut: "The notes in sequence..." The phrase "in sequence" is used to distinguish them from "twisted" melodic fragments <term>kuta-tana — non-sequential or scrambled note patterns</term>. Of the seven...
