In this Ṣaḍjodīcyavā mode, Madhyama (Ma) is the <term>final note</term> <note>nyāsa: the note that concludes a melodic phrase or composition</note>. Ṣaḍja (Sa) and Dhaivata (Dha) are the <term>intermediate final notes</term> <note>apanyāsa: notes used as secondary points of rest within a melody</note>.

(Siṃhabhūpāla's Commentary) He characterizes the Ṣaḍjodīcyavā mode with the words: **The dominant notes...**. In the Ṣaḍjodīcyavā mode, Ṣaḍja (Sa), Madhyama (Ma), Niṣāda (Ni), and Dhaivata (Dha) are the <term>dominant notes</term> <note>aṃśa: the primary notes that define the character of the mode</note>. There is a mutual connection between these dominant notes. There is an abundance of <term>Gāndhāra in the lower register</term> <note>mandra-gāndhāra: the note Ga played in the bottom octave</note>. There is an extreme abundance of Ṣaḍja (Sa) and Ṛṣabha (Ri). Through the omission of Ṛṣabha (Ri), it becomes <term>six-noted</term> <note>ṣāḍava: a hexatonic scale</note>. Through the omission of Ṛṣabha (Ri) and Dhaivata (Dha), it becomes <term>five-noted</term> <note>auḍuvita: a pentatonic scale</note>. When Dhaivata (Dha) is chosen as the dominant note, the six-note variation is not permitted. The singing style, rhythmic cycle, and other elements are similar to the Ṣāḍjī mode. The <term>parent scale</term> <note>mūrchhanā: the specific sequence of seven notes used as a basis</note> begins with Gāndhāra (Ga). The <term>rhythmic cycle</term> <note>tāla</note> is Caccatpuṭa. It consists of twelve <term>time units</term> <note>kalā: basic measures of duration</note>. Its application is for the second performance segment of the <term>Dhruvā</term> <note>sacred songs used to mark transitions or moods in ancient Indian drama</note> songs. || 81–83 ||

11. Gāṃ Sa Sa Sa Sa Sa Sa Gāṃ
    <note>Text:</note> De     vā     su re     śa
    <note>original: "Devāsureśa" meaning "Lord of gods and demons"</note>

    <note>Text:</note> Ta va ru ci raṃ
    <note>original: "Tava ruciram" meaning "Your beautiful [face/eye]"</note>

->The first unit is formed by the two syllables of *Śaile*, while the second is by *Śasūnu*.<-
->The third consists of those five syllables; the seventh is formed with the syllables of *Adhika*.<-
->The eighth unit is with *Mukhendu*, and the ninth unit (kalā) is composed of those six.<-

(Kallinātha's Commentary) In the tuning of the pure notes belonging to the <term>Ṣaḍja scale</term> <note>ṣāḍjagrāmika: the primary scale system of ancient Indian music based on the note Ṣaḍja</note>, there are four Ṣaḍjas (Sa) in the middle register; two Madhyamas (Ma) in the <term>lower register</term> <note>mandra: the lowest of the three primary octaves</note>; and two Gāndhāras (Ga); thus making eight <term>short beats</term> <note>laghu: a fundamental unit of time in the ancient rhythmic system</note>. With the two syllables of the word *Śaile*, the first and fifth notes are occupied; the others are the remaining notes (1). 

In the second unit, there are eight short beats in the <term>middle register</term> <note>madhya: the middle octave</note>: Ga Ma Pa Ma Ga Ma Ma Dha. With the syllables of *Śasūnu*, the first, third, and eighth notes are occupied; the others are the remaining (2). 

In the third unit, there are eight short beats in the middle register: Sa Sa Ma Ga Pa Pa Ni Dha. The syllables used are *Śaileśasūnu*; the second, fourth, and seventh notes are the remaining (3). 

In the fourth unit, there are eight short beats in the middle register: Dha Ni Sa Sa Dha Ni Pa Ma. The syllables are *Praṇaya-prasaṅga*; the fourth and seventh are the remaining (4). 

In the fifth unit, there is one Gāndhāra (Ga) in the lower register; six Ṣaḍjas (Sa) in the middle register; and one Gāndhāra (Ga) in the lower register; thus eight short beats. The syllables are *Savilāsa-khela*; the fourth and seventh are the remaining (5). 

In the sixth unit, there are eight short beats in the middle register: Dha Dha Pa Dha Pa Ni Dha Dha. The syllables are *Navinodaṃ*—the syllables *na-vi-no* fall on Dha Dha Pa; the syllable *daṃ* is the seventh; the others...

In the seventh <note>referring to the seventh kalā or musical unit</note>, there is one middle-register Ṣaḍja (Sa); five <term>lower-register</term> <note>mandra: the lowest octave</note> Gāndhāras (Ga); two middle-register Sa; thus making eight <term>short beats</term> <note>laghu: a basic unit of time in ancient Indian music</note>. In order to demonstrate the arrangement of songs like the <term>Māgadhī</term> <note>an ancient song style where phrases are repeated three times at different speeds</note> and others within all musical modes (*jātis*), the author shows the application of the <term>Ardhamāgadhī</term> <note>a "half-Māgadhī" style where phrases are repeated twice</note> song structure in this mode, following the defined characteristics. He does this with the section starting with "By the syllables of *Śaile*..." and so on. "The first" means the first <term>musical unit</term> <note>kalā</note> should be joined with the two syllables of the word *Śai-le*. "The second with *Śasūnu*" means the second unit is joined with the three syllables *Śa-sū-nu* <note>referring to the "Son/Daughter of the Mountain"</note>. "The third is formed by those five" means the third unit is joined with those five syllables: *Śai-le-śa-sū-nu*. "The seventh with the syllables of *Adhika*" refers to those three syllables: *A-dhi-ka*. "The eighth with *Mukhendu*" refers to the three syllables *Mu-khen-du*. "The ninth with those" means the ninth unit is composed of those six syllables: *A-dhi-ka-mu-khen-du*. In the other units, the application of the song should be understood according to the technical definitions. || 84, 85- || Thus ends the description of the Ṣaḍjodīcyavā mode || 9 ||

<header>The Ocean of Music [On Jātis—</header>

### Now, the Ṣaḍjamadhyamā [Mode]

> In the *Ṣaḍjamadhyamā* mode, all seven notes serve as dominant notes (*aṃśas*), and they occur in combination with one another. (85)
> Except when it is the dominant note, the note Niṣāda (Ni) is generally weak <note>original: "niralpaḥ"; used sparingly</note>. Hexatonic and pentatonic forms are recognized by the omission of Niṣāda, or both Niṣāda and Gāndhāra (Ga). (86)
> In the hexatonic and pentatonic forms, however, the two-microtone notes <note>Niṣāda and Gāndhāra are termed "dvi-śrutī" because they possess only two units of pitch measurement</note> create a contradiction <note>meaning they cannot be both dominant and omitted simultaneously</note>. The song-styles, rhythms, and musical units are like those of the *Ṣāḍjī* mode. (87)
> Furthermore, the scale-sequence (*mūrchanā*) should be understood as beginning with the note Madhyama (Ma), and the application of notes is as described previously.

**(Su.)** <note>Sudhākara: the commentary by Siṃhabhūpāla</note> He explains the rules for assigning syllables to the musical units (*kalās*) with the phrase "With the syllables in *Śaile*." The first unit is to be performed with the two syllables of the name of the god Śiva <note>referring to "Śarva"</note>. The second unit is performed with the name of the god Gaṇeśa. The third unit consists of five syllables from the names of Śiva and Gaṇeśa. The seventh unit uses additional syllables. The eighth unit uses the word *Mukhendu* <note>meaning "moon-like face"</note>. The ninth unit uses six syllables. (84, 84-)

**(Ka.)** <note>Kalānidhi: the commentary by Kallinātha</note> **Regarding "All seven notes are dominant"**: He says "not weak" <note>original: "niralpaḥ"</note>, meaning that in the full heptatonic state (using all seven notes), the note Niṣāda should be made weak. **Regarding "Acceptance based on dominance"**: The idea is that even in that state, when Gāndhāra (Ga) is the dominant note, the weakness of Niṣāda is not desired because it is a consonant note (*saṃvādī*) to Gāndhāra. **Regarding "Without being the enunciator"**: This means if the note itself is the enunciator (*vādi* or dominant), there is an even greater absence of weakness. The two-microtone notes are Niṣāda and Gāndhāra; here it is implied they are the dominant notes. They would be "contradictory" in hexatonic and pentatonic forms because these forms are prescribed by dropping Niṣāda or both Niṣāda and Gāndhāra. There is a contradiction between the property of being a "dominant note" and the property of being "omitted." The sense is that in such cases, the hexatonic and pentatonic forms do not occur. Since the two notes Niṣāda and Gāndhāra are required to be present when they are dominant, one must consider the seventeen varieties of dominant notes mentioned by the sage Matanga: five for hexatonic, five for pentatonic, and seven for the full heptatonic scale. **Regarding "Song-styles, rhythms, and units like Ṣāḍjī"**: The song-styles (*gītis*) are the three known as Māgadhī, Sambhāvitā, and Pṛthulā. The rhythm (*tāla*) is also of three types—one, two, or four units—known as the *Pañcapāṇi*. The units (*kalās*) are twelve, consisting of eight beats each. By the word "and others," he refers to the musical paths named *Citra*, *Vṛtti*, and *Dakṣiṇa*...

<summary>This page defines the Ṣaḍjamadhyamā mode, noting that all seven notes can be dominant and explaining how hexatonic and pentatonic versions are formed. The commentaries clarify the syllable-to-rhythm mapping and resolve technical contradictions regarding dominant notes that would otherwise be omitted.</summary>

In this *Ṣaḍjamadhyamā* mode, the notes Ṣaḍja (Sa) and Madhyama (Ma) are the <term>nyāsas<gloss>final or concluding notes</gloss></term>. All seven notes serve as the <term>apanyāsas<gloss>semi-final notes used to end intermediate phrases</gloss></term>. Its <term>prastāra<gloss>notation-structure or rhythmic expansion</gloss></term> is as follows:

These elements, such as the song-styles (*gītis*) and others, are taken "as in the *Ṣāḍjī* mode"; this is an <term>atideśa<gloss>extension of rules by analogy</gloss></term>, meaning they should be performed here just as they were prescribed for the *Ṣāḍjī* mode. Furthermore, the scale-sequence (*mūrchanā*) here should be understood as beginning with the note Madhyama (Ma). Since this mode belongs to the Ṣaḍja-grama <note>the basic parent scale starting on Sa</note>, this refers to the *matsarīkṛtā* scale <note>original: "matsarīkṛtā mūrchanā"; the technical name for the scale starting on the 4th degree, Ma, within the Sa-grama</note>. The application (*viniyoga*) is as before; meaning that, as with the previous *Ṣaḍjodīcyavā* mode, it is used for the *Dhruvā* song in the second stage-scene <note>original: "dvitīye prekṣaṇe"; refers to specific types of songs used in ancient Indian theater</note>. —85—87—

**(Su.)** <note>Sudhākara: the commentary by King Siṃhabhūpāla</note> He defines the *Ṣaḍjamadhyamā*: "All seven notes are dominant notes." In the *Ṣaḍjamadhyamā*, all seven notes function as the <term>aṃśas<gloss>dominant or tonic-like notes</gloss></term>. There is a mutual association among these dominant notes. The note Niṣāda (Ni) is used sparingly <note>original: "alpa"</note>. 

When Gāndhāra (Ga) is the dominant note, then the scarcity of Niṣāda is not observed. Similarly, when Niṣāda is the "enunciator" note (*vādī*), its scarcity is not observed. 

The hexatonic form (*ṣāḍava*) is created by omitting Niṣāda. The pentatonic form (*auḍuvita*) is created by omitting both Niṣāda and Gāndhāra. When these hexatonic and pentatonic forms are being performed, the notes Niṣāda and Gāndhāra act as discordant notes (*vivādī*). The song-styles, rhythms, units (*kalās*), and so on, are like those of the *Ṣāḍjī* mode. The scale-sequence starts with Madhyama. The application is like that of the *Ṣaḍjodīcyavā* mode. —85—87—

The commentaries clarify that while Niṣāda is usually weak, its role changes when it or Gāndhāra acts as the dominant note.</summary>

<note>The following is the commentary (Kallinātha's *Kalānidhi*) explaining the rules of this mode.</note>

**[Kallinātha’s Commentary]:** Regarding the statement, "**Ṣaḍja and Madhyama are the final notes (*nyāsas*)**": this means that either Ṣaḍja or Madhyama must be used to conclude the melodic phrase. 

Regarding the statement, "**All seven notes are semi-finals (*apanyāsas*)**": it should be understood that, depending on the melodic beauty (*rakti*) governed by the starting note (*graha*) and the dominant note (*aṃśa*), all seven notes may alternately serve as semi-final resting points as appropriate.

In the scale of pure notes of the <term>Ṣaḍja-grāma<gloss>the standard ancient Indian parent scale</gloss></term>, in the first rhythmic unit (*kalā*), there are two notes in the middle register, Ma and Ga; one Sa-Ga; one Pa; one Dha-Pa; one Ma; one Ni-Dha; and one Ni-Ma. Thus, there are eight <term>laghus<gloss>short beats or time units</gloss></term>. 

The syllables of the phrase "**Rajanivadhūmukha**" (the face of the night-bride) are mapped as follows: 
- The syllables *Ra-ja-ni* correspond to the notes Ma, Ga, and Sa. 
- The remainder of that beat is Ga. 
- The syllables *va-dhū* correspond to Pa and Dha. 
- The remaining notes are Pa and Ma. 
- The syllable *mu* corresponds to Ni. 
- The remainder is Dha. 
- The syllable *kha* corresponds to Ni. 
- The remainder is Ma (1).

In the second rhythmic unit, in the high register (*tāra*), there are three notes, Ma-Ma-Sa; one Ri-Ga; one Ma-Ga; in the middle register, one Ni-Dha; one Pa-Dha; and one Pa. Thus, there are eight *laghus*. The syllables of the phrase "**Vilasaloce**" (with charming eyes) are mapped beginning with the syllables *vi-la*...

<header>236 Saṅgītaratnākara [On Modes—</header>

### Now, the Gāndhārodīcyavā Mode

In the **Gāndhārodīcyavā** <note>original: "gāndhārodīcyavā"; likely meaning the "Northern" (udīcyavā) variation of the Gāndhāra mode</note> mode, the two tonics <term>aṃśas</term> are **Ṣaḍja** (Sa) and **Madhyama** (Ma). || 88 ||

It is known to be hexatonic <term>ṣāḍava</term> <note>A six-note scale</note> when the note **Ri** is omitted. When it is complete (heptatonic), the non-tonic notes are considered weak <term>alpatā</term>. In the hexatonic state, the notes **Ni**, **Dha**, **Pa**, and **Ga** are declared to be weak. || 89 ||

A specific movement <term>saṅgati</term> is known between **Ri** and **Dha**. The scale <term>mūrcchanā</term> begins with the note **Dhaivata** (Dha). The rhythm <term>tāla</term> is known as **Catpuṭa**, consisting of sixteen units <term>kalās</term>. || 90 ||

Its application <term>viniyoga</term> is prescribed for sacred stage songs <term>dhruva-gāna</term> and during the fourth act of a theatrical performance <term>prekṣaṇa</term>.

***

<note>The following section details the mapping of syllables to specific notes for the song following the pattern on the previous page</note>

**Pa-Ma-Gā** is one; **Ga-Ma** are two; thus making eight <term>laghus</term> <note>short beats</note>. Regarding the syllables of **"Pra-ṇa-mā-mi de-vam"**:
With **"pra"** and **"ṇā"** are the two **Ma** notes; the remainders are **Ga** and **Ma**; with **"mā"** is **Ma**; the remainders are **Ni** and **Dha**; with **"mi"** is **Pa**. 
The remainder is **Dha**; with **"de"** is **Pa**; the remainders are **Ma** and **Ga**; with **"vam"** is **Ga**; the remainder is **Ma** (10).

In the eleventh [measure], in the **middle register**, one is **Dha**; one is **Pa-Dha**; one is **Pa-Ri**; one is **Ri-Ga**; one is **Ma-Ga**; one is **Ri-Ga**; one is **Sa-Dha-Sa**; and one is **Sa**; thus making eight **laghus**. Regarding the syllables of **"Ku-mu-dā-dhi-vā-sī"**:
With **"ku"** and **"mu"** are **Dha** and **Pa**; the remainder is **Dha**; with **"dā"** is **Pa**; the remainder is **Ri**; with **"dhi"** is **Ri**; the remainder is **Ga**; with **"vā"** is **Ma**; the remainders are **Ga, Ri, Ga, Sa, Dha, Sa**; with **"sī"** is **Sa** (11).

In the twelfth, in the **middle register**, one is **Ni-Dha**; two are **Sa-Ri**; one is **Ma-Ga-Ma**; and there are four **Ma** notes; thus making eight **laghus**. With **"nam"** is **Ni**; the others are the remainders (12).

> The eyes that are the playful charm of the Night-bride's face,
> Resplendent like the foam on the petals of a blooming water-lily;
> Bringing joy to the eyes and hearts of all lovers—
> I bow to that God who dwells within the lily. 
> —Thus ends the **Ṣaḍjamadhyamā** mode. || 10 ||

***

**Kallinātha's Commentary:** Regarding the verse "In the **Gāndhārodīcyavā**...": "In the state of completeness" <note>original: "pūrṇatve"</note> refers to the heptatonic condition. "Weakness of the non-tonics" means that because the two tonics (Sa and Ma) are equal and dominant, the other notes—Ri, Ga, Pa, Dha, and Ni—are used sparingly. In the hexatonic state...

### The Sangītaratnākara [On the Melodic Modes]

### Now, Raktagāndhārī

The dominant notes in the mode **Raktagāndhārī** are five, excluding **Dhaivata** (Dha) and **Rishabha** (Ri). || 91 ||
Skipping over **Rishabha** (Ri), one should perform a close transition between **Shadja** (Sa) and **Gāndhāra** (Ga).
By omitting **Rishabha** (Ri) or **Dhaivata** (Dha), it is considered <term>hexatonic</term> <note>A six-note scale, called ṣāḍava</note> or <term>pentatonic</term> <note>A five-note scale, called auḍuva</note> respectively. || 92 ||
The notes **Nishāda** (Ni) and **Dhaivata** (Dha) are used frequently. The fifth note, **Pañcama** (Pa), forbids the hexatonic form.
The notes **Shadja** (Sa), **Nishāda** (Ni), **Madhyama** (Ma), and **Pañcama** (Pa) forbid the pentatonic form. **Shadja** (Sa) and **Gāndhāra** (Ga) are played in conjunction. || 93 ||
The rhythm used is the <term>pañcapāṇi</term> <note>A specific ancient rhythmic pattern</note>; the <term>mūrchanā</term> <note>The underlying scale or sequence of notes</note> begins with **Rishabha** (Ri) in the Shāḍjī group.
This mode is to be employed in the <term>dhruvā</term> <note>A formal stage song</note> during the third act of a theatrical performance. || 94 ||

In the **fourteenth unit**, in the **high register**, the notes are **Ni, Ni, Pa, Dha, Ni**—making five notes; then three **Ga** notes; thus making eight <term>laghus</term> <note>short beats</note>. The syllables of the song are <gloss>I bow to Gauri</gloss> <note>original Sanskrit: "praṇamāmi gaurī"</note>; the fourth and seventh beats are the remaining durations. (14) In the **fifteenth unit**, in the **high register**, the notes are **Ni, Ni, Dha, Pa, Dha, Pa, Ma, Pa**—eight laghus. The syllables are <gloss>having approached the pair of feet</gloss> <note>original Sanskrit: "caraṇayugamanupe"</note>. (15) In the **sixteenth unit**, in the **high register**, the notes are **Dha, Pa, Sa, Sa**—four notes; then four **Ma** notes; thus making eight laghus. The syllable *maṃ* is the note **Dha**; the others follow. (16)

> I bow to the incomparable pair of feet of the Goddess Gauri, which are kissed by the divine mark on her lovely lotus-like face; feet that shine like a fully blossomed golden lotus; a pure abode for the mirrors of her exceedingly beautiful nails; the ones that once struck the body of the God of Love <note>Referring to a mythological episode where the Goddess's feet are involved in the subduing of Kama, the god of desire</note>.

->The Gāndhārodīcyavā Mode || 11 ||<-

(Kallinātha's Commentary:) **Regarding "The dominant notes":** The five dominant notes are **Sa, Ga, Ma, Pa,** and **Ni**, excluding **Dhaivata** and **Rishabha**. Regarding "Skipping over **Rishabha**, a close transition between **Sa** and **Ga** should be performed": "Skipping over **Rishabha**" means without using the note **Rishabha**.

<margin>As stated: "In this mode, the movement between Gāndhāra and Shadja occurs without Rishabha."</margin>

# Chapter 7] The First Section on Musical Notes

...as stated in the words of the Sage <note>Referring to the ancient authority Bharata Muni</note>. In this context, regarding the notes **Shadja** (Sa) and **Gāndhāra** (Ga), there is a "proximity" and "union" with the other notes—**Madhyama** (Ma), **Pañcama** (Pa), **Dhaivata** (Dha), and **Nishāda** (Ni)—as appropriate. Here, <term>proximity</term> <note>Sanskrit: saṃnidhi</note> refers to the uninterrupted succession of two notes that have different <term>short-beat</term> <note>Sanskrit: laghu</note> durations. <term>Union</term> <note>Sanskrit: melana</note> is intended to mean the uninterrupted succession of two or three notes within the duration of a single short-beat. These two techniques should be performed to the best of one's ability.

The terms **hexatonic** and **pentatonic** <note>Sanskrit: ṣāḍava-auḍuvam</note> are treated here as a compound in the singular. Regarding the "frequency" <note>Sanskrit: bahutvam</note> of **Nishāda** (Ni) and **Dhaivata** (Dha): although **Nishāda** (Ni) already attains frequency by being a dominant note, its mention here is for the sake of emphasis. As for **Dhaivata** (Dha), which normally causes the pentatonic state <note>by being omitted</note>, even though it is absent in the pentatonic stage, it is assigned "frequency" as an exception to its usual weakness in the full and hexatonic stages. This is understood from the Sage's words:

> "In this mode, the **Dhaivata** and the **seventh** <note>Nishāda</note> are both strong."

The dominant note **Pañcama** (Pa) "hates" <note>forbids or is incompatible with</note> the hexatonic form. The sense is that when **Pañcama** itself becomes the dominant note, it does not permit the hexatonic form produced by the omission of **Rishabha** (Ri). This is because in the <term>Madhyama-grāma</term> <note>One of the two standard parent scales of ancient Indian music</note>, there is a consonance between **Pañcama** and **Rishabha**.

The notes **Shadja** (Sa), **Nishāda** (Ni), **Madhyama** (Ma), and **Pañcama** (Pa) "hate" the pentatonic form. That is to say, when Sa, Ni, Ma, or Pa are the dominant notes, they do not permit the pentatonic form produced by the omission of **Rishabha** (Ri) and **Dhaivata** (Dha). Only **Gāndhāra** (Ga) as a dominant note permits the pentatonic form. On this point, even though **Nishāda** (Ni) and **Dhaivata** (Dha) lack a consonant relationship with the dominant **Shadja** (Sa) and others, the rejection of the pentatonic form is understood from the Sage’s words:

> "In the modes **Gāndhārī** and **Raktagāndhārī**, the notes **Shadja**, **Madhyama**, **Pañcama**,
> and the **seventh** <note>Nishāda</note> are to be known; in these, the pentatonic state shall not occur."

Therefore, in hexatonic and similar modes, the prohibition of the hexatonic form is occasionally fixed because the omission of a note consonant with the dominant is not accepted. As the Sage's words state:

> "These seven are excluded from hexatonic forms due to the omission of a consonant note."

It should be observed that in pentatonic and similar modes, the prohibition of a potentially applicable pentatonic form arises sometimes from the omission of the dominant and sometimes simply from the scriptural injunction itself. Regarding the statement: "**Shadja** (Sa) and **Gāndhāra** (Ga) are played in conjunction..."

<header>The Ocean of Music [Section on Melodic Modes-</header>

In this **Raktagāndhārī** mode, the <term>final note</term> <note>Sanskrit: nyāsa; the note on which a melody must end</note> is **Gāndhāra** (Ga). The <term>intermediate final note</term> <note>Sanskrit: apanyāsa; a note used for secondary pauses within the melody</note> is **Madhyama** (Ma).

The musical arrangement <note>Sanskrit: prastāra</note> of this mode is as follows:

### 12. Raktagāndhārī

1. ->Pa Ni Sa Sa Ga Ga Sa Pa Ni<-
->Him, whose forehead-mark is the young moon<- <note>original: "taṃ bāla-rajani-kara-tilaka-bhū-"</note>

2. ->Sā Mā Pa Pa Ma Ma Ga Ga<-
->the protector of the world, the Lord<- <note>original: "ka-ra-ti-la-ka-bhū-pa"</note>

3. ->Ma Pa Dha Pa Ma Pa Ri* Ga<- <note>*The transcription "ऋप म्ग" likely refers to the notes Rishabha (Ri) and Gāndhāra (Ga)</note>
->of the hosts [of spirits]<- <note>original: "ṇa-vi-bhū-"</note>

4. ->Ma Ma Ma Ma Ma Ma Ma Ma<-
->...[continued]<- <note>original: "tiṃ"</note>

5. ->Dhā Nī Pā Ma-Pa Dhā Nī Pā Pā<-
->[Rhythmic syllables/No lyrics]<-

6. ->Mā Pā Mā Dha-Ni Pā Pā Pā Pā<-
->[Rhythmic syllables/No lyrics]<-

---

Regarding the pairing of the two notes <note>Shadja (Sa) and Gāndhāra (Ga)</note>: as stated previously, there is a "union" and "proximity" involving notes other than **Rishabha** (Ri). This means that these two notes should occasionally be performed in relation to one another. The mention of rhythmic patterns like the **five-handed clap** <note>Sanskrit: pañcapāṇi</note> and others is for the sake of clarity. || 91—94 ||

<gloss>Commentary by Simhabhūpāla (The Sudhākara):</gloss> He defines **Raktagāndhārī** starting with the words "The dominants should be..." In the Raktagāndhārī mode, there are five <term>dominant notes</term> <note>Sanskrit: amshas; the most important notes that govern the melody's character</note>, excluding **Dhaivata** (Dha) and **Rishabha** (Ri). By skipping the note **Rishabha**, a melodic link is formed between **Shadja** (Sa) and **Gāndhāra** (Ga). 

The <term>hexatonic</term> <note>Sanskrit: ṣāḍava; a six-note scale</note> form of this mode is created by omitting **Rishabha**. The <term>pentatonic</term> <note>Sanskrit: auḍuvita; a five-note scale</note> form is created by omitting both **Rishabha** and **Dhaivata**. There is an abundance of the notes **Nishāda** (Ni) and **Dhaivata** (Dha). 

When **Pañcama** (Pa) is the dominant note, the hexatonic form is not used. When **Shadja** (Sa), **Nishāda** (Ni), **Madhyama** (Ma), or **Pañcama** (Pa) are the dominant notes, the pentatonic form is not used. There is a melodic association between **Shadja** and **Gāndhāra**. The <term>parent scale</term> <note>Sanskrit: mūrchanā</note> begins with **Rishabha**. The application of rhythmic units <note>Sanskrit: kalā</note> and time follows the rules of the **Shāḍjī** mode. || 91—94 ||

### Now, the Kaiśikī Mode

In the Kaiśikī mode, any note except Rishabha <term>Ri; the second note</term> can serve as the dominant note <term>aṃśa</term>. When Nishāda <term>Ni; the seventh note</term> and Dhaivata <term>Dha; the sixth note</term> are the dominant notes, the final note <term>nyāsa</term> must be Pañcama <term>Pa; the fifth note</term>. In other instances, the two notes with two microtones <note>Gāndhāra (Ga) and Niṣāda (Ni)</note> are considered the concluding notes. ॥ 95 ॥

Some authorities hold that when Nishāda and Dhaivata are the dominant notes, the concluding notes are Niṣāda, Gāndhāra, and Pañcama. The hexatonic <term>ṣāḍava</term> and pentatonic <term>auḍuvita</term> forms of this mode are achieved by omitting Ri and Dha, or Ri and Ga. ॥ 96 ॥

The note Rishabha <term>Ri</term> should be used sparingly, while Niṣāda and Pañcama are used frequently. There is a mutual melodic relationship between the dominant notes. In the hexatonic and pentatonic forms, Pañcama and Dhaivata are prescribed as the final notes respectively. ॥ 97 ॥

The rhythmic structures like *pañcapāṇi* should be applied as they are in the *Ṣāḍjī* mode. The scale <term>mūrcchanā</term> begins with Gāndhāra. This mode is to be employed in the *Dhruvā* songs of the theatrical performance known as *Pañcama-prekṣaṇa*. ॥ 98 ॥

In the seventh time-unit, the notes are as previously stated. The syllables are "the lotus-like face" <note>original: "va-da-nā-ra-vim"</note>; the fourth, seventh, and eighth beats are rests (8). 

In the ninth time-unit, in the middle register, there are eight short beats of **Pa**. The first beat corresponds to the syllable "da" <note>from "ravindam"</note>; the rest follow (9).

In the tenth time-unit, in the middle register, the notes are **Ri Ga Sa Sa Ri Ga Ga Ga**, making eight short beats. These correspond to the syllables "causing delight" <note>original: "prī-ti-ka-ram"</note>; here, the final **Ga** notes are rests (10).

In the eleventh time-unit, in the high register <term>tāra</term>, there are two **Ga** notes; one **Pa**; one **Dha-Ma** combination; one **Dha**; one **Ni-Dha** combination; and two **Pa** notes. This totals eight short beats. All these are sustained notes (11).

In the twelfth time-unit, in the high register, there are three **Ma-Pa** notes; one **Pa-Ri-Ga**; and four **Ga** notes. This totals eight short beats. All these are sustained notes (12).

> I bow to Him <note>Shiva</note>, who is adorned with the splendor of the young moon as His crest-ornament. 
> I prostrate before Him, who brings delight to the lotus-face of Gauri. 
> Thus ends the *Raktagāndhārī* mode. ॥ 12 ॥

<gloss>Commentary by Kallinātha:</gloss> 
Regarding the verse beginning "In the Kaiśikī...": "Except for Rishabha" <note>original: "ṛṣabhānye"</note> means that the six notes—Shadja, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, Dhaivata, and Niṣāda—are the dominant notes <term>aṃśas</term>. The phrase "when Ni and Dha are dominant..." explains that the ending note <term>nyāsa</term> is Pañcama. As it is said:

->'When Dhaivata or Niṣāda is the dominant note, the final note is desired to be Pañcama.'<-

<header>Chapter 7] First Section on Notes 245</header>

In this *Kaiśikī* mode, the notes Gāndhāra <term>Ga</term>, Pañcama <term>Pa</term>, and Niṣāda <term>Ni</term> are the final notes <term>nyāsa</term>. All six or seven notes, excluding Rishabha <term>Ri</term>, serve as intermediate stop-notes <term>apanyāsa</term>. The structural arrangement <term>prastāra</term> of this mode is as follows:

### 13. Kaiśikī

| | | | | | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | Pa | Dha-Ni | Pa | Dha-Ni | Ga | Ga | Ga | Ga |
| | Ke | | lī | | ha | | ta | |
<note>The syllables "Ke-lī-ha-ta" likely refer to a phrase like "destroyed by sport" or "playful strike," part of a hymn to a deity.</note>

This is regulated according to the words of the Sage <note>The "Sage" refers to Bharata Muni, the semi-divine author of the Nāṭyaśāstra</note>. The meaning is that at other times, the notes excluding Niṣāda and Dhaivata—namely Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, and Pa—can serve as dominant notes <term>aṃśa</term>. The notes with two microtones <term>śrutis</term>, Niṣāda and Gāndhāra, are traditionally accepted as the final notes.

However, other authorities such as Mataṅga <note>Mataṅga is the author of the *Bṛhaddeśī*, a pivotal 8th-century musicological text</note> maintain that when Niṣāda and Dhaivata are the dominant notes, all three—Niṣāda, Gāndhāra, and Pañcama—can be the final notes. This is because Mataṅga stated: "When Dhaivata and Niṣāda are the dominant notes, Pañcama is also a final note." This view effectively restricts the finality of Pañcama to the specific case where Niṣāda and Dhaivata are the dominant notes. 

The terms "omission of Ri" and "omission of Dha" are treated here as a single concept. This means that Rishabha is used sparingly even in the "complete" seven-note version of the scale. Regarding the frequency of Niṣāda and Pañcama: even though they are frequently used as dominant notes, the Sage's decree that "the final note and Pañcama are powerful" means they are used much more often than the other dominant notes. 

When Pañcama and Dhaivata become the dominant notes, the mode is seen in its hexatonic <term>ṣāḍava</term> and pentatonic <term>auḍuvita</term> forms respectively. The sequence is: Pañcama results in the six-note form, and Dhaivata results in the five-note form. This is because, in the *Madhyama-grāma* <term>the scale based on the middle note</term>, Rishabha is a consonant with Pañcama, and thus in the Dhaivata-dominant version, it cannot be omitted. The comparison to the *Ṣāḍjī* mode and other details are easily understood. ॥ 95—98 ॥

---

**The Sudhākara Commentary**
Simhabhūpāla defines the *Kaiśikī* mode: In *Kaiśikī*, all six notes except Rishabha can be dominant notes. When Niṣāda and Dhaivata are the dominant notes, only Pañcama is the final note; otherwise, Niṣāda and Gāndhāra are the final notes. However, some others consider Niṣāda, Gāndhāra, and Pañcama as final notes when Niṣāda and Dhaivata are dominant. 

By omitting Rishabha, it becomes hexatonic; by omitting Rishabha and Dhaivata, it becomes pentatonic. Rishabha is used sparingly. Niṣāda and Pañcama are used frequently. There is a mutual melodic agreement between the dominant notes. When Pañcama is the dominant note, the hexatonic form is not used. When Dhaivata is the dominant note, the pentatonic form is not used. Rhythmic patterns like *Ṣaṭpitāputraka* and others should be used as in the *Ṣāḍjī* mode. The scale <term>mūrcchanā</term> begins with Gāndhāra. It is employed in the *Dhruvā* songs during the *Pañcama-prekṣaṇa* <note>A specific act or scene in ancient Sanskrit theater</note>. ॥ 95—98 ॥

### Section 7] First Chapter on Notes (Svaras)

->(Kallinātha) Six or seven notes, excluding Rishabha (Re), serve as secondary cadences (*apanyāsa*).<-

> “Sometimes even Rishabha may be a secondary cadence here”

This is according to the statement of the Sage <note>original: *munivacanāt*; referring to Bharata Muni, the author of the *Nāṭyaśāstra*</note>. The word “sometimes” implies this is an option even when the scale is full <note>meaning a heptatonic or seven-note scale</note>. In the arrangement of pure notes belonging to the Middle Scale <term>mādhyamagrāmika: a fundamental scale in ancient Indian music starting on the note Madhyama</term>, in the **first segment** (*kalā*), in the middle register, there is one Pa; one Dha-Ni; one Pa; one Dha-Ni; and four Ga notes; thus, there are eight short beats (*laghus*). For the syllables *Ke-lī-ha-ta*: the two syllables *Ke-lī* correspond to the two Pa notes; *ha-ta* correspond to the first and third Ga notes; the remaining notes are assigned to the other syllables (1).

In the **second segment**, in the middle register, there are two Pa notes; one Ma; two pairs of Ni-Dha; and three Pa notes; totaling eight short beats. For the syllables *kāma-tanu* <note>meaning "the body of the God of Love"</note>: the syllable *kā* is Pa; the following is Pa; the syllables *ma* and *ta* are Ma and Ni; the remainder is Dha; the syllable *nu* is Ni; and the rest are the subsequent notes (2).

In the **third segment**, in the middle register, there are two Dha-Ni; one high-register Sa; one middle-register Sa; and four Rishabhas (Ri); totaling eight short beats. These correspond to the syllables *vibhrama-vilāsam* <note>meaning "playful manifestation"</note>; the second and seventh beats are the remaining notes (3).

In the **fourth segment**, in the middle register, there are three Sa notes; two Ri-Ga notes; and three Ma notes; totaling eight short beats. These correspond to the syllables *tilaka-yutam* <note>meaning "adorned with a forehead mark"</note>; the remaining notes are the Ma notes (4).

In the **fifth segment**, in the lower register <note>original: *mandra*</note>, the notes are Ma-Dha-Ni-Dha-Ma-Dha-Ma-Pa, making eight short beats. For the syllables *mūrdhordhva-bālā* <note>meaning "the young moon/girl high upon the head"</note>; the second, fourth, and seventh notes are the remaining ones (5).

In the **sixth segment**, in the middle register, there are Ga, Ri, and three Sa notes; one Dha-Ni; and four Rishabhas; totaling eight short beats. For the syllables *soma-nibham* <note>meaning "resembling the moon"</note>: *so-ma-ni* correspond to Ga, Sa, and Dha; the syllable *bham* is the first Ri; the rest are the other notes (6).

In the **seventh segment**, in the middle register, there are two Ga-Ri; two Sa; two Dha; and two Ma; totaling eight short beats. For the syllables *mukha-kamalam* <note>meaning "the lotus-like face"</note>; the notes from the sixth beat onwards are the remaining ones (7).

In the **eighth segment**, in the middle register, there are three Ga; two Ma; one Ni-Dha-Ni; and two Ni; totaling eight short beats. For the syllables *asama-hāṭa* <note>meaning "incomparable gold"</note>: *a-sa-ma* are the Ga notes; the rest is Ma; *hā* is the Ma note; the rest are the Ni-Dha-Ni sequence; *ṭa* is the Ni note; and the rest is the final Ni (8).

In the **ninth segment**, in the middle register, there are two Ga; two Ni; and four Ga; totaling eight short beats. For the syllables *ka-saroja* <note>meaning "lotus flower"</note>: the syllables *ka-sa-ro-ja* correspond to the Ga and Ni notes; the syllable *ja* is specifically the fifth Ga; the rest are the other notes (9).

In the **tenth segment**, in the high register <note>original: *tāra*</note>, there are two Ga; two Ni; one Ni-Dha; and three Pa notes...

### Now, the Madhyamodīcyavā Mode

> The Madhyamodīcyavā mode is considered to have the fifth note <term>Pañcama: the fifth note, 'Pa', equivalent to G in the C-major scale</term> as its dominant note <term>Aṃśa: the primary note that carries the melody's weight</term>, and it is always "full" <note>pūrṇā: a heptatonic scale containing all seven notes</note>. Its remaining characteristics should be understood as being the same as the Gāndhārodīcyavā mode. || 99 ||

> Its parent scale <term>Mūrcchanā: the specific sequence of seven notes</term> begins with the middle note <note>Madhyama or 'Ma'</note>, and its rhythm is set to the *Cañcatpuṭa* meter. It is traditionally used in the *Dhruvā* <note>a specific type of stage song in ancient Indian drama</note> of the fourth act of a theatrical performance. || 100 ||

In this way, there are eight short beats <term>Laghus: a unit of time in ancient rhythm</term>. For the phrase *hṛdi sukhadām* <note>meaning "giving pleasure to the heart"</note>, there are five beats in sequence; the remaining ten are for the other syllables. In the **eleventh segment**, in the high register, the notes are Ma-Pa-Ma; then two Ma notes; thus making eight short beats. These correspond to the syllables *pra-ṇa-mā-mi lo-ca* <note>meaning "I bow to the eye..."</note>; the fourth and eighth beats are the remaining notes (11). In the **twelfth segment**, in the high register, the notes are Sa-Ma-Ga; then one note as the conclusion; then two Ni notes; then two Ma-Ga notes; thus making eight short beats. For the syllables *na-vi-śe-ṣam* <note>meaning "the special one"</note>—the syllables *na-vi-śe-ṣi* correspond to Sa-Ma-Ga; the seventh note is Ni; the others are the remaining notes (12).

->The song for the Kaiśikī mode:<-

> He whose playful movements and charms are joined with a decorative mark <note>tilaka</note>, who resembles the crescent moon rising above the head, whose lotus-face is like refined gold, and who grants joy to the heart—I bow to that special Eye <note>referring to the third eye of Lord Shiva</note>.
->This concludes the Kaiśikī mode. || 13 ||<-

(Kallinātha) **Pañcama as the dominant**: This means the fifth note (Pa) alone is the *aṃśa* <note>dominant note</note>. **Always full**: This means it never becomes hexatonic <note>ṣāḍava: six notes</note> or pentatonic <note>auḍuva: five notes</note>. The "remaining characteristics"—such as the specific relationship between the notes Ri and Dha, or the fact that it consists of sixteen rhythmic segments—should be known from the description of the Gāndhārodīcyavā mode; those traits are to be applied here as well. The parent scale beginning with Madhyama is known as *Sauvīrī*. The rest is easy to understand. || 99, 100 ||

(Siṃhabhūpāla) He defines the Madhyamodīcyavā mode: **Pañcama as the dominant**. In this mode, the fifth note is the primary tone. Its "fullness" refers to it having all seven notes. It never lacks notes to become six-toned or five-toned. The rest of the characteristics are to be known as being like the Gāndhārodīcyavā mode. The scale is *Madhyamādi* <note>starting on Ma</note>. The meter is *Cañcatpuṭa*. Its application is in the fourth act's song (*Dhruvā*). || 99, 100 ||

### The Section on Melodic Modes [Jātis]

### Now, the Kārmāravī Mode

In the **Kārmāravī** mode, the prevailing notes <term>aṃśas: the structural, "soul" notes of a melody</term> are Niṣāda (Ni), Riṣabha (Ri), and Dhaivata (Dha). Many other notes are also described as non-prevailing <term>anaṃśas: notes that do not serve as the tonic or dominant</term> because of the use of "interstitial movement" <term>antaramārga: a melodic technique where subordinate notes are used frequently to bridge the gaps between dominant notes</term>. || 101 ||

The note Gāndhāra (Ga) is used very frequently and is associated with all the prevailing notes. The rhythm used here is the *Caccatpuṭa* <note>A traditional rhythmic meter consisting of specific patterns of long and short beats</note>, consisting of sixteen segments <term>kalās: rhythmic units</term>. The scale progression <term>mūrcchanā</term> begins with the note Șaḍja (Sa). || 102 ||

It is employed in the *Dhruvā* <note>A specific type of theatrical song used in ancient Sanskrit drama</note> during the scenic presentation <term>prekṣaṇa</term> associated with the note Pañcama (Pa).

> I bow to Lord Shiva, whose form is half-bodied <note>original: "dehārdharūpam" — a reference to Ardhanārīśvara, the form of Shiva and Parvati joined as one</note>, possessing a pure and immense radiance like the stainless moon, the jasmine, and the white water-lily. 
> He is the invincible one, worshiped by the noble divine hosts, possessing the divine luster of a golden lotus. 
> Praised by the gods, he is as swift as the wind or the mind; his voice resonates like thunderclouds and the ocean; he is ever-smiling.
> I bow to the peaceful Shiva, the crusher of the demon armies, at whose feet the three worlds bow in reverence.

->Thus ends the Madhyamodīcyavā mode. || 14 ||<-

**(Commentary by Kallinātha)** Regarding the phrase *In the Kārmāravī*: The non-prevailing notes mentioned here are Sa, Ga, and Ma. Because they are non-prevailing, they are also considered minor in importance. However, due to the technique of *antaramārga* (interstitial movement) and their association with all the dominant notes, they are used repeatedly and thus appear "frequent" in performance. 

One might ask: if both the dominant and non-dominant notes are used frequently, what is the difference between them? It is explained thus: The note that is used frequently as a stable, resting point <term>sthāyitva</term> is the dominant (*aṃśa*). However, the note that is used frequently for the sake of melodic movement and transition <term>saṃcāritva</term> is the subordinate note (*anaṃśa*) relying on the interstitial path. This is the distinction to be made. Even though the general rule states that "abundance in usage is a characteristic of the dominant note," we must understand that this "abundance" specifically refers to the note's role as a stable melodic anchor <note>original: "ya raktti" — referring to the note that provides the specific aesthetic color or 'rasa' to the mode</note>. 

By this, it is meant that in this specific mode, the technique of interstitial movement must be performed. As the sage Bharata says:

> "Subordinate notes can indeed become strong through constant application in practice."

The note Gāndhāra (Ga) is especially frequent because it is associated with all the dominant notes, including their various secondary forms. This association with all dominant notes is also...

In this Kārmāravī mode, the note Pañcama <note>the fifth note, 'Pa'</note> serves as the final cadence <term>nyāsa: the note that concludes a melodic phrase or composition</term>. The prevailing notes <term>aṃśas</term> themselves serve as the secondary cadences <term>apanyāsas: notes used for intermediate pauses</term>.

> “The note Gāndhāra <note>Ga</note> should specifically have movement in all directions.” 

This is according to the words of the Sage <note>original: "munivacanāt" — referring to Bharata Muni, the legendary author of the Nāṭyaśāstra</note>. The rhythmic pattern *Caccatpuṭa* and other details are easy to understand. || 101—102 ||

(Su.) Simhabhūpāla defines Kārmāravī: **In the Kārmāravī...** In this mode, the prevailing notes <term>aṃśas</term> are Niṣāda (Ni), Riṣabha (Ri), Pañcama (Pa), and Dhaivata (Dha). Aside from these dominant notes, the notes Șaḍja (Sa), Gāndhāra (Ga), and Madhyama (Ma) are used frequently according to the rules of "interstitial movement" <term>antaramārga: a technique where non-dominant notes are woven between dominant ones to enrich the melody</term>. The note Gāndhāra is used with extreme frequency. It is compatible with all the prevailing notes. The rhythm is *Caccatpuṭa*. There are sixteen rhythmic units <term>kalās</term>. The scale <term>mūrcchanā</term> begins with Șaḍja. It is used in the *Dhruvā* song for the stage presentation <term>prekṣaṇa</term> associated with the note Pañcama <note>This likely refers to scenes involving specific emotional states or characters tied to the fifth note</note>. || 101—102 ||

### Section 7] First Section: On Notes (Svaras)

In the second <term>kalā: a rhythmic unit or time-measure</term>, in the middle register, there are five notes: *Ma-Ga-Sa-Ga-Sa* <note>original: "मगसगसाः"</note>; then three *Nishadas* <term>the seventh note 'Ni'</term>; thus making eight short time-units <term>laghus</term> in total. The syllables of the lyrics are: *vāmāṅgasakta* <note>meaning: "clinging to the left side of His body," referring to the Goddess Parvati as Shiva's half</note>; the second, fourth, and seventh beats are the remaining sustains (2).

In the third unit, in the low register <term>mandra</term>, there are six notes: *Ni-Ma-Ni-Ma-Pa-Pa*; in the middle register, there are two *Gandharas* <term>the third note 'Ga'</term>; thus making eight short units. The syllables are: *matitajeḥprasara*; the fourth beat is the remainder (3).

In the fourth unit, in the middle register, there are four notes: *Ga-Pa-Ma-Pa*; and four *Nishadas*; thus making eight short units. The syllables are: *saudhāṃśukāntī* <note>meaning: "possessing the luster of the moon"</note>; the second, fourth, and seventh beats are the remainders (4).

In the fifth unit, in the high register <term>tāra</term>, there are eight short units: *Ri-Ga-Sa-Ni-Ri-Ga-Ri-Ma*. The syllables are: *phaṇipatimusukham* <note>meaning: "the face of the King of Serpents," referencing Shiva’s snake ornaments</note>; the penultimate and final beats are the remainders (5).

In the sixth unit, in the middle register, there are five notes: *Ri-Ga-Ri-Sa-Ni*; one *Dha-Ni*; and two *Pa-s*; thus making eight short units. The syllables are: *urovipulasāge*; the seventh and eighth beats are the remainders (6).

In the seventh unit, in the high register, there are three notes: *Ma-Pa-Ma*; one *Pa-Ri-Ga*; and in the middle register, four *Ga-s*; thus making eight short units. The syllables are: *raniketam*—the notes *Ma-Pa-Ma* correspond to the syllables *ra-ni-ke*; the seventh beat is the syllable *tam*; the others are the remainders (7).

In the eighth unit, in the middle register, there are three notes: *Ri-Ri-Ga*; one *Sa-Ma*; two *Ma-s*; and two *Pa-s*; thus making eight short units. The syllables are: *sitapannagendra* <note>meaning: "the white king of serpents"</note>; the fourth, fifth, and eighth beats are the remainders (8).

In the ninth unit, in the middle register, there are three notes: *Ma-Pa-Ma*; one *Pa-Ri-Ga*; and four *Ga-s*; thus making eight short units. The syllables are: *matikāntām* <note>meaning: "pleasing to the mind"</note>—the notes *Ma-Pa-Ma* correspond to the syllables *ma-ti-kān*; the seventh beat is the syllable *tām*; others are the remainders (9).

In the tenth unit, in the middle register, there are eight notes: *Dha-Ni-Pa-Ma-Dha-Ni-Sa-Sa*. The syllables are: *ṣaṇmukhavinoda* <note>meaning: "the delight of the Six-Faced One," referring to Shiva’s son Kartikeya</note>; the second and seventh beats are the remainders (10).

In the eleventh unit, in the middle register, there are eight *Nishada* notes; eight short units. The syllables are: *karapallavāṅgvi* <note>meaning: "fingers like tender leaves"</note>; the fourth and seventh beats are the remainders (11).

In the twelfth unit, in the low register, there are four notes: *Ma-Ma-Dha-Ni*; in the middle register, the note group *Sa-Ni-Ni* counts as one; then three notes: *Dha-Pa-Pa*; thus making eight short units. The syllables are: *lilāvilāsakīle* <note>meaning: "playful like a flame"</note>; the fourth, sixth, seventh, and ninth beats are the remainders (12).

In the thirteenth unit, in the middle register, the notes are the same as the ninth unit. The syllables are: *ninodam*—the notes *Ma-Pa-Ma* correspond to the syllables *ni-no*; the seventh beat is the syllable *dam*; others are the remainders (13).

In the fourteenth unit, in the middle register, there are three notes: *Ni-Ni-Pa*; one *Dha-Ni*; and four *Ga-s*; thus making eight short units. The syllables are: *praṇamāmi deva* <note>meaning: "I bow to the Lord"</note>; the fourth, fifth, and eighth beats are the remainders (14).

In the fifteenth unit, in the high register, there are four notes: *Sa-Ri-Ga-Sa*...

### Now, the Gāndhārapañcamī Mode

In the **Gāndhārapañcamī** mode, the dominant note is the fifth <term>aṃśa: the primary or "soul" note of a melody</term>, which is *Pañcama* (Pa). Furthermore, melodic combinations <term>saṅgati: the grouping or pairing of notes</term> — 103 —

should be performed here extensively with many notes, just as they are in the *Gāndhārī* and *Pañcamī* modes. The rhythm is *Caccatpuṭa* <term>a specific rhythmic cycle or tāla</term> containing sixteen units <term>kalā: a rhythmic beat or measure</term>, and the scale <term>mūrcchanā: a sequential melodic structure</term> begins with the note *Gāndhāra* (Ga). — 104 —

It is employed in the singing of the *Dhruvā* songs <term>fixed songs used in classical drama</term> related to the fourth theatrical performance <note>original: "turyaprekṣaṇa," likely referring to the fourth stage or act of a play</note>.

<note>This section continues the notation from the previous page</note>
There are four *Nishādas* <term>the seventh note 'Ni'</term>; thus making eight short time-units <term>laghus</term>. The syllables of the lyrics are: *yajñopavīta* <note>meaning: "the sacred thread worn by the twice-born"</note>; the second, fourth, and seventh beats are the remaining sustains (15). In the sixteenth unit, in the high register <term>tāra</term>, there are two *Nis*; two *Dhas* <term>the sixth note 'Dhaivata'</term>; and four *Pas*; thus making eight short units. The syllable *kam* <note>the final syllable of the word "yajñopavīta-kam"</note> is the first *Ni*; the others follow as sustains (16).

> I bow to the Sacred Thread of the God—to Him who is the immovable Shiva <note>Sthāṇu</note>, to whose lovely left side She [the Goddess Parvati] is attached, whose splendor spreads like the light of the moon-mansion, whose chest is a vast ocean-abode, whose face is adorned by the Lord of Serpents, who is exceedingly beautiful, and who delights in the play of the fingers of the six-faced child [the god Kartikeya].
> — Thus concludes the song in the **Kārmāravī** mode. || 15 ||

**(Kallinātha's Commentary):** Regarding the verse "In the **Gāndhārapañcamī**...": The melodic combinations <term>saṅgati</term> should be performed with many notes, as in the *Gāndhārī* and *Pañcamī* modes. In the description of *Gāndhārī*, it was stated: "Combinations of the others should be made with the final note <term>nyāsa</term> and the dominant note <term>aṃśa</term>." Just so, here, with the notes *Gāndhāra* and *Pañcama* acting as the final and dominant notes, combinations are made with the other notes: *Sa, Ri, Ma, Dha,* and *Ni*. Furthermore, because it was said of the *Pañcamī* mode that combinations occur "of *Ri* and *Ma*," here too the notes *Ṛṣabha* (Ri) and *Madhyama* (Ma) should be combined with each other. This is the meaning of the instruction to perform combinations with many notes. The rest is easy to understand. — 103 — 104 —

**(Siṃhabhūpāla's Commentary):** He defines the **Gāndhārapañcamī** mode: In *Gāndhārapañcamī*, the dominant note is *Pañcama*. The melodic combination of notes is similar to *Gāndhārī* and *Pañcamī*. The rhythm is *Caccatpuṭa*. There are sixteen units. The scale begins with the note *Gāndhāra*. It is used in the *Dhruvā* song for the fourth theatrical spectacle. — 103 — 104 —

In this **Gāndhārapañcamī** mode, the note *Gāndhāra* (Ga) is the final note <term>nyāsa: the note on which a musical phrase or the entire composition ends</term>. The notes *Riṣabha* (Ri) and *Pañcama* (Pa) are the secondary final notes <term>apanyāsa: notes used to conclude intermediate sections of a melody</term>. Its rhythmic notation <term>prastāra: a step-by-step layout of musical notes and their corresponding lyrics</term> is as follows:

### [Chapter 7] First Chapter on Musical Notes [Jāti Section]

### Now the Āndhrī Mode

In the <term>Āndhrī</term> <note>a specific melodic mode or 'jāti' in the ancient musical system</note> mode, the <term>aṃśas</term> <note>dominant or 'soul' notes of the melody</note> are <term>Ni</term>, <term>Ri</term>, <term>Ga</term>, and <term>Pa</term> <note>the notes Niṣāda, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, and Pañcama</note>. Likewise, there is a <term>saṅgati</term> <note>melodic pairing or transition</note> between <term>Ri</term> and <term>Ga</term>, and between <term>Ni</term> and <term>Dha</term> <note>Dhaivata</note>. || 105 ||

The melody should proceed according to the sequence of the dominant notes until it reaches the <term>nyāsa</term> <note>the final or concluding note</note>. Its six-note form <note>original: "ṣāḍavaṃ"</note> is created by omitting the note <term>Ṣaḍja</term> <note>the note Sa</note>, and its scale-type <note>original: "mūrchanā"</note> is <term>Madhyamādi</term> <note>the scale starting on the note Madhyama or Ma</note>. || 106 ||

The application of the rhythmic sections and time units <note>original: "kalākālaviniyogāḥ"</note> are said to be the same as previously described <note>referring to the previous mode, Gāndhārapañcamī</note>.

(Kallinātha) "In the Āndhrī the dominant notes..." refers to the fact that <term>Ni</term>, <term>Ri</term>, <term>Ga</term>, and <term>Pa</term> serve alternately as the <term>aṃśas</term> <note>dominant notes</note> and the <term>grahas</term> <note>starting notes</note>. "...likewise <term>Ri</term> and <term>Ga</term>, and <term>Ni</term> and <term>Dha</term>": Here the word "likewise" <note>original: "tathā"</note> is a particle used for conjunction, meaning "and also <term>Ni</term> and <term>Dha</term>." <term>Saṅgati</term> refers to a relationship based on mutual proximity or blending; it should be understood that this pairing "is to be performed."

To provide a rule where there might otherwise be irregularity regarding this mutual pairing, the author says: "it should proceed according to the sequence of the dominant notes until the final note." "According to the sequence of dominant notes" means that among <term>Ni</term>, <term>Ri</term>, <term>Ga</term>, and <term>Pa</term>, whichever note is chosen as the dominant at that time, one should follow its sequence. The rule is that the singer should perform by first sounding that dominant note and then sounding the non-dominant or the alternate dominant notes, until reaching the <term>nyāsa</term>—which is the note that ends the song—meaning until the completion of the song. Thus Bharata <note>the legendary sage and author of the Nāṭyaśāstra</note> says:

> "In this mode, there is a mutual movement between <term>Gāndhāra</term> and <term>Ṛṣabha</term>,
> And also between the seventh <note>Niṣāda</note> and the sixth <note>Dhaivata</note> notes,
> following the sequence toward the final note."

And in another text:

> "Following the sequence of its own dominant note and its pervasiveness, one should proceed until the final note."

The rest of the details are without distinction <note>i.e., they are the same as the previous mode</note>. || 105—106 ||

(Siṃhabhūpāla) He defines the Āndhrī mode: "In the Āndhrī..." In the Āndhrī mode, <term>Niṣāda</term>, <term>Ṛṣabha</term>, <term>Gāndhāra</term>, and <term>Pañcama</term> are the dominant notes. There is a pairing of <term>Ṛṣabha</term> with <term>Gāndhāra</term> and <term>Niṣāda</term> with <term>Dhaivata</term>. There is an ascent from the dominant notes to the final note. It becomes six-noted through the omission of <term>Ṣaḍja</term>. The scale-type is <term>Madhyamādi</term>. The application of rhythmic units and time is like that of <term>Gāndhārapañcamī</term>. || 105—106 ||

<summary>This page defines the technical characteristics of the Āndhrī mode (jāti), specifying its dominant and starting notes, its hexatonic structure (omitting Sa), and its melodic relationships, while noting its rhythmic similarity to the previous mode.</summary>

## [Section 7] First Chapter on Musical Notes

In this <term>Āndhrī</term> <note>a specific musical mode or 'jāti'</note> mode, the note <term>Gāndhāra</term> <note>the note Ga</note> is the <term>nyāsa</term> <note>the concluding note of a musical composition</note>. The <term>aṃśas</term> <note>the dominant or primary notes</note> themselves serve as the <term>apanyāsas</term> <note>the notes used for intermediate pauses within a melodic section</note>. Its <term>prastāra</term> <note>systematic melodic expansion or notation example</note> is as follows:

### 17. Āndhrī

1. Ga Ri Ri Ri Ri Ri Gī Ri
   The young moon flow-er <note>original: "taruṇendu kusuma"; refers to the crescent moon in Lord Shiva's hair</note>

2. Ri Gā Ri Gā Ri Ri Ri Ri
   Set in mat-ted locks <note>original: "khacita jaṭaṃ"</note>

3. Ri Ri Gā Gā Ri Ri Mā Mā
   Wa-ters of the heav-en-ly riv-er <note>original: "tridiva nadī salila"; referring to the Ganges</note>

4. Ri Gā Sā Dha-Ni Nī Nī Nī Nī
   Face washed clean <note>original: "dhauta mukhaṃ"</note>

5. Nī Ri Nī Ri Dha-Ni Dha-Ni Pā Pā
   Loved by the daugh-ter of the moun-tain <note>original: "naga sūnu praṇayaṃ"; referring to the goddess Parvati</note>

6. Mā Pā Mā Ri-Ga Gā Gā Gā Gā
   Trea-sure of the Ve-das <note>original: "veda nidhiṃ"</note>

7. Ri Ri Gā Sa-Sa Mā Mā Pā Pā
   The sprawl-ing snow <note>original: "pariṇāhi tuhina"</note>

8. Mā Pā Mā Ri-Ga Gā Gā Gā Gā
   Moun-tain home <note>original: "śaila gṛhaṃ"</note>

9. Dhā Nī Gā Gā Gā Gā Gā Gā
   Born of nec-tar <note>original: "amṛta bhavaṃ"</note>

10. Pā Pā Mā Ri-Ga Gā Gā Gā Gā
    Be-yond all qual-i-ties <note>original: "guṇa rahitaṃ"; referring to the absolute nature of the Divine</note>

# Saṅgītaratnākara [On Musical Modes]

11. Nī Nī Nī Nī Rī Rī Rī Rī
    Dark-ness, earth, the sun, and moon <note>original: "ta ma va ni ra vi śa śi"; these represent four of the eight forms of Shiva</note>

12. Rī Rī Gā Nī Sā Sā Nī Nī
    Fire, wa-ter, and the wind <note>original: "jva la na ja la pa va na"; continuing the elements that compose Shiva’s cosmic body</note>

13. Pā Pā Māṃ Riṃ Gā Gāṃ Gāṃ Gāṃ
    To the one whose bod-y is the sky <note>original: "ga ga na ta nuṃ"; the eighth element, space or ether</note>

14. Rī' Rī' Gāṃ Saṃ Maṃ Māṃ Māṃ Pā Pāṃ
    I go for ref-uge <note>original: "śa ra ṇaṃ va jā mi"</note>

15. Māṃ Māṃ Nī Nī' Sā Rī' Gāṃ Pāṃ
    With a pure mind, seek-ing the a-bode <note>original: "śu bha ma ti kṛ ta ni la yaṃ"; referring to the practitioner focusing their mind on the deity's dwelling</note>

16. Riṃ Gāṃ Gāṃ Gāṃ Gāṃ Gāṃ Gāṃ Gāṃ
    Him. <note>original: "yaṃ"; the concluding syllable of the prayer</note>

**[Commentary by Kallinātha]**

In the arrangement of pure notes belonging to the <term>Madhyamagrāma</term> <note>the "Middle Scale," one of the two foundational scales in ancient Indian music</note>:

In the first <term>kalā</term> <note>a rhythmic division or phrase</note>, there is one <term>Gāndhāra</term> <note>the note Ga</note> in the middle register; seven <term>Ṛṣabhas</term> <note>the note Ri</note>; thus making eight <term>laghus</term> <note>short beats or units of time</note>. The syllables are "ta-ru-ṇen-du-ku-su-ma" <note>referring back to the start of the hymn on the previous page</note>; the fourth beat is the remainder (1).

In the second section, there are four notes—Ri, Ga, Ri, and Ga—in the middle register; then four Ris; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. The five syllables are "kha-ci-ta-ja-ṭa-m" in order; the others are the remainder (2).

In the third section, there are two of each in the middle register: two Rīs, two Gās, two Rīs, and two Mās; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. The syllables are "tri-di-va-na-dī-sa-li-la" (3).

In the fourth section, there are three notes—Ri, Ga, and Sa—in the middle register; one Dha-Ni <note>a combined melodic unit</note>; and four <term>Niṣādas</term> <note>the note Ni</note> in the lower register; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. The syllables are "dhau-ta-mu-kha-m"—"dhau" is Ri; Ga is the remainder; "ta-mu" are Sa and Dha; Ni is the remainder; "kha-m" is Ni; the others are the remainder (4).

In the fifth section, there is one Ni in the lower register; one Ri in the middle; again one Ni in the lower; one Ri in the middle; two each of Dha and Ni in the lower register; and two Pas; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. The syllables are "na-ga-sū-nu-pra-ṇa-ya-m"; the fourth, sixth, and seventh beats are the remainder (5).

In the sixth section, there are three notes—Ma, Pa, and Ma—in the lower register; one Ri-Ga combination in the middle; and four Gās; thus eight <term>laghus</term>.

### Chapter 7] First Section on Musical Notes

For the syllables "Ve-da-ni-dhi-m": "Ve" is <term>Madhyama</term> <note>the note Ma</note>; the remainder is <term>Pañcama</term> <note>the note Pa</note>; "da-ni" are <term>Madhyama</term> and <term>Ṛṣabha</term> <note>Ma and Ri</note>; the remainder is <term>Gāndhāra</term> <note>the note Ga</note>; "dhi-m" is <term>Gāndhāra</term>; the rest are others (6).

In the seventh <term>kalā</term> <note>rhythmic phrase</note>, in the middle register, there are three notes: Ri-Ri-Ga; Sa-Sa counts as one; two Ma-s; two Pa-s; thus making eight <term>laghus</term> <note>short beats</note>. The syllables are "pa-ri-ṇā-hi-tu-hi-ne"; the fourth and fifth beats are the remainder (7).

In the eighth <term>kalā</term>, the notes are the same as those mentioned for the sixth. The syllables are "śai-la-gṛ-ha-mi-m": "Śai" is Ma; its remainder is Pa; "la-gṛ" are Ma-Ri; the remainder is Ga; "ha-m" is Ga; the rest are others (8).

In the ninth <term>kalā</term>, in the lower register, <term>Dhaivata</term> and <term>Niṣāda</term> <note>Dha and Ni</note> are two; in the middle register, there are six Ga-s; thus making eight <term>laghus</term>. The syllables "a-mṛ-ta-bha-va-m" are continuous; the rest are others (9).

In the tenth <term>kalā</term>, in the middle register, there are three notes: Pa-Pa-Ma; Ri-Ga is one; four Ga-s; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. For the syllables "gu-ṇa-ra-hi-ta-m": "gu-ṇa-ra-hi" correspond to Pa-Pa-Ma-Ri; the remainder is Ga; "ta-m" is Ga; the rest are others (10).

In the eleventh <term>kalā</term>, in the middle register, there are four <term>Niṣādas</term> <note>the note Ni</note> and four <term>Ṛṣabhas</term> <note>the note Ri</note>; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. The syllables are "ta-ma-va-ni-vi-śa-śī" <note>referring to darkness, earth, and the moon</note> (11).

In the twelfth <term>kalā</term>, in the middle register, Ri-Ri-Ga-Ni are four; two Sa-s; two Ni-s; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. The syllables are "jva-la-na-ja-la-pa-va-na" <note>referring to fire, water, and wind</note> (12).

In the thirteenth <term>kalā</term>, in the high register, Pa-Pa-Ma are three; Ri-Ga is one; four Ga-s; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. For the syllables "ga-ga-na-ta-nu-m" <note>referring to the sky-bodied lord</note>: "ga-ga-na-ta" are the first four; "nu-m" is the sixth; others are the rest (13).

In the fourteenth <term>kalā</term>, in the high register, Ri-Ri-Ga are three; Sa-Ma is one; two Ma-s; two Pa-s; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. The syllables are "śa-ra-ṇa-m vra-jā-mi" <note>meaning "I go for refuge"</note>; the fourth, fifth, and eighth are the remainders (14).

In the fifteenth <term>kalā</term>, in the high register, there are two Ma-s; two Ni-s; Sa-Ri-Ga-Pa are four; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. The syllables are "śu-bha-ma-ti-kṛ-ta-ni-la-ya" <note>meaning "the one who abides in a pure mind"</note> (15).

In the sixteenth <term>kalā</term>, in the high register, Ri-Ga is one; there are seven Ga-s; thus eight <term>laghus</term>. "Ya-m" <note>the final syllable of the prayer</note> is Ri; the rest are others (16).

->His matted hair is adorned with flowers and the crescent moon,<-
->His face is washed by the waters of the heavenly river,<-
->The beloved of the daughter of the mountain, a treasure of the Vedas,<-
->Whose home is the expansive, snowy mountain.<-

->Born of nectar, devoid of material qualities,<-
->Whose body is composed of darkness, earth, moon, fire, water, wind, and sky,<-
->I go for refuge to Him, who has made His dwelling in the pure mind.<-
->Thus ends the Āndhrī mode. || 17 ||<-

### The Ocean of Music [Modes-

### Now, the Nandayantī Mode

In the Nandayantī mode, the note <term>Pañcama</term> <note>the fifth note, Pa</note> is the predominant note <note><term>aṃśa</term></note>, while <term>Gāndhāra</term> <note>the third note, Ga</note> is remembered as the starting note <note><term>graha</term></note>. ॥ 107 ॥

However, some scholars of song have stated that <term>Pañcama</term> is the starting note in this mode. There is an abundance of the note <term>Ṛṣabha</term> <note>the second note, Ri</note> in the lower register. This mode is hexatonic <note><term>ṣāḍava</term>, meaning it uses a six-note scale</note> due to the omission of the note <term>Ṣaḍja</term> <note>the first note, Sa</note>. ॥ 108 ॥

The melodic scale <note><term>mūrcchanā</term></note> is *Hṛṣyakā*. The rhythmic cycle <note><term>tāla</term></note> is as described previously, but the rhythmic units <note><term>kalās</term></note> are doubled. Its application is for the singing of <term>Dhruvā</term> songs <note>theatrical songs used to establish a mood</note> during the first act of a performance. ॥ 109 ॥

In this Nandayantī mode, <term>Gāndhāra</term> is the concluding note <note><term>nyāsa</term></note>. <term>Madhyama</term> <note>the fourth note, Ma</note> and <term>Pañcama</term> serve as the intermediate ending notes <note><term>apanyāsas</term></note>.
Its musical arrangement <note><term>prastāra</term></note> follows:

18. Nandayantī

| 2. | Dha Dha Dha Dha Dha Ni Sa-Ni-Ni Dha | <gloss>peaceful <note>original: "myam"</note></gloss> |
| 3. | Pa Pa Pa Pa Pa Pa Pa Pa | <gloss>... <note>original: "myam" continued</note></gloss> |

| 29. | Dhā Dhā Sā Nī Dhā Nī Pā Pā | Slayer of the demon Madhu... <note>original: "Ma-dhu-sū-da-na-su"; Madhusudana is a title for Lord Vishnu.</note> |

**(Commentary by Kallinatha)**
Regarding the **Nandayantī** mode: it is stated that "the note **Gāndhāra** <note>the third note, equivalent to 'Mi'</note> is known as the **starting note** (*graha*)." 

Here, one must understand a point of technical logic. There is a general rule by the Sage Bharata stating that "the **dominant note** (*aṃśa*) should also be the **starting note** (*graha*)." According to this general rule, since **Pañcama** <note>the fifth note, 'Sol'</note> is the dominant note of this mode, it should be the starting note. However, a specific rule exists stating that "the note **Gāndhāra** is to be the starting note in this particular mode." Following the **logic of buttermilk and Kaundinya** <term>takra-kauṇḍinya-nyaya; a principle where a specific rule overrides a general one, similar to saying "give buttermilk to everyone, but give curds to Kaundinya"</term>, the specific rule overrides the general one. 

However, some other masters who are experts in the characteristics of songs suggest an alternative view: they claim that **Pañcama** is indeed the starting note for this mode.

Regarding the instruction "an **abundance of the low Rishabha** <note>the second note, 'Re'</note>": Since the **Nandayantī** mode belongs to the **Middle Scale** (*madhyama-grāma*), it technically does not descend to the low register of the **Rishabha** note. However, it relies on the **Hṛṣyakā scale-sequence** (*mūrcchanā*) which begins from the low **Pañcama**. Because this low **Pañcama** resonates with the **Rishabha**, an abundance of the **Rishabha** note should be performed in the lower register compared to other positions. 

As the Sage **Bharata** himself said: 
> "In this mode, there is an abundance of **Rishabha**, and that is remembered as occurring in the lower register."

Regarding the rhythm, it is said "the rhythm is as before." This means the rhythm is the **Caccatpuṭa** pattern <note>a traditional rhythmic cycle</note>, just as it was in the previously discussed **Āndhrī** mode. 

Regarding the phrase "**double the units** (*kalā*)": This means the duration is doubled compared to the previous example. Where the previous mode had sixteen units, this one has thirty-two. This indicates that the **Caccatpuṭa** rhythm is repeated four times in the "Southern Style" of performance. 

The rest of the text is easy to understand. In the first rhythmic unit of the pure scale of the **Middle Scale**...

<vocab>Nandayantī (a specific melodic mode), Gāndhāra (the third note 'Mi'), Svara (musical note), Madhyama-grāma (the Middle Scale), Rishabha (the second note 'Re'), Mandra-pañcama (the fifth note 'Sol' in the lower register), Caccatpuṭa (a rhythmic cycle), Bharata (the foundational sage of Indian performing arts), Hṛṣyakā-mūrcchanā (a specific melodic scale-sequence), Bāhulya (abundance or frequent repetition of a note), Takra-kauṇḍinya-nyaya (a rule of specific exception in logic).</vocab>

२७१
### Chapter 7] First Chapter on Notes

Where it is not specifically mentioned, the **rhythmic cycle** <term>tāla; the repeating rhythmic framework</term> should be three-fold, beginning with a single **unit** <term>kalā; a basic unit of time or beat</term>. The **paths** <term>mārgas; the styles of rhythmic pacing</term> are, in order: the **Ornate**, the **Expressive**, and the **Elaborate** <note>original: "citra, vṛtti, and dakṣiṇa"</note>. Furthermore, the **song styles** <term>gītis; methods of melodic phrasing</term> are stated to be, in order: (110) **Māgadhī**, **Saṃbhāvitā**, and **Pṛthulā**.

The **Gāndhārodīcyavā**, **Kārmāravī**, **Gāndhārapañcamī**, **Madhyamodīcyavā**, and **Āndhrī** melodies, as well as **Ṣadja-kaiśikī**, these five have **eight units** <note>kalās</note> each. The melodies **Pañcamī**, **Ārṣabhī**, and **Madhyamā** also have eight units. A single melody, known as **Nandayantī**, is celebrated as having **thirty-two units**. (107–109)

**(Sudhākara)**: He defines the characteristics of the Nandayantī melody in the section "In Nandayantī...": In the Nandayantī melody, the **dominant note** <term>aṃśa; the most significant note in a mode</term> is **Pañcama** <note>the fifth note, Pa</note>. The **starting note** <term>graha</term> is **Gāndhāra** <note>the third note, Ga</note>. One might object, saying it was stated earlier that the dominant note itself must be the starting note. This is not so; that was merely a general rule which is set aside here. In other schools of thought, however, Pañcama is cited as the starting note. There is an abundance of the note **Ṛṣabha** <note>the second note, Ri</note> in the **lower register** <term>mandra sthāna</term>. It is **hexatonic** <term>ṣāḍava; a six-note scale</term> because the note **Ṣaḍja** <note>the first note, Sa</note> is omitted. Its **parent scale** <term>mūrchanā</term> is **Hṛṣyakā**. The rhythm used is the **Cañcatpuṭa** cycle. It consists of **thirty-two units**. Its **application** <term>viniyoga; the ritual or theatrical use</term> is for the first performance of a play. (107–109)

**(Kalānidhi)**: Earlier, in the definition of the **Ṣāḍjī** melody alone, it was stated that "The rhythm is three-fold, using the five-handed movement" and so on; thus, in the various rhythmic divisions, the three paths (Ornate, etc.) and the three song styles (Māgadhī, etc.) should be applied in their respective order. Similarly, in the definitions of certain melodies like **Dhaivatī**, the text indicates by extension that "the rhythm, path, and song style, and the application, are like those of Ṣāḍjī," or "the song styles and rhythms are like Ṣāḍjī." However, in the definitions of others, such as **Ārṣabhī**, only the rhythm and the number of units are mentioned, such as "the rhythm is considered to be Cañcatpuṭa" and "there are eight units," or "sixteen units are celebrated." In those cases, there is an absence of instructions regarding the specific path or song style for those rhythms. To address the question of how to perform them in such instances, he says: "Where it is not specifically mentioned..." Here, in the context of defining the melody types, if the specific divisions of rhythm, path, and song style are not stated, the rhythm should be the one mentioned in the general definitions—the "five-handed" **Cañcatpuṭa**—and it should be three-fold, beginning with one unit. The phrase "beginning with one unit"...

२७२
### Saṅgītaratnākara [On Melodic Types]

**The count of rhythmic units that we have mentioned pertains to the Elaborate Path. || 111 ||**
**It should be known as double in the Expressive Path, and fourfold in the Ornate Path. In all melodic types, one should recognize the aesthetic sentiment associated with the dominant note. || 112 ||**

This serves as a qualifying description. The phrase "three-fold" and so on was already explained in the section on the **Ṣāḍjī melody**; it should be understood from that context. || 110, 110- ||

**(Sudhākara)**: Where a specific detail is not mentioned, the author provides the general characteristic with the phrase **"In those not specified..."** Where no specific **rhythmic cycle** <term>tāla; the repeating rhythmic framework</term> is mentioned, the *Cañcatpuṭa* <note>a specific rhythmic pattern of eight beats</note> consisting of one, two, or four units should be understood. And the **paths** <term>mārgas; styles of rhythmic pacing or tempo</term> associated with one unit and so on are, in order: the **Ornate**, the **Expressive**, and the **Elaborate** <note>original: "citra, vṛtti, and dakṣiṇa"</note>. The **song styles** <term>gītis; methods of melodic phrasing</term> are likewise **Māgadhī**, **Saṃbhāvitā**, and **Pṛthulā**, respectively. || 110, 110- ||

**(Kallinātha)**: Since a count of rhythmic units was given in the descriptions of the *Ṣāḍjī* and other melodies, a question arises: to which specific variation of rhythmic cycle, path, or song style does that count belong? To answer this inquiry, he says: **"The count of units that we have mentioned..."** "By us" refers to ourselves and others who follow the tradition of **Sage Bharata** <note>the legendary author of the Natyasastra, the foundational text on Indian performing arts</note>. 

The count of units—such as twelve in the *Pañcapāṇi* cycle, or eight, sixteen, or even thirty-two (as in one particular case) in the *Cañcatpuṭa* cycle—was stated in the descriptions of the *Ṣāḍjī* and other melodic types. That count should be understood as belonging to the **Elaborate Path** <note>original: "dakṣiṇa-mārga"</note>. By associating it with this specific path, it implies that the **rhythmic cycle** here consists of four units and the **song style** is the **Pṛthulā** <note>the 'Extensive' style of melodic phrasing</note>. 

Having established that the rhythmic units mentioned here belong to the Elaborate Path, he now shows how a singer, if they so desire, may employ other paths. He does this with the phrase: **"In the Expressive Path..."** and so on. That same count of units assigned to a path should be known as being doubled when performing in the **Expressive Path** <note>original: "vārttika"</note>. 

This means that for the *Ṣāḍjī* melody, where twelve units were prescribed for the Elaborate path, there would be twenty-four in the Expressive path. The intention is that instead of units consisting of eight short syllables, one should employ units of four short syllables <note>this refers to the subdivision of time: as the tempo speeds up, the number of units increases relative to the duration</note>. The phrase "that same" <note>original: "saiva"</note> is repeated to emphasize continuity. That...

<summary>This page explains the relationship between rhythmic units (kalās) and the three musical paths (mārgas), establishing that standard counts apply to the Elaborate path but double or quadruple in faster styles. It also notes that the dominant note of a melody determines its emotional character (rasa).</summary>

The number of units <term>kalā; a basic unit of rhythmic time</term> mentioned for the **Elaborate Path** <note>original: "dakṣiṇa mārga"; the slowest, most sophisticated tempo</note> should be known as fourfold in the **Ornate Path** <note>original: "citra mārga"; the fastest, most decorated tempo</note>. This means that in the *Ṣāḍjī* melody, there are forty-eight units. The intention is that these units should be divided into parts consisting of two short beats <term>laghus</term>. By this same logic, in the **Expressive Path** <note>original: "vārtika"; the medium tempo</note>, the rhythm is two-unit and the song style is *Saṃbhāvitā*; whereas in the Ornate Path, the rhythm is one-unit and the song style is *Māgadhī*. This should be inferred for the other melodic types as well. Regarding the aesthetic sentiments <term>rasas; emotional essences</term> in the descriptions: fearing that repeating the sentiments for each melody would be tedious, he shows the application of sentiment for all of them briefly, saying: **"In all melodic types..."** In whichever melodic type a particular note becomes the **dominant note** <term>aṃśa; the melodic center</term>, one should recognize the aesthetic sentiment associated with that note, according to the rule: "Sa and Ri in the Heroic," etc. <note>Refers to the notes Shadja and Rishabha being associated with the Heroic (Vira) sentiment</note>. Having recognized this, one should sing using lyrics that manifest those specific sentiments. || 111, 112 ||

**(Sudhākara)**: He describes the specific rhythmic units according to the specific path: **"That which was mentioned by us..."** The number of units stated as "eight long beats make a unit" refers to the Elaborate Path. In the Expressive Path, sixteen long beats make a unit. In the Ornate Path, thirty-two long beats make a unit. The aesthetic sentiments of the notes were previously stated as: "Sa and Ri in the Heroic, Amazing, and Furious," and so on. In whatever melodic type a note is dominant, its corresponding sentiment should be understood in that melodic type. || 111, 112 ||

**(Kallinātha)**: Previously, in some melodic types like *Ṣāḍjī*, the components of **derived melodies** <term>janya-rāgas; melodies born from the parent scales</term> were shown only as a mere indication with phrases like "The *Varāṭī* melody is seen here"; in others, they were not shown at all.
