# [Chapter 7] First Chapter on Notes
## 274
### Saṅgītaratnākara: [Section 7 on Melodic Types]

**Melodic components** <term>rāgāṃśa; constituent parts of a rāga</term>. Even the ten varieties of melodies, such as the "village-melodies" <term>grāmarāga</term> and others, are indeed derived from the parent melodic types <term>jātis</term>, whether directly or through a traditional lineage. These components are their constituent parts. As the author will state later: "A melodic component is a limb of another melody." This means they are portions of a melody. In the parent melodic types—those that give birth to these melodies, whether directly or through a tradition—these components are observed and conceptualized by experts who understand the different varieties of melodies.

Now, he demonstrates the extraordinary spiritual merit <term>adṛṣṭa; "unseen" karmic reward</term> gained by singing these melodic types according to the rules, starting with the words: **"Spoken by Brahma."** In ancient times, regarding the praise of Lord Shiva, the four-faced Creator, Lord Brahma, composed and spoke specific lyrics <note>original: "padaiḥ"; lyrics or word-sequences</note> such as "Him of the white forehead..." <note>original: "taṃ dhavalalāṭa"; a famous hymn fragment addressed to Shiva</note>. When these melodic types, such as the *Ṣāḍjī* and others, are performed perfectly—neither lacking nor exceeding the prescribed rules—they purify a person even if they have committed the sin of killing a Brahmin <note>original: "brahmahaṇam"; traditionally the most severe sin in the ancient social and spiritual order</note>, releasing them from that spiritual debt. By this, the proper singing of melodic types is declared to be a form of atonement <term>prāyaścitta</term> for the gravest of sins.

Having established the power of these melodic types when bound by the stated rules—treating them as equal to the mantras of the *Rig Veda* and others—he now prohibits their use without strict adherence to the rules, stating: **"The Rig verses."** Just as the verses of the *Rig*, *Yajur*, and *Sama Vedas* are never altered—meaning they are never performed contrary to the correct pronunciation of notes or syllables—likewise, the melodic types are born from the *Samaveda* <note>The Veda associated specifically with chanting and musical melody</note> and are thus equal to the Vedas. They must not be altered; meaning, they should not be performed with any deviation in note <term>svara</term>, lyric <term>pada</term>, or rhythm <term>tāla</term>. This implies that performing them incorrectly incurs a spiritual transgression <term>pratyavāya</term>. || 113—114 ||

<note>Commentary titled Sudhākara</note>

**Regarding "They are observed":** In those derived melodic types where specific melodic components are not explicitly mentioned, the components of their parent melodic types should be understood as applying to them. He praises the mentioned melodic types by saying: **"With lyrics spoken by Brahma."** The lyrics mentioned in the arrangement for the praise of Lord Shiva were spoken by Brahma. When melodic types are performed with these words, adhering strictly to their definitions without deviation, they purify even a killer of a Brahmin; how much more so, then, a person with lesser sins? He states the fault in performing melodic types incorrectly: **"The Rig verses."** Since melodic types are equal to the Vedas, they must be performed perfectly because of the spiritual defect caused by improper performance. || 113—114 ||

->Thus ends the seventh section on melodic types in the first chapter concerning notes. <-

# Now, the Eighth Section on Songs

I shall now describe the **Kapālas** <term>Kapāla; literally "skull-shards," referring to a specific set of ancient sacred songs associated with the worship of Lord Shiva</term> that arise from the pure melodic types <term>jāti</term>. The melodies <term>rāga</term> that spring from these parent types are mirrored within these Kapālas. || 1 ||

Where the note *Ṣaḍja* <note>The tonic or first note, "Sa"</note> is the starting note <term>graha</term>, the dominant note <term>aṃśa</term>, and the secondary ending note <term>apanyāsa</term>; where *Gāndhāra* <note>The third note, "Ga"</note> is the final note <term>nyāsa</term>; where *Gāndhāra* and *Madhyama* <note>The fourth note, "Ma"</note> occur very frequently; || 2 ||

where *Ṛṣabha* (Ri), *Pañcama* (Pa), *Niṣāda* (Ni), and *Dhaivata* (Dha) are used infrequently, and *Ṛṣabha* is often skipped <term>laṅghya</term>; and which consists of twelve rhythmic units <term>kalā</term>—that is declared by experts in song <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "gītavedibhiḥ"; the gloss suggests an alternative reading "mārgavedibhiḥ" meaning "experts in the high classical path"</note> to be the **Ṣāḍjī-kapāla**. Where the note *Ṛṣabha* is the dominant and secondary ending, and *Madhyama* is the final, and Ga, Ni, Pa, and Dha are infrequent... || 3 ||

---

(Commentary by Kallinātha) Now, to define the Kapālas according to the order of the list, he first shows their origin and makes a vow to describe them: **"Arising from pure..."**. Now, after defining the nature of the melodic types <term>jāti</term>, he describes the Kapālas arising from the pure ones—specifically from the seven pure Jātis like *Ṣāḍjī*. This implies that Kapālas do not arise from "mixed" <term>saṃsargaja</term> melodic types. One might ask: "Since they are all Jātis, why don't they also arise from mixed ones?" The answer: The mixed ones themselves are born from the pure ones. The Kapālas also come from those same pure sources. Since both [mixed Jātis and Kapālas] arise directly from the same cause, the mixed ones cannot be considered the cause of the Kapālas.

He then shows the practical purpose of knowing these Kapālas: **"The melodies..."**. Regarding the "parent types" <term>janaka-jāti</term>, the pure Jātis are intended here as the parents. Their "offspring melodies" <term>rāga</term> are those like the *Śrīrāga*, which the author will later describe as: "The *Śrīrāga* arises from the *Ṣāḍjī* melody." These melodies are seen to have forms similar to the Kapālas of those parent types. The meaning is that the purpose here is to understand the nature of the Rāgas. 

Just as a shard <term>kapāla</term> of a pot, being a part of it, allows one to recognize the pot itself, so too these melodic units are called "Kapālas" because they cause one to recognize the full melody <term>rāga</term> as they are parts of it. Their name is also...

<note>The term Kapāla (skull) also refers to the legend of Lord Shiva carrying the skull of Brahma; these songs were traditionally sung as part of that specific ritual enactment.</note>

...where that [Dhaivata] is infrequent, and which consists of eight rhythmic units <term>kalā</term>—that is the **Ārṣabhī-kapāla**. In this melody, the note *Madhyama* <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "gāndhāro"; the gloss suggests that some traditions consider Gāndhāra (Ga) to be the dominant note here instead of Madhyama (Ma)</note> is the dominant <term>aṃśa</term>, the starting note <term>graha</term>, the final note <term>nyāsa</term>, and the secondary ending <term>apanyāsa</term>, while *Dhaivata* (Dha) is used frequently. || 4 ||

Where the notes *Ṣaḍja* (Sa), *Ṛṣabha* (Ri), and *Gāndhāra* (Ga) are infrequent, and where it becomes pentatonic <term>auḍuva</term> through the omission of *Ṛṣabha* and *Pañcama* (Pa)—that is the **Gāndhārī-kapāla**, which is constructed with eight rhythmic units. || 5 ||

Where *Madhyama* (Ma) is the dominant note, and where *Niṣāda* (Ni), *Ṛṣabha*, *Gāndhāra*, and *Pañcama* are very infrequent, and which consists of nine rhythmic units—that is the **Madhyama-kapāla**, according to the tradition of Niḥśaṅka <note>A title for the author, Śārṅgadeva, meaning "the Fearless One"</note>. || 6 ||

Where *Ṛṣabha* and *Gāndhāra* are absent, the dominant and starting note is *Ṣaḍja*, and it is characterized by the notes *Niṣāda*, *Dhaivata*, and *Ṣaḍja*—experts know this as the **Pañcamī-kapāla**, born from the *Pañcamī-jāti*, consisting of eight rhythmic units. || 7 ||

Where *Ṛṣabha* and *Gāndhāra* are extremely infrequent, *Pañcama* is the secondary ending, and *Madhyama* is frequent—that is the eight-unit **Dhaivatī-kapāla**, which is similar in nature to the *Ṣāḍjī* melody. || 8 ||

Where *Ṣaḍja* serves as the starting, dominant, and final note, and where *Ṛṣabha* and *Gāndhāra* are infrequent while *Niṣāda*, *Dhaivata*, and *Madhyama* are very frequent—that eight-unit song is the **Naiṣādī-kapāla**. || 9 ||

By singing these seven Kapālas with the words uttered by Lord Brahma and with these specific notes, the devotee who praises the Beloved of Parvati <note>Lord Shiva</note> shall obtain auspiciousness. || 10 ||

->**Commentary**<-

The meaning of the verses is easily understood. However, a legend <term>aitihya</term> is told: In ancient times, during the occasion of his wandering for alms <note>original: "bhikṣāṭana"; referring to a famous myth where Shiva wanders as a naked beggar</note>, Lord Shambhu (Shiva) sang these melodies like *Ṣāḍjī* and the others. Because of the expression of unsurpassed aesthetic delight <term>rasa</term>, the moon-digit on his forehead—which is the essence of nectar—began to flow. The skulls of Brahma <term>brahma-kapāla</term> that served as his ornaments were sprinkled with that nectar and came to life. They then sang by imitating his own singing. Therefore, because they were "songs of the skulls," they are known as the **Kapālas**. The characteristics of the *Ṣāḍjī-kapāla* and the others are clear. The difference in form between these and the parent *Jātis* should be understood through the differences in their ending notes <term>nyāsa</term> and other technical factors. The author also mentions the spiritual reward <term>adṛṣṭa-phala</term> for the singer who follows these rules of the Kapālas.

This concludes the section on the seven Kapālas. || 1–10 ||

### **Where the starting note, the dominant, and the secondary ending is Pañcama, but Ṛṣabha is frequent;**
### **where that [Ṛṣabha] is the final note, and Madhyama and Gāndhāra are infrequent—that is known as the Kambala. || 11 ||**

(Su) <note>original: "kapālani ca kambalam... iti padārthasaṅgrahokta..."</note> In accordance with the sequence of subjects mentioned in the summary of contents—"...the Kapālas and the Kambala; and the various types of songs"—and without deviating from that intended order because of its practical utility, the author begins by defining the Kapālas, saying: "From the pure modes <term>jāti</term>..." Whichever Kapāla <note>Literally "Skull-Song," these were ancient, sacred melodies associated with religious rituals</note> is born from a particular melodic mode <term>jāti</term>, the derivative melodies <term>rāga</term> of that mode should be understood to reside within that Kapāla. || 1 ||

He defines the **Ṣāḍjī-kapāla**: "In the note Ṣaḍja..." <note>original: "ṣaḍja iti"</note>. That in which the note *Ṣaḍja* (Sa) is the starting note <term>graha</term>, the dominant <term>aṃśa</term>, and the secondary ending <term>apanyāsa</term>; where the final note <term>nyāsa</term> is *Gāndhāra* (Ga); where *Gāndhāra* and *Madhyama* (Ma) are used with great frequency; where *Ṛṣabha* (Ri), *Pañcama* (Pa), *Niṣāda* (Ni), and *Dhaivata* (Dha) are infrequent; where *Ṛṣabha* is "leaped over" <note>original: "laṅghanam," meaning a note is skipped or barely touched</note> or touched only slightly; and which consists of twelve rhythmic units <term>kalā</term>—that is the **Ṣāḍjī-kapāla**, as declared by the sage Bharata and others. || 2 ||

He defines the **Ārṣabhī-kapāla**: "Where..." <note>original: "yatreti"</note>. Where *Ṛṣabha* (Ri) is the dominant and the secondary ending; *Madhyama* (Ma) is the final note; however, *Gāndhāra* (Ga), *Niṣāda* (Ni), *Pañcama* (Pa), and *Dhaivata* (Dha) are infrequent; *Ṣaḍja* (Sa) is extremely infrequent; and it consists of eight rhythmic units—that is the **Ārṣabhī-kapāla**. || 3 ||

He defines the **Gāndhārī-kapāla**: "Madhyama is the dominant..." <note>original: "madhyamo 'ṃśa iti"</note>. Where the note *Madhyama* (Ma) is the dominant, the starting note, the final note, and the secondary ending; *Dhaivata* (Dha) is used frequently; *Ṣaḍja* (Sa), *Ṛṣabha* (Ri), *Gāndhāra* (Ga), and *Pañcama* (Pa) are infrequent; and because *Ṛṣabha* and *Pañcama* are omitted, it becomes pentatonic <term>auḍuva</term>; it consists of eight rhythmic units—that is the **Gāndhārī-kapāla**. || 4, 5 ||

He defines the **Madhyamā-kapāla**: "Madhyama is the dominant..." Where *Madhyama* (Ma) is the dominant note; *Niṣāda* (Ni), *Ṛṣabha* (Ri), *Gāndhāra* (Ga), and *Pañcama* (Pa) are very infrequent; and it consists of nine rhythmic units—that is the **Madhyamā-kapāla**. || 6 ||

He defines the **Pañcamī-kapāla**: "Ṛṣabha is the dominant..." <note>original: "ṛṣabhāṃśam iti"</note>. Where *Ṛṣabha* (Ri) is the dominant note; *Ṣaḍja* (Sa) is the starting note; *Niṣāda* (Ni), *Dhaivata* (Dha), *Ṣaḍja* (Sa), *Gāndhāra* (Ga), and *Madhyama* (Ma) are infrequent; and it consists of eight rhythmic units—that is the **Pañcamī-kapāla**. || 7 ||

He defines the **Dhaivatī-kapāla**: "Extremely infrequent..." <note>original: "atyalpa..."</note>. Where *Ṛṣabha* (Ri) and *Gāndhāra* (Ga) are extremely infrequent; *Pañcama* (Pa) is the final note; *Madhyama* (Ma) and *Dhaivata* (Dha) are frequent; it consists of eight rhythmic units; and the rest is similar to the Ṣāḍjī-kapāla—that is the **Dhaivatī-kapāla**. || 8 ||

He defines the **Naiṣādī-kapāla**: "Starting note and dominant..." <note>original: "grahāṃśa..."</note>. Where *Ṣaḍja* (Sa) is the starting note, the dominant, and the final note; *Ṛṣabha* (Ri) and *Gāndhāra* (Ga) are infrequent; *Niṣāda* (Ni), *Dhaivata* (Dha), and *Madhyama* (Ma) are used very frequently; and it consists of eight rhythmic units—that is the **Naiṣādī-kapāla**. || 9 ||

Regarding the result of singing these Kapālas, he says: "Thus..." <note>original: "itīti"</note>. By singing these seven Kapālas with the words and notes prescribed in the arrangements of melodic modes <term>jāti</term> as taught by the god Brahma, one attains auspiciousness and well-being. || 10 ||

**Saṅgītaratnākara**
**[Section on Songs—**

### **Many varieties of this [melody], born from the *Pañcamī* mode <term>jāti</term>, have been described by the ancients based on the infrequency or frequency of its notes. || 12 ||**

### **In ancient times, Shiva <note>original: "Purāri," an epithet for Shiva as the destroyer of the three cities</note> was so pleased by the singing of the *Kambala* melody that he granted a boon to the Naga Kambala; even today, Shiva is delighted by those songs. || 13 ||**

### **We shall now recite, in order, the sequence of verses for the *Kapālas* <note>Sacred "Skull-songs" used in ancient ritual worship</note> as they were spoken by the creator god Brahma.**

*Jhandum, jhandum* <note>Musical vocables or rhythmic syllables</note> || 1 || [To the] Wearer of the skull-topped staff <term>khaṭṭāṅga</term> || 2 || [To the one] Terrifying with fangs || 3 || [To the one] With a tongue like a lightning bolt || 4 || *Hau hau hau hau hau hau hau hau* <note>original: "stobha," musical interjections with no lexical meaning but religious significance</note> || 5 || [To the] Multi-faced one with a voice like deep, thundering clouds || 6 || *Hau hau hau hau hau hau hau hau* || 7 || *Ūṃ ūṃ hāṃ rau hauṃ hauṃ hauṃ hauṃ* <note>Esoteric seed-syllables or mantras</note> || 8 || [To the one] Adorned with human skulls || 9 || *Hūṃ hūṃ kaha kaha hūṃ hūṃ* || 10 || [To the one] Who makes a fierce, distorted face || 11 || **I bow to the Lord Bhairava.** || 12 || **These are the lyrics for the Ṣāḍjī-kapāla.** || 1 ||

The text above is self-explanatory. This melody is called **Kambala** because it was sung by the lord of serpents, Kambala, who wears a crescent moon <note>original: "khaṇḍaparaśu," usually an axe, but here associated with the serpent’s adornments</note> as an earring. || 11—13 ||

**(Su) <note>Sudhākara commentary by Siṃhabhūpāla</note>** He defines the **Kambala**: "Where..." <note>original: "yatreti"</note>. That in which the note *Pañcama* (Pa) is the starting note <term>graha</term>, the dominant <term>aṃśa</term>, and the secondary ending <term>apanyāsa</term>; where there is an abundance of *Ṛṣabha* (Ri); where *Ṣaḍja* (Sa) is the final note <term>nyāsa</term>; and where *Madhyama* (Ma), *Dhaivata* (Dha), and *Gāndhāra* (Ga) are infrequent—that is the **Kambala**, born from the *Pañcamī* mode <term>jāti</term>. Many varieties of this Kambala melody, distinguished by the frequency or infrequency of its notes, were described by ancient masters such as Bharata; those should be sought in their respective treatises. They are not detailed here for fear of making the book too long. He then explains the reason for the name and the benefit of the Kambala song: "Pleased..." <note>original: "prīta iti"</note>. Because the Naga <note>Serpent deity</note> named Kambala sang it, it is called the Kambala-song. The Lord [Shiva] is pleased by it. By his pleasure, the fruit is the attainment of all human goals <term>puruṣārtha</term>. || 11—13 || This concludes the definition of the Kambala.

**(क०) <note>Kalānidhi commentary by Kallinātha</note>** Regarding the rule for singing *Kapālas*, "Singing with the verses spoken by Brahma," he describes those verses. The nature of the verses spoken by Brahma, including the *stobha* syllables <note>Intercalated musical sounds</note> such as *hum*, is determined by the number of rhythmic units <term>kalā</term> prescribed for each *Kapāla*...

२८१
# Section 8: The First Chapter on Notes #
### 36 ###

**For example—**

| Ma | Ga | Ma | Dha |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| De | | vam | |
<note>Notes: Ma (Madhyama), Ga (Gāndhāra), Dha (Dhaivata). The word "Devam" (God) is stretched across four beats in a slow tempo.</note>

| Dha-Ni | Dha-Ni | Sa-Ni | Dha |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| De | vam | Ru | dram |
<note>Notes: Ni (Niṣāda), Sa (Ṣaḍja). The words "Devam Rudram" (God Rudra) are sung in medium tempo.</note>

| Ri-Ga | Ri-Ga | Ma-Ga | Ri-Sa |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| De-vam | Rud-ram | vam | de |
<note>Notes: Ri (Ṛṣabha). The full phrase "Devam Rudram vande" (I bow to God Rudra) is sung in fast tempo.</note>

...and so on. To define them in their proper sequence, [the author] says: **"Of these..."** He defines **Māgadhī** with the verse starting **"Having sung..."** For the sake of illustration, one should imagine <term>kalās</term> <note>units of musical time</note> consisting of four beats each. 

In the first of these units, the word is set to a **slow tempo** <term>vilambita-laya</term>, where the duration of the rest <note>the time between musical actions</note> is four times the base unit. Here, after singing the word "Devam" <note>original: "devam," meaning "to the God"</note>, which consists of two syllables, one sings each syllable for the duration of two beats. 

In the second <term>kalā</term>, one sings in a **medium tempo** <term>madhya-laya</term>, where the rest duration is doubled <note>i.e., twice as fast as the slow tempo</note>, joined with another word. The word "Devam" from the first unit is repeated and joined with the additional word "Rudram" <note>a name for the god Shiva</note>. One must understand that the instruction "having sung" applies here as well: having sung the two words "Devam Rudram," one should sing each syllable using either two notes or a single note.

In the third <term>kalā</term>, performed in a **fast tempo** <term>druta-laya</term>—which is much quicker in its rest intervals compared to the slow and medium tempos—the phrase is joined with a third word, "vande" <note>meaning "I bow"</note>. This unit includes the words "Devam" and "Rudram" previously sung in the second unit. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> in the verse implies that the instruction to "sing" continues here. In this unit, one sings by assigning "Devam" to the first beat, "Rudram" to the second, the syllable "vam" to the third, and "de" to the fourth.

In the manner described, the word "Devam" is repeated three times across the three units of time. Because of this triple repetition, the wise—those learned in the **science of music** <term>saṅgīta-śāstra</term>—call this song-style **Māgadhī**. One should infer this same structure in other examples beyond the one illustrated here. The sage **Matanga** provides the etymology for this term, stating it is called **Māgadhī** because it originated in the Magadha region <note>an ancient kingdom in east-central India</note>. || 14 — 17- ||

<summary>This page explains the Māgadhī song-style, characterized by repeating words across three time units (kalās) in progressively faster tempos (slow, medium, and fast).</summary>
<keywords>Māgadhī, Gīti, kalā, tempo, laya, vilambita, madhya, druta, Matanga, Shiva, Rudra, musical notation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of song-styles (gītis). Having finished the description of the Māgadhī style, the text now introduces the second style, Ardhamāgadhī, while providing a broader definition of what constitutes a "song-style" in Indian musicology.</meta>

२८२
संगीतरत्नाकरः [Song-styles—]

# When the final halves of the first two words are uttered twice¹ ॥ १८ ॥
# ...then they call it Ardhamāgadhī ("Half-Magadhan").

**For example—**
-> Ma Ri Ga Sa <-
-> De vam <-
<note>Notes: Ma (Madhyama), Ri (Ṛṣabha), Ga (Gāndhāra), Sa (Ṣaḍja). The syllables "De-vam" (God) are distributed across these notes.</note>

<margin>(Sudhākara)</margin> The author has previously mentioned the use of "caste-songs" <term>jāti-gīta</term> <note>ancient melodic frameworks that preceded the modern Raga system</note>. In response to the question "What are the characteristics of these song-styles?", he says: **"Adorned with melodic movements and ornaments..."** 

"Melodic movements" <term>varṇa</term> refers to the four types of musical patterns (such as steady, ascending, descending, or circling notes). The "and so on" implies "ornaments" <term>alaṃkāra</term> <note>specific melodic flourishes like tremors or slides</note> such as the "bright" <note>prasanna</note> ornament. 

A "song-style" <term>gīti</term> is defined as the act of singing which is endowed with these movements and ornaments, as well as with:
1. **Lyrics** <term>pada</term> (the well-known verbal content).
2. **Tempo** <term>laya</term> (the intervals of time within a rhythmic cycle, categorized as fast, medium, or slow, which will be discussed in the Chapter on Rhythm).

This song-style is of four types: **Māgadhī, Ardhamāgadhī, Sambhāvitā, and Pṛthulā**. 

Here, he describes the characteristics of **Māgadhī** by saying **"Having sung..."**: 
In the first unit of time <term>kalā</term>, one should sing a word in a **slow tempo**. In the second unit, one should sing that same word joined with a second word in a **medium tempo**. In the third unit, one should sing those two words along with a third word in a **fast tempo**. The wise experts in song have declared this three-unit style, with its three-fold repetition of words, to be Māgadhī. 

For instance, having sung "Devam" <note>original: "devam"; God</note> in a slow tempo, one then sings "Devam Rudram" <note>original: "devam rudram"; God Rudra</note> in a medium tempo in the second unit. In the third unit, one sings the two words "Devam Rudram" together with another word "vande" <note>original: "vande"; I bow</note> as "Devam Rudram vande" in a fast tempo. ॥ १७-१४- ॥

<margin>(Kalānidhi)</margin> He defines **Ardhamāgadhī** with the phrase **"Of the first two..."**. Among the three words mentioned (Devam, Rudram, Vande), one looks at the "final halves" of the first two words. The final half of the word "Devam" is "-vam"; the final half of the word "Rudram" is "-dram". When both these halves, "-vam" and "-dram", are uttered twice, they call it Ardhamāgadhī. 

The meaning is this: In the first unit of time, following the method of Māgadhī, one utters the word "Devam." In the second unit, one should utter "-vam Rudram" <note>the end of the first word plus the second word</note>.

---
¹ Variation: "When the final half of the first two words is spoken twice."

<summary>This page defines the general concept of "song-style" (gīti) as a combination of melody, lyrics, and tempo, and specifically details the "Ardhamāgadhī" style where word fragments are repeated across rhythmic units.</summary>

[Chapter 8] First Chapter on Musical Notes

Sa&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sa&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Dha&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ni
-vam&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ru&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;draṃ
<note>Musical notes: Sa (Ṣaḍja), Dha (Dhaivata), Ni (Niṣāda). The lyrics correspond to the end of the word "Devam" and the start of "Rudram".</note>

Pa&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Dha&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Pa&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma
draṃ&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;vam&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;de
<note>Musical notes: Pa (Pañcama), Dha (Dhaivata), Ma (Madhyama). The lyrics are "Rudram vande" (I bow to Rudra).</note>

->Others say it has words repeated twice.¹<-

**For example—**

Ma&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma
Dru&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;va
<note>Musical note: Ma (Madhyama). Lyric: "Druva".</note>

Dha&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Dha&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ni
de&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;vam&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ru&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;draṃ

Pa&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ni-Dha&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma
Ru&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;draṃ&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;vam&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;de

<margin>¹ In the middle of words repeated twice.</margin>

Then, in the third time-unit <term>kalā</term>, one should utter "draṃ vande" <note>original: "dram vande" (I bow to [Ru]dra)</note>. In this way, there is a double repetition of the final meanings of the previous two words. 

Regarding the phrase **"Others say it has words repeated twice"**: "Others" refers to teachers who claim that **Ardhamāgadhī** <note>literally "Half-Magadhan," a specific ancient singing style</note> involves this: the word "Devam" <note>God</note> spoken in the first unit is repeated in the second unit as "Devam Rudram," and the word "Rudram" is repeated in the third unit as "Rudram vande." This pattern of repeating words is what they call Ardhamāgadhī. 

**Matanga** <note>an influential early medieval musicologist</note>, however, describes this as a specific variety of the **Māgadhī** style. As he says: "Others, however, read Māgadhī as having two repetitions." Furthermore, since Ardhamāgadhī is technically included within the broader category of Māgadhī, the use of Ardhamāgadhī in place of Māgadhī is considered acceptable in certain contexts. 

Here, anticipating the potential criticism of redundancy <note>the fault of "punarukti" or repeating oneself</note> or the loss of meaning when words are broken into parts, Matanga resolves the doubt by stating: "In the **Samaveda** <note>the Veda of Melodies</note>, where the song-element is primary, the literal meanings are not strictly observed during repetitions." 

This is also illustrated by the Veda itself: in the famous verse "Udu tyaṃ jātavedasam" <note>a hymn to the Sun-god</note>, after singing through a sequence of repetitions until the word "veda"...

It cites the sage Matanga and Vedic tradition to justify why repeating or splitting words is musically valid despite potential loss of literal meaning.</summary>

[Chapter 8] First Chapter on Musical Notes

### Sambhāvitā is considered to have compressed words and many long syllables. || 19 ||

**For example—**

->Dha&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ma&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ri&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ga<-
->Bhak&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;tyā<-
<note>Musical notes: Dha (Dhaivata), Ma (Madhyama), Ri (Ṛṣabha), Ga (Gāndhāra). Lyric: "Bhaktyā" (With devotion).</note>

->Rī&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Gā&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sā&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Mā<-
->de&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;vam<-
<note>Lyric: "Devam" (The God).</note>

->Nī&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Dhā&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sā&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nī<-
->ru&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;draṃ<-
<note>Lyric: "Rudram" (Rudra/Shiva).</note>

->Dhā&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nī&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Mā&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Mā<-
->van&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;de<-
<note>Lyric: "Vande" (I bow).</note>

One sings "I bow to the God Rudra with devotion" <note>original: "bhaktyā devaṃ rudraṃ vande"</note>. Even here, there is no loss of meaning <note>arthabhaṅga</note> despite the breaking of word fragments across the music. Therefore, in music which essentially originates from the *Sāmaveda* <note>The Veda of melodies, known for stretching and repeating syllables for ritual chant</note>, it should be understood that the repetition of words or the utterance of partial words is not a fault if necessitated by the singing. || 18, 18 ||

**(Su.)** <note>Sudhākara commentary by Siṃhabhūpāla</note> He defines the *Ardhamāgadhī* style: "Regarding the previous two..." and so on. When the final half of the previous two words is repeated twice—for example, having sung the word "God" <note>original: "devam"</note> in the first time-unit <term>kalā</term>, then in the second unit one sings the word "Rudra" <note>original: "rudram"</note> alongside the syllable "vam," which is the final half of the first word. Thus, one sings "vam Rudram." In the third unit, one sings the word "vande" <note>I bow</note> along with the syllable "dram," which is the final half of the second word. In this case, the slow, medium, and fast tempos <term>laya</term> should be understood across the three time-units. || 18, 18 ||

**(Ka.)** <note>Kalānidhi commentary by Kallinātha</note> He defines the *Sambhāvitā* style: "Compressed words..." and so on. A style is so called if its words are compressed. Here, "expansion" of words refers to applying a syllable to every single note within a time-unit; the "compression" <term>saṃkṣepa</term> of that is the opposite. From the word "saṃkṣepi" <note>to shorten</note>, the form "saṃkṣepinā" is derived. This implies that the singer should only apply syllables to a few of the notes within the rhythmic units. "Many long syllables" <term>bhūriguru</term> means there is a prevalence of heavy or long vowels...

<vocab>saṃkṣepipada (compressed words), bhūriguru (many long syllables), sambhāvitā (the 'manifest' song-style), ardhamāgadhī (the 'half-Magadhi' style), Sāmaveda (Scripture of Chants), kalā (rhythmic unit), laya (tempo), svara (musical note)</vocab>

<summary>This page defines the Sambhāvitā song-style, characterized by using fewer syllables than notes (compression) and long vowels, while defending the practice of breaking and repeating words as seen in Vedic chanting.</summary>
<keywords>Sambhāvitā, Ardhamāgadhī, word repetition, musical semantics, Sāmaveda influence, rhythmic units, medieval Indian music theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the four types of Gītis (song styles), moving from the Sambhāvitā style to the Pṛthulā style. It provides technical instructions on how syllables are mapped to musical notes (svaras) and rhythmic units (kalās).</meta>

२८५
[Chapter 8] First Chapter on Musical Notes २८५

### Pṛthulā is considered by the wise to have words with many short syllables. || 19 ||

**For example—**
-> Mā &nbsp;&nbsp; Gā &nbsp;&nbsp; Rī &nbsp;&nbsp; Gā <-
-> Su &nbsp;&nbsp; ra &nbsp;&nbsp; na &nbsp;&nbsp; ta <-
<note>Musical notes: Mā (Madhyama), Gā (Gāndhāra), Rī (Ṛṣabha). Lyrics: "Suranata" (One to whom the gods bow).</note>

In this style, the use of occasional sparse short syllables is also accepted. In the time units <term>kalā: a rhythmic cycle or division</term> consisting of four measures, one should sing the five notes of the first unit by joining the first two to a long syllable <term>guru: a long vowel or heavy syllable</term>, then the third note to a long syllable, and the remaining two notes as part of that same syllable's extension.

In the four notes of the second unit, the first and third should be joined with the long syllables of the word "God" <note>original: "devam"</note>. Likewise, in the third unit, the first and third notes join with the syllables of the word "Rudra" <note>original: "rudram"</note>. In the fourth unit, the first and third notes join with the syllables of "I bow" <note>original: "vande"</note>, with the other notes sung as extensions of those syllables. The words are thus compressed into the phrase: "I bow with devotion to the God Rudra" <note>original: "bhaktyā devaṃ rudraṃ vande"</note>. 

This method shown in the written example should be applied to other cases as well. The specific notes for each unit should be used according to whatever melodic scale <term>jāti: the ancient precursor to the raga</term> the song is based on. A song performed in this way is considered to be in the *Sambhāvitā* style. The etymology <note>original: "nirukti"</note> given by the sage Matanga is: "That in which the compression of words is possible is called *Sambhāvitā*." || 19 ||

**(Su.)** <note>Sudhākara commentary by Siṃhabhūpāla</note> He defines the *Sambhāvitā* style: "Repeated twice..." and so on. *Sambhāvitā* is a song style where words are compressed and many long syllables are used. After singing four words in the first unit as "I bow with devotion to the God Rudra," the two middle words are sung twice in the second unit as "to the God, to the God, to Rudra, to Rudra" <note>original: "devaṃ devaṃ rudraṃ rudram"</note>. In the third unit, it returns to the form of the first unit: "I bow with devotion to the God Rudra." || 19 ||

**(Ka.)** <note>Kalanidhi commentary by Kallinātha</note> He defines the *Pṛthulā* style: "Words with many short syllables..." and so on. The meaning is clear. Regarding the phrase "Bow to the pair of feet of the Lord who is bowed to by the gods," <note>original: "suranataharapadayugalaṃ praṇamata"</note> syllables are applied to every note across the four rhythmic units. The etymology provided by Matanga says: "It is called *Pṛthulā* (the Broad) because of the abundance of short word-units." || 19 ||

<vocab>Svaragatādhyāya, Pṛthulā, Sambhāvitā, Matanga, Nirukti, Kalā, Gīti, Bhaktyā devaṃ rudraṃ vande</vocab>

### Saṅgītaratnākara [Song Styles]

<note>This table shows the musical notation. The top row contains the notes: Sā (Ṣaḍja), Dha (Dhaivata), Ni (Niṣāda), etc. The bottom row contains the syllables of the lyrics: "Hara-pada-yugalaṃ praṇamata," which means "Bow to the pair of Shiva's feet."</note>

-> Or alternatively, just as in the "Even" rhythm <term>Yugma: a rhythmic category including the Chaccatpuṭa meter</term>, when the first two long syllables, <-
-> each employing the "Elegant" path <term>Chitra-mārga: a fast-paced musical tempo/style</term>, consist of the Chagaṇa group¹, <-
-> and are joined with eight beats in the "Southern" path <term>Dakṣiṇa-mārga: a slow, sophisticated musical tempo</term> using gestures such as the Dhruvakā; || 21 || <-
-> when this is performed, it is called the "Intellect of Song Paths" <note>original: "gītimārgadhī"</note>. <-

**(Sudhākara Commentary)** He defines the **Pṛthulā** style: *bhūri-laghu-akṣara-padā*. This means a style in which there are many short syllables. Another characteristic is that it includes the features of the *Sambhāvitā* style. This is Pṛthulā. For example, after singing the four words of the phrase "Bow to the pair of Shiva's feet worshipped by the gods" <note>original: "suranata-hara-pada-yugalaṃ praṇamata"</note> in the first unit <term>kalā: a rhythmic division</term>, the middle two words are repeated in the second unit. The third unit is then performed like the first. This is the definition of Pṛthulā according to a different tradition. || 19 ||

**(Kalānidhi Commentary)** Having thus defined the singing styles <term>Gīti</term> based on their relationship to the words <note>original: "padāśritatvena"</note>, he now defines them based on their relationship to the rhythm <note>original: "tālāśritatvena"</note> with the verse beginning "Or alternatively" <note>original: "yadvā"</note>. In the "Even" rhythm <note>Yugma</note>—specifically the *Chaccatpuṭa* rhythm which consists of two long syllables, one short, and one prolonged syllable—one should take the first two long syllables, which are each two beats long. Because they are naturally two beats, they are suitable for the "Elegant" path <term>Chitra-mārga</term>. After performing them with gestures like the **Dhruvakā** <note>a specific hand gesture used to mark time</note>, they are made to consist of a **Chagaṇa**. A Chagaṇa is a specific rhythmic group consisting of four beats <term>mātras</term>; as the text will say later: "From that group come the Sha, Pa, Cha, Ta, and Dau groups." 

One should repeat the phrase "consisting of a Chagaṇa"; by performing it this way, the units are doubled. By following the "Commentary" path <term>Vārttika-mārga: a medium tempo</term>, each long syllable is made into four beats using the hand gestures known as **Dhruvakā**, **Sarpiṇī**, **Patākā**, and **Patitā**...

¹ Endowed with Chagaṇa. <note>original: "chagaṇānvitam"</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of Gītis (ancient song styles) within the Saṅgītaratnākara. Having previously discussed the Māgadhī style, the text now concludes the commentary on Māgadhī and introduces the definition of the Ardhamāgadhī (Half-Magadhi) style, focusing on its complex relationship with rhythmic meters like Chaccatpuṭa and specific hand gestures (mātrās).</meta>

Section 8] First Chapter on Tones 287
287

-> When the third syllable, a short one in the "Even" rhythm, <-
-> is joined with half of a *Chagaṇa* rhythmic unit; || 22 || <-
-> And is combined with the first and final two beats; <-
-> Then the extra-long syllable is performed, joined with one and a half units. || 23 || <-

This means each should be performed with those [beats]. Then, in the **Southern path** <term>Dakṣiṇa-mārga: the slowest and most sophisticated of the three ancient musical tempos</term>, one uses the eight beats known as *Dhruvakā*, *Sarpiṇī*, *Kṛṣṇā*, *Padminī*, *Visarjitā*, *Vikṣiptā*, *Patākā*, and *Patitā*. These will be defined later by their specific characteristics. Here, one should view the use of these beats (beginning with *Dhruvakā*) through the lens of "identity between the attribute and the attributed" <note>This is a Sanskrit philosophical concept where the gesture and the time-unit it represents are treated as one</note>. This means each long syllable is expanded into four units (*kalās*). When it is performed in this way, it is called the **Māgadhī** song-style. The intention is that the pair of long syllables is repeated three times.

**(Sudhākara Commentary)** He provides an alternative definition for these song-styles: "Or..." In the "Even" rhythm <term>Yugma: here referring specifically to the Chaccatpuṭa rhythm</term>, one takes each of the first two long syllables and performs them in the **Elegant path** <term>Chitra-mārga: the fast-paced musical tempo</term> joined with a *Chagaṇa* unit. (He will explain these rhythmic units <note>original: "gaṇas"</note> later in the Chapter on Musical Compositions). When those same first two long syllables of the *Chaccatpuṭa* meter are performed in the Southern path, joined with the eight beats—*Dhruvakā*, *Sarpiṇī*, *Kṛṣṇā*, *Padminī*, *Visarjitā*, *Vikṣiptā*, *Patākā*, and the eighth, *Patitā*—which are to be described in the Chapter on Rhythm <note>original: "Tālādhyāya"</note>, then it is known as the **Māgadhī** song-style.

**(Kalānidhi Commentary)** Now he defines **Ardhamāgadhī** (Half-Magadhi): "The third..." Within the "Even" rhythm <note>original: "Yugma"</note>, specifically the *Chaccatpuṭa* meter as it is written, the third rhythmic component is a short syllable (*laghu*) that follows the two long syllables. This is "joined with half of a *Chagaṇa*." A *Chagaṇa* is a specific rhythmic group consisting of six beats; half of that is three beats. Joined with its own single beat, it is made into a four-beat unit. This is then combined with the "first two beats" (*Dhruvakā* and *Sarpiṇī*) and the "final two" (*Patākā* and *Patitā*). Following this, the extra-long syllable <term>pluta: a vowel held for three beats</term>, which is the final component of the *Chaccatpuṭa* meter, is performed joined with "one and a half units." Here, the general word "unit" (*gaṇa*) refers to the *Chagaṇa* mentioned previously, and "half" refers to half of that unit. Therefore, "one and a half" means a full unit plus three additional beats.

### [Song-styles — Header]

-> When performed with the eight gestures starting with *Dhruvakā* and by repeating the final two twice, <-
-> then it is **Ardhamāgadhī**; these two should be used similarly in other rhythms as well. || 24 || <-
-> **Sambhāvitā** is considered to have many long syllables in the two-unit **Middle path** <term>Vārttika-mārga: the moderate musical tempo</term>. <-
-> **Pṛthulā** is considered to have many short syllables in the four-unit **Southern path** <term>Dakṣiṇa-mārga: the slow, elaborate tempo</term>. || 25 || <-

-> Thus ends the eighth section on song-styles in the first chapter on Tones. || 8 || <-

-> Thus concludes the first chapter on Tones in the *Saṅgītaratnākara* composed by <-
-> the illustrious Śārṅgadeva, the "Undoubted" <note>original: *Niḥśaṅka*, a title meaning one who has no doubts</note>, son of the venerable <-
-> Śrī Soḍhala, the head of the royal treasury and a delight to the wise. <-

**(Sudhākara Commentary)**
It is "joined with one and a half rhythmic units." A *Chagaṇa* unit consists of six beats <term>mātrās: the basic unit of time</term>; half of that is three beats. Thus, by combining them with nine beats, an extra-long syllable (*pluta*), which normally lasts three beats, is expanded to consist of twelve beats. 

When this extra-long syllable is structured this way and performed using the eight hand gestures starting with *Dhruvakā* in sequence, the remaining four beats are filled by "repeating the final two." This means the last two beats—the *Patākā* and *Patitā* gestures—are doubled or repeated. When it is performed using those repeated final gestures, this is the meaning.

The point is this: if the remaining four beats are performed in the sequence of *Patākā-Patitā* and then *Patākā-Patitā* again, it is called **Ardhamāgadhī** (Half-Magadhi). These two—Māgadhī and Ardhamāgadhī—should be applied to other rhythmic structures like the *Pañcapāṇi* rhythm just as they were applied to the *Chaccatpuṭa* rhythm.

The definitions for **Sambhāvitā** and **Pṛthulā** are clear in their meaning. It should be understood that these song-styles (*Gītis*) are to be applied to the primary melodic scales <term>Jātis: the ancient precursors to Ragas</term>, such as *Ṣāḍjī*, according to the rules of the musical "paths" (fast, middle, or slow) and their specific requirements. || 22—25 ||

-> has himself explained this chapter on Tones here on earth. <-

-> composed by the venerable and clever Kallinātha, son of Lakṣmaṇārya and <-
-> protégé of the King of Kings, the new Bharata, Toḍaramalla. || 1 || <-

# 289
### [Section 8] First Chapter on Tones

**(Sudhākara Commentary)**
He defines **Ardhamāgadhī**: "The third..." The third [syllable] of the even-beat *cañcatpuṭa* <term>cañcatpuṭa: a fundamental rhythmic pattern in ancient Indian music</term> is a short syllable (*laghu*). When this is combined with half of a *chagaṇa* unit <note>original: *chagaṇa*, a specific rhythmic grouping of six units</note>, it is performed using the first two hand-gestures, *Dhruvakā* and *Sarpini*, and the final two, *Patākā* and *Patitā*. 

Then, when the fourth syllable of the *cañcatpuṭa*—known as the extra-long syllable (*pluta*)—is combined with one and a half units (by adding half of a *chagaṇa*), and is performed with the eight gestures starting with *Dhruvakā*, and where the final *Patākā* and *Patitā* gestures are doubled, then it is called **Ardhamāgadhī**. Just as these two styles, *Māgadhī* and *Ardhamāgadhī*, are described in relation to the *cañcatpuṭa* rhythm, they should also be understood to apply to other rhythms such as *cācapuṭa*.

He [next] defines **Sambhāvitā**: "Sambhāvitā..." In the two-unit *cañcatpuṭa* rhythm, when following the **Middle path** <term>Vārttika-mārga: the moderate tempo</term>, a song-style that consists of many long syllables (*guru*) according to the previously mentioned rule is called *Sambhāvitā*. 

In the four-unit **Southern path** <term>Dakṣiṇa-mārga: the slow, elaborate tempo</term>, a song-style that consists of many short syllables (*laghu*) according to the previously mentioned method is known as **Pṛthulā**. || 22—25 || 

Thus ends the definition of song-styles. || 8 ||

### [Section 8] First Chapter on Tones

**(Sudhākara Commentary)**
He defines **Ardhamāgadhī**: "The third..." The third syllable of the even-beat *cañcatpuṭa* <term>cañcatpuṭa: a fundamental rhythmic pattern in ancient Indian music consisting of eight units</term> is a short syllable (*laghu*). When this is combined with half of a *chagaṇa* unit <note>original: *chagaṇa*, a specific rhythmic grouping of six units</note>, it is performed using the first two hand-gestures, *Dhruvakā* and *Sarpini*, and the final two, *Patākā* and *Patitā*. 

Then, when the fourth syllable of the *cañcatpuṭa*—known as the extra-long syllable (*pluta*)—is combined with one and a half units (by adding half of a *chagaṇa*), and is performed with the eight gestures starting with *Dhruvakā*, and where the final *Patākā* and *Patitā* gestures are doubled, then it is called **Ardhamāgadhī**. Just as these two styles, *Māgadhī* and *Ardhamāgadhī*, are described in relation to the *cañcatpuṭa* rhythm, they should also be understood to apply to other rhythms such as *cācapuṭa* <note>original: *cācapuṭa*, an odd-beat rhythmic pattern</note>.

He next defines **Sambhāvitā**: "Sambhāvitā..." In the two-unit *cañcatpuṭa* rhythm, when following the **Middle path** <term>Vārttika-mārga: the moderate tempo or performance style</term>, a song-style that consists of many long syllables (*guru*) according to the previously mentioned rule is called **Sambhāvitā**. 

In the four-unit **Southern path** <term>Dakṣiṇa-mārga: the slow, elaborate tempo or style of performance</term>, a song-style that consists of many short syllables (*laghu*) according to the previously mentioned method is known as **Pṛthulā**. || 22—25 ||

# Table of Natural and Modified Notes

<image-desc>A rectangular grid diagram used for musical classification. Above the grid are four notations: ^3^"Hair-fine" Seventh Note <note>original: Kaiśiki-Nishāda</note>, ^4^"Pleasing" Sharp Seventh <note>original: Kākalī-Nishāda</note>, ^2^Lowered Tonic <note>original: Cyuta-Ṣaḍja</note>, and ^Fixed 4^Natural Tonic <note>original: Acyuta/Śuddha-Ṣaḍja</note>. To the left are ^2^Natural Seventh <note>original: Śuddha-Niṣāda</note> and Lowered Sixth; Natural Sixth <note>original: Cyuta-Dhaivata; Śuddha-Dhaivata</note>. To the right are ^3^Natural Second <note>original: Śuddha-Riṣabha</note>; ^4^Lowered Second <note>original: Cyuta-Riṣabha</note>, ^2^Natural Third <note>original: Śuddha-Gāndhāra</note>, ^3^Common Third <note>original: Sādhāraṇa-Gāndhāra</note>, and ^4^Intermediate Third <note>original: Antara-Gāndhāra</note>. Below the grid are two clusters of text: "Natural Fifth (4), Three-microtone Fifth (3), 'Hair-fine' Fifth (4)" on the left and "Natural Fourth (4), Lowered Fourth (2), Unlowered Fourth (2)" on the right.</image-desc>

The "hair-fine" seventh note <note>original: kaiśika (niṣāda)</note>, the lowered tonic <note>original: cyuta ṣaḍja</note>, and the modified second <note>original: vikṛta ṛṣabha</note> are to be employed in the Scale of the Tonic <note>original: ṣaḍja-grāma</note>; these are considered "enemies" <note>This technical term refers to notes that are incompatible or create dissonance within a specific grammatical structure.</note> of the Scale of the Fourth <note>original: madhyama-grāma</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

Only in the Scale of the Fourth <term>Madhyama-grāma: The second of the three ancient Indian scales, characterized by a specific arrangement of intervals starting from the fourth note.</term> should the lowered fourth <note>original: cyuta-madhyama</note> be used. Likewise, the common third <note>original: sādhāraṇa gāndhāra</note> and the two modified fifths <note>original: vikṛta pañcamau</note> are used there. ॥ 2 ॥

The modified sixth <note>original: vikṛta dhaivata</note> is also used there, while the remaining notes are "both-travelers" <note>original: ubhayacāriṇaḥ; meaning they can appear in either scale</note>. These "enemies" of the Scale of the Fourth depend upon their mutual existence. ॥ 3 ॥

The common third, the "hair-fine" fifth <note>original: kaiśika-pañcama</note>, and the lowered fourth are notes that act as mutual companions <note>original: sahacarāḥ</note>. ॥ 4 ॥

The "pleasing" sharp seventh <note>original: kākalī</note> and the unlowered tonic <note>original: acyuta-ṣaḍja</note> depend upon their mutual existence. In the same way, the intermediate third <note>original: antara-gāndhāra</note> and the unlowered fourth <note>original: acyuta-madhyama</note> are related notes. ॥ 5 ॥

The three-microtone fifth <note>original: triśruti-pañcama</note> should be considered an "enemy" of the lowered fourth. The modified sixth is considered to be dependent on the Scale of the Fourth. ॥ 6 ॥

# Permutations of Notes <note>original: Svaraprastāraḥ; this refers to the systematic mathematical arrangement of musical notes to show all possible combinations.</note>

Permutations of one note <note>original: Ārcikasvaraprastāraḥ; referring to the "Ārcika" style of chanting the Rigveda which traditionally uses a single melodic accent.</note>—(1) <term>Sa</term>. (2) <term>Ri</term>. (3) <term>Ga</term>. (4) <term>Ma</term>. (5) <term>Pa</term>. (6) <term>Dha</term>. (7) <term>Ni</term>. <note>These are the seven notes of the Indian scale: Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, Dhaivata, and Niṣāda, roughly equivalent to Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ti.</note>

Permutations of two notes <note>original: Gāthikasvaraprastāraḥ; referring to the "Gāthika" style of chanting which employs two notes.</note>—(1) Sa-Ri, Ri-Sa. (2) Sa-Ga, Ga-Sa. (3) Sa-Ma, Ma-Sa. (4) Sa-Pa, Pa-Sa. (5) Sa-Dha, Dha-Sa. (6) Sa-Ni, Ni-Sa. (7) Ri-Ga, Ga-Ri. (8) Ri-Ma, Ma-Ri. (9) Ri-Pa, Pa-Ri. (10) Ri-Dha, Dha-Ri. (11) Ri-Ni, Ni-Ri. (12) Ga-Ma, Ma-Ga. (13) Ga-Pa, Pa-Ga. (14) Ga-Dha, Dha-Ga. (15) Ga-Ni, Ni-Ga. (16) Ma-Pa, Pa-Ma. (17) Ma-Dha, Dha-Ma. (18) Ma-Ni, Ni-Ma. (19) Pa-Dha, Dha-Pa. (20) Pa-Ni, Ni-Pa. (21) Dha-Ni, Ni-Dha.

Permutations of three notes <note>original: Sāmikasvaraprastāraḥ; referring to the "Sāmika" style of chanting associated with the Sāmaveda, which utilizes three notes.</note>—(1) Sa-Ri-Ga, Ri-Sa-Ga, Sa-Ga-Ri, Ga-Sa-Ri, Ri-Ga-Sa, Ga-Ri-Sa. (2) Sa-Ri-Ma, Ri-Sa-Ma, Sa-Ma-Ri, Ma-Sa-Ri, Ri-Ma-Sa, Ma-Ri-Sa. (3) Sa-Ri-Pa, Ri-Sa-Pa, Sa-Pa-Ri, Pa-Sa-Ri, Ri-Pa-Sa, Pa-Ri-Sa. (4) Sa-Ri-Dha, Ri-Sa-Dha, Sa-Dha-Ri, Dha-Sa-Ri, Ri-Dha-Sa, Dha-Ri-Sa. (5) Sa-Ri-Ni, Ri-Sa-Ni, Sa-Ni-Ri, Ni-Sa-Ri, Ri-Ni-Sa, Ni-Ri-Sa. (6) Sa-Ga-Ma, Ga-Sa-Ma, Sa-Ma-Ga, Ma-Sa-Ga, Ga-Ma-Sa, Ma-Ga-Sa. (7) Sa-Ga-Pa, Ga-Sa-Pa, Sa-Pa-Ga, Pa-Sa-Ga, Ga-Pa-Sa, Pa-Ga-Sa. (8) Sa-Ga-Dha, Ga-Sa-Dha, Sa-Dha-Ga, Dha-Sa-Ga, Ga-Dha-Sa, Dha-Ga-Sa. (9) Sa-Ga-Ni, Ga-Sa-Ni, Sa-Ni-Ga, Ni-Sa-Ga, Ga-Ni-Sa, Ni-Ga-Sa. (10) Sa-Ma-Pa, Ma-Sa-Pa, Sa-Pa-Ma, Pa-Sa-Ma, Ma-Pa-Sa, Pa-Ma-Sa. (11) Sa-Ma-Dha, Ma-Sa-Dha, Sa-Dha-Ma, Dha-Sa-Ma, Ma-Dha-Sa, Dha-Ma-Sa. (12) Sa-Ma-Ni, Ma-Sa-Ni, Sa-Ni-Ma, Ni-Sa-Ma, Ma-Ni-Sa, Ni-Ma-Sa. (13) Sa-Pa-Dha, Pa-Sa-Dha, Sa-Dha-Pa, Dha-Sa-Pa, Pa-Dha-Sa, Dha-Pa-Sa. (14) Sa-Pa-Ni, Pa-Sa-Ni, Sa-Ni-Pa, Ni-Sa-Pa, Pa-Ni-Sa, Ni-Pa-Sa. (15) Sa-Dha-Ni, Dha-Sa-Ni, Sa-Ni-Dha, Ni-Sa-Dha, Dha-Ni-Sa, Ni-Dha-Sa. (16) Ri-Ga-Ma, Ga-Ri-Ma, Ri-Ma-Ga, Ma-Ri-Ga, Ga-Ma-Ri, Ma-Ga-Ri. (17) Ri-Ga-Pa, Ga-Ri-Pa, Ri-Pa-Ga, Pa-Ri-Ga, Ga-Pa-Ri, Pa-Ga-Ri. (18) Ri-Ga-Dha, Ga-Ri-Dha, Ri-Dha-Ga, Dha-Ri-Ga, Ga-Dha-Ri, <insert>Dha-Ga-Ri</insert> <note>The text breaks off here; the logic of the permutation requires the final sequence Dha-Ga-Ri to complete the set of six.</note>

<summary>This page catalogs the mathematical permutations of musical notes used in early Vedic chanting, specifically categorizing sequences of one, two, and three notes. These arrangements illustrate how ancient Indian musicology systematically explored all possible melodic variations within limited note-sets.</summary>
